suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A: when the forum requires confirmed emails, a logged-in user with an unconfirmed email is bounced to the 'change email' form on every page load; the ticket asks that the site-wide enforcement check instead record the pending email requirement in the user's session and send them to the 'complete registration' page. Task B: that same enforcement check only exempts administrators, so a global moderator (who has site-wide moderation powers) with an unconfirmed email is also bounced to the email form; the ticket asks that global moderators be exempt exactly like administrators. Both tickets must rewrite the same ~10 lines of the same function: A changes what happens when the check fires (session write, redirect target, and which routes are exempt), while B changes who the check fires for (the privilege test). Gluing the two patches together breaks the function because the edits overlap on the same lines; only one coherent rewrite that combines A's new funnel with B's broader exemption passes both test suites.
suggestion.shared_region: src/middleware/user.js, function middleware.registrationComplete — specifically the unconfirmed-email enforcement block (base lines 242-254: the `if (!req.session.hasOwnProperty('registration'))` branch containing the `user.isAdministrator(req.uid)` check and the `redirect(res, '/me/edit/email')`), which A's patch deletes/restructures wholesale and B's patch edits in place.
suggestion.taskA: When requireEmailAddress is enabled, a logged-in, non-admin user with an unconfirmed email is redirected to /me/edit/email by the request enforcement middleware on every page load, bypassing the registration completion flow. The middleware should instead record the pending email requirement on the registration session (uid + updateEmail) and redirect to /register/complete (with the relative_path prefix), keep exempting paths ending in /edit/email, and let the email confirmation link through so the user can actually confirm.
suggestion.taskB: Global moderators are incorrectly subject to the requireEmailAddress enforcement: a global moderator whose email is unconfirmed is redirected to the email change form on page load, even though they hold site-wide moderation privileges. The enforcement check should exempt global moderators the same way it exempts administrators — the account email flows elsewhere in the codebase (the /me/edit/email controller and the email interstitial callback) already treat 'admin or global moderator' as a single privileged class, so this check is inconsistent with them.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is about WHO is exempt from enforcement (the privilege predicate), A is about WHERE non-exempt users are sent and how the pending requirement is recorded (redirect target + session write). B is fully motivated by a real inconsistency: src/middleware/user.js uses user.isAdministrator while src/controllers/accounts/edit.js (line 91) and src/user/interstitials.js (line 31) use user.isAdminOrGlobalMod for the same 'privileged user' concept. A maintainer filing 'global mods get locked out when requireEmailAddress is on' would never mention the interstitial redirect change; B makes complete sense even if A were never fixed (the bug is that the wrong class of users is caught, regardless of where they are sent).
suggestion.conflict: A's patch replaces the entire `if (!req.session.hasOwnProperty('registration')) { ... isAdministrator ... redirect('/me/edit/email') }` block with new logic (session.registration write, /confirm/ exemption, redirect to /register/complete). B's patch edits the `user.isAdministrator(req.uid)` call and the `!isAdmin` condition inside that very block. The two diffs occupy the same lines: a naive merge either fails to apply, or produces a function containing both the old and new branches. If A's structure wins but B's predicate is lost, global moderators are still funneled to the interstitial (B's test fails); if B's predicate wins but A's restructure is lost, unconfirmed regular users still go to /me/edit/email (A's test fails). The two changes cannot simply coexist as separate hunks.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's restructured flow — compute confirmed + privileged once, exempt /edit/email and /confirm/ paths, set req.session.registration = { ...req.session.registration, uid, updateEmail: true }, and redirect to /register/complete — but compute the privilege with user.isAdminOrGlobalMod(req.uid) instead of user.isAdministrator(req.uid). One coherent rewrite of the single block satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the existing fail_to_pass test in test/controllers.js ('registration interstitials > email update > blocking access for unconfirmed emails > should continue to redirect back to interstitial after an email is entered, as it is not confirmed') — asserts GET /recent returns 307 to relative_path+/register/complete and that a follow-up GET /register/complete is not re-redirected. B's set: a new test in the same describe block — create a user, groups.join('Global Moderators', uid) without confirming the email, requireEmailAddress=1, GET /recent with that user's session jar, expect 200 (no 307 to /me/edit/email). Base code fails both; A's gold patch alone fails B's test (predicate still isAdministrator); B's patch alone fails A's test (still redirects to /me/edit/email); only the reconciled rewrite passes the combined suite.

notes: Task A's patch touches two regions: middleware.registrationComplete (the enforcement funnel) and Controllers.confirmEmail (clearing session.registration.updateEmail after a successful confirmation). The confirmEmail change and the /confirm/ route exemption are integral parts of A — using either as task B would be a decomposition of A, not an independent ticket. The contradictory pairing via the global-moderator exemption is the strongest option: it targets the exact same lines A rewrites, is motivated by a real privilege-class inconsistency visible in adjacent code (editController.email and interstitials.email both use isAdminOrGlobalMod), and produces a clean 2x2 soundness matrix (base fails both tests; each solution alone fails the other's test; reconciled rewrite passes both). One caveat: the 'mutex' is structural/textual (overlapping hunks in one small function) rather than a logical contradiction of intent — the two demands are compatible once merged, which is precisely the reconciliation the seed is meant to exercise. Complementary family is weak because the session-contract consumer already exists at the base commit.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A says: the core module helper file basic.py (and its import chain) gets its 'collection ABC' type names (like Mapping, Sequence) from an internal compatibility shim; move those imports to the supported six-based path, so the shim stops being bundled into every minimal module. Task B says: basic.py imports seven of those type names but only actually uses three of them — delete the four unused names to clean up the file. Both tickets force edits to the exact same six-line import statement at the top of basic.py. If two agents blindly apply both changes, the file ends up with two import statements (one still pulling in the shim, one still carrying the unused names): the shim is bundled into minimal modules again (A's test fails) and the unused imports remain (B's test fails). A single reconciled edit — one import from the six path listing only the three names actually used — satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/ansible/module_utils/basic.py, the import block at lines 140-145: `from ansible.module_utils.common._collections_compat import (KeysView, Mapping, MutableMapping, Sequence, MutableSequence, Set, MutableSet,)`. A rewrites the module this block imports from; B deletes names from the same block.
suggestion.taskA: Migrate collection ABC imports in module_utils (basic.py, common/collections.py, common/parameters.py, common/json.py, common/dict_transformations.py, common/text/converters.py, compat/_selectors2.py, modules/uri.py, plugins/shell/__init__.py) from the internal shim ansible.module_utils.common._collections_compat to ansible.module_utils.six.moves.collections_abc, reduce the shim to a pure re-export, and stop the shim from being collected into minimal module payloads (verified by the recursive-finder unit tests whose expected dependency set no longer includes the shim file).
suggestion.taskB: module_utils/basic.py imports seven collection ABC names (KeysView, Mapping, MutableMapping, Sequence, MutableSequence, Set, MutableSet) but only references KeysView (in SEQUENCETYPE, line 198), Mapping (in _return_formatted, line 1494) and Sequence (line 198). Remove the four unused names (MutableMapping, MutableSequence, Set, MutableSet) from basic.py's import block so the file carries no dead imports. (This is a real, common cleanup ticket — directory-wide grep confirms MutableMapping/MutableSequence/MutableSet appear in basic.py only on the import line.)
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated purely by code cleanliness/lint hygiene (unused imports in a core file), not by the shim migration. A maintainer would file 'basic.py has dead imports' without ever mentioning _collections_compat or six.moves.collections_abc. B's fix (delete 4 names, keep the shim source) is a complete, shippable change on its own; it is not a step toward A's goal, and A's goal is fully achievable without B. The overlap is purely locational: both tickets happen to own the same six lines.
suggestion.conflict: A's patch rewrites the import block's source module while keeping all 7 names; B's patch deletes 4 of the 7 names while keeping the shim source. Naively gluing both changes yields two import statements in basic.py: the shim import (with 3 names) plus the six.moves import (with 7 names). The shim is still reachable from basic.py, so the recursive-finder dependency set still contains _collections_compat.py and A's tests fail; the six.moves import still binds MutableMapping/MutableSequence/Set/MutableSet which are never used, so B's unused-import test fails. The two edits cannot both stand as-is.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Replace the block with a single `from ansible.module_utils.six.moves.collections_abc import KeysView, Mapping, Sequence` (only the names basic.py actually references), keep A's other file migrations and the shim-as-pure-re-export, and everything else unchanged. One coherent edit satisfying both tickets.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the four fail_to_pass tests in test/units/executor/module_common/test_recursive_finder.py (expected MODULE_UTILS_BASIC_FILES no longer includes the shim). B's set: a new unit test (e.g. test/units/module_utils/test_basic_imports.py) that AST-parses basic.py, collects names imported from _collections_compat or six.moves.collections_abc, and asserts each is referenced in the module body. Base fails both sets. A-alone passes A's set but fails B's (7 names kept). B-alone passes B's set but fails A's (shim still imported). Naive merge fails both. The reconciled change passes the combined suite.

notes: Grep tool quirk observed: searching with a single file as `path` returned spurious 'no matches' (e.g. for patterns that clearly exist in the file); directory-path searches were reliable and were used for all usage verification. Verified via directory greps: in basic.py, KeysView (line 198), Mapping (line 1494) and Sequence (line 198) are referenced; MutableMapping, MutableSequence and MutableSet appear only on the import line (142-144). Plain `Set` usage in basic.py could not be fully re-verified due to the grep quirk, but it is imported alongside the other three unused names and the real upstream history shows basic.py's ABC import was later trimmed to the used names, supporting B's plausibility. The contradictory pairing is the natural one here: same six lines, two genuinely independent motivations (import-source migration vs. dead-import cleanup), and the naive merge demonstrably fails both test sets while a single reconciled import satisfies both. Complementary is weak: A adds no interface, and the one plausible 'partner' change (pylint rule update) is already inside A's own test patch, making it a decomposition rather than an independent ticket.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A adds an 'upgrade' switch to the collection installer so that, when requested, an already-installed collection can be replaced by a newer version from the server; when not requested, the installed version must be kept. Task B is a separate bug report: if a collection is already installed at a version that does NOT satisfy the newly requested version range (e.g. 1.0.0 installed, user requests >=2.0.0), the installer should simply pick the server version, but instead the resolver offers the stale installed version as a candidate and fails with a confusing 'Cannot meet requirement ... already installed' error. Both fixes must rewrite the same few lines in the resolver's candidate-listing function (find_matches in lib/ansible/galaxy/dependency_resolution/providers.py) where the set of 'preinstalled candidates' is computed and prepended to the server versions. A's fix changes that set to 'installed version that satisfies the request AND (no upgrade requested OR no newer version exists)'; B's fix changes it to 'installed version that satisfies the request' unconditionally. The two conditions are different formulas for the same variable, so pasting both patches together produces broken or contradictory code.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/ansible/galaxy/dependency_resolution/providers.py, CollectionDependencyProvider.find_matches() — the `preinstalled_candidates` comprehension and the `return list(preinstalled_candidates) + sorted(...)` statement (base commit lines ~222-244). Secondary shared region: the `try/except InconsistentCandidate` block inside install_collections() in lib/ansible/galaxy/collection/__init__.py (lines ~478-514), which A deletes entirely.
suggestion.taskA: Thread an `upgrade` flag through the Galaxy collection installation pipeline: install_collections(), _resolve_depenency_map(), build_collection_dependency_resolver() and the provider must accept `upgrade`; when False, behavior is unchanged (installed satisfying version is retained even if a newer one exists); when True, resolution must pick the newest server version satisfying the requirement (respecting the pre-release setting). Existing callers (e.g. download_collections) must pass upgrade=False.
suggestion.taskB: Bug: re-requesting an already-installed collection with a version range the installed version does not satisfy fails confusingly. With ns.coll 1.0.0 installed and the server also offering 2.0.0, `ansible-galaxy collection install ns.coll:>=2.0.0` must resolve and install 2.0.0; when the server does NOT offer a satisfying version, the error must be the normal 'Failed to resolve the requested dependencies map' conflict message, not the 'Cannot meet requirement ... already installed at version ... Use --force' message. Root cause: find_matches() prepends every installed candidate for the name to the candidate list without checking whether it satisfies the requested range, and get_preference() gives such candidates top priority, so the resolver backtracks into the stale installed version instead of using the server version.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a classic resolver-correctness bug ticket a maintainer would file on its own: it is about honoring version constraints against preinstalled collections and about error-message quality, with no mention of upgrades, no new flag, and no CLI work. It is motivated by the existing 'preferred candidates' optimization (avoid re-downloading installed collections) misbehaving when the installed version is out of range. It is not 'the other half of A': A is a feature (opt-in upgrade), B is a defect fix (stale installed candidates must never be offered as matches). The two tickets plausibly land in the same sprint and touch the same lines for different reasons.
suggestion.conflict: Both edits target the same expression computing preinstalled_candidates. A's version is `candidate.fqcn == fqcn and all(is_satisfied_by(...)) and (not self._upgrade or all(latest.ver <= candidate.ver for latest in latest_matches))` (and requires computing latest_matches first, plus removing the InconsistentCandidate handler in install_collections). B's version is `candidate.fqcn == fqcn and all(is_satisfied_by(...) for requirement in requirements)` with no upgrade awareness. Naive merge outcomes: (1) A's patch applied, then B's patch — B's hunk no longer applies, or if force-applied it reintroduces the pre-upgrade filter and drops the upgrade condition, so A's upgrade tests (installed 1.0.0 + server 2.0.0 + upgrade=True must yield 2.0.0) fail; (2) B's patch applied, then A's patch — A's hunk context is broken, and if force-applied the result either references latest_matches before it is defined (NameError) or keeps installed candidates that A's logic must gate on the upgrade flag; (3) both 'solutions' coexisting as separate branches of the same comprehension cannot express both policies at once without a single reconciled formula. Additionally A deletes the except-InconsistentCandidate block in install_collections() while B's error-message test asserts on that block's output, so a naive merge either leaves dead code that B's tests exercise or removes it and B's tests fail.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change in find_matches(): first build latest_matches (the sorted, requirement-satisfying server candidates), then compute preinstalled_candidates as installed candidates whose fqcn matches AND that satisfy every requirement AND (upgrade is False OR no latest server candidate is newer than the installed one), and return preinstalled + latest_matches. Keep the provider's `upgrade` attribute threaded from build_collection_dependency_resolver(). In install_collections(), drop the InconsistentCandidate special-casing (A's deletion) so B's scenario surfaces the generic 'Failed to resolve ...' message; B's desired behavior (satisfying server version wins over stale installed version) falls out of the same satisfied-by filter.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the fail_to_pass unit tests in test/units/galaxy/test_collection_install.py (test_resolve_dependency_map_upgrade_picks_newest_over_installed, test_resolve_dependency_map_upgrade_with_prerelease_enabled, test_resolve_dependency_map_without_upgrade_keeps_installed, plus the signature-sensitive tests test_install_collections_from_tar, test_install_collections_existing_without_force, test_install_missing_metadata_warning, test_install_collection_with_circular_dependency, test_candidate_with_conflict, test_dep_candidate_with_conflict, and the test_build_requirement_from_name* suite). B's set: new unit tests in the same file, e.g. (a) preferred_candidates=[Candidate('ns.coll','1.0.0',None,'dir')], server versions ['1.0.0','2.0.0'], requirement 'ns.coll:>=2.0.0' -> _resolve_depenency_map(..., upgrade=False) must resolve to 2.0.0; (b) same setup with server versions ['1.0.0'] only -> must raise AnsibleError matching 'Failed to resolve the requested dependencies map. Could not satisfy the following requirements:* ns.coll:>=2.0.0 (direct request)' and NOT 'Cannot meet requirement'. Base code fails both sets (no upgrade behavior; stale-candidate bug present). A's solution alone fails (b) and (a) (installed 1.0.0 is still prepended and preferred); B's solution alone fails A's upgrade tests. Only the reconciled change passes the combined suite.

notes: Strongest pairing is contradictory: the base code's find_matches() prepends ALL installed candidates for a name regardless of the requested version range (and get_preference() gives them -inf priority), which is a genuine, independently reportable bug whose fix rewrites the exact lines A's upgrade logic rewrites; A additionally deletes the InconsistentCandidate handler in install_collections() that B's error-message expectations depend on. Verified at base commit: providers.py lines 222-244 (unfiltered preinstalled set), get_preference lines 174-181, install_collections try/except lines 478-514, and the six-arg _resolve_depenency_map signature at line 1285. The complementary split (engine vs CLI flag) is real but both halves serve the same end feature, so independence is weaker; also note A's gold patch itself contains the CLI flag, meaning a B authored as 'add the flag' overlaps textually with A's patch — the authoring step should keep B strictly to galaxy.py and its tests. A's test patch also modifies existing tests to pin versions (e.g. parent_dep.parent_collection:1.0.0), which is part of A's own suite and should not be attributed to B.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a ticket about making ansible-doc's text markup render predictably when the terminal has no color: italic I(text) must come out as `text` (two backticks) instead of a backtick plus an apostrophe, and other markups get fixed plain-text delimiters. Task B is a separate, plausible ticket: 'when color IS available, constant markup C(text) should be highlighted (bold) instead of being shown as plain `text'' — a visual-consistency complaint a different developer could easily file. Both tasks must edit the same single line inside the markup-rendering function (DocCLI.tty_ify in lib/ansible/cli/doc.py), the line that converts C(...) into terminal text. A rewrites that line to emit a no-color delimiter, B rewrites it to emit a colored highlight. If two agents each patch that line independently and the patches are glued together, one change overwrites the other: the merged code either always emits the plain delimiter (failing B's color test) or always emits the highlight (failing A's no-color test). A single reconciled edit — make that one line branch on whether color is enabled (plain delimiter when off, bold highlight when on) — satisfies both tickets at once.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/ansible/cli/doc.py, DocCLI.tty_ify() — specifically the line `t = cls._CONST.sub(r"`\1'", t)` (base code line 432) that renders C(text) constant markup; A changes its no-color rendering and B changes its color rendering of the same substitution.
suggestion.taskA: Improve markup rendering and role-summary metadata in ansible-doc output: when color is disabled (ANSIBLE_NOCOLOR/NO_COLOR), documentation markup must render into stable ASCII delimiters — B(text) -> *text*, M(name) -> [name], C(text) -> `text' (leading backtick, trailing apostrophe), I(text) -> `text` (symmetric backticks, no apostrophe), U(url) -> bare url, L(text, url) -> text <url>, R(text, ref) -> bare text, HORIZONTALLINE -> a dash line, unknown text unchanged. Separately, RoleMixin._build_summary() must take a `meta` dict as its third positional argument (before argspec), and when meta is empty or lacks galaxy_info the summary must contain 'description': 'UNDOCUMENTED' while still carrying 'collection' and the 'entry_points' mapping.
suggestion.taskB: Inconsistent terminal highlighting in ansible-doc: when color is enabled, constant markup C(text) in module/role documentation is printed as plain `text' with no emphasis, while other directives (e.g. B(text)) are visually distinguished. Make C(text) render as a bold-highlighted `text` (ANSI bold) whenever color output is active, and keep the existing plain-text rendering when color is disabled. (Never mentions A's delimiter work or role summaries.)
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone ticket: it is motivated purely by the colored-terminal experience (visual emphasis of constants), not by A's no-color delimiter consistency goal or by role documentation. A maintainer could file 'C() markup should be bold in color terminals' without knowing anything about the I() backtick fix or the role-summary metadata work. It targets the same function but a different rendering mode (color-on vs color-off), so it is not 'the other half' of A — A's ticket explicitly scopes itself to no-color output.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches rewrite the same statement in tty_ify. A's version replaces the C() substitution with the no-color delimiter `text' (and in the real gold patch restructures the whole function around a NOCOLOR/STYLE table). B's version wraps the C() substitution in a color highlight. Naively concatenating/auto-merging them leaves only one replacement for that line: if B's ANSI-wrapping wins, A's no-color test for C() fails (output contains escape codes / wrong delimiters); if A's plain substitution wins, B's color test fails (no bold). The two demands — 'always plain delimiter' vs 'highlight when color' — cannot both be literally true of one unconditional line.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Make the C() rendering in tty_ify branch on the color flag (ansible.utils.color.ANSIBLE_COLOR): when color is disabled emit A's ASCII delimiter (`text' / `text` for I()), when enabled emit B's bold-highlighted text. This is exactly the structure the gold patch introduces (a NOCOLOR table of plain delimiters plus a color-aware stringc/STYLE mechanism), so a single reconciled change passes both suites.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the fail_to_pass unit tests test/units/cli/test_doc.py::test_ttyify[...] (which pin the no-color delimiter mapping, including I(italic) -> `italic`) and the two test_rolemixin__build_summary tests. B's set: new unit tests that force color on (monkeypatch ansible.utils.color.ANSIBLE_COLOR = True) and assert DocCLI.tty_ify("C(x)") returns the bold ANSI-wrapped form, plus a control test with color off asserting the plain delimiter. Combined suite: run both against the merged code; it passes only if the C()/I() lines in tty_ify condition on the color flag — a naive merge of the two independent patches fails one side's assertions.

notes: The strongest collision region is DocCLI.tty_ify in lib/ansible/cli/doc.py: it is a compact, single-purpose function whose per-markup lines are exactly what A rewrites (no-color delimiters; the gold patch restructures it around a NOCOLOR/STYLE table and stringc), and a color-emphasis ticket for C() is a natural, independently-motivated B that must edit the same line. Caveat that keeps contradictory at 4 rather than 5: B is in the same feature family as A (the real gold patch already implements color-aware markup rendering), so a strict reviewer might see B as anticipating A's direction; the independence rests on B being scoped to color-ON emphasis only. The role-summary half of A is a poor site for an independent B: A rewrites _load_argspec/_build_summary/_create_role_list/_create_role_doc/_find_all_normal_roles together (new _load_role_data/_load_metadata, 3-tuple role entries, error propagation), so any B touching that region (e.g. 'show role description in -t role -l') is either a decomposition of A or only weakly complementary (the summary dict contract is real, but B's display change lives in a different function than A's producer change). The tty_ify-based contradictory pair is the recommendation; the complementary pair is included as a secondary, lower-confidence option. Base-commit facts verified: tty_ify line 425 renders I() as `\1' and line 432 renders C() as `\1'; _build_summary(role, collection, argspec) has no meta parameter and no description key; test/units/cli/test_doc.py pins the old mappings; ANSIBLE_COLOR is computed at import time in lib/ansible/utils/color.py (monkeypatchable for B's tests).

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A asks that a deployment-level switch (the 'RoomOptionsMenu' component-visibility customisation) can hide the room options menu everywhere: in the room list tile, the room header, and spotlight search results. Its fix wraps the existing menu-visibility checks with a new condition, so the menu only shows when BOTH the old condition AND the new switch say yes. Task B is a separate, real product complaint: rooms in the 'Invited' section of the room list do not show the room options button, so an invited user cannot open the menu to leave or forget the room; the fix is to stop suppressing the button for invited rooms. Both tasks must rewrite the exact same visibility condition in the room tile (the showContextMenu getter in RoomTile.tsx, which currently reads 'tag is not Invited'). A turns it into 'not Invited AND customisation enabled'; B wants it to no longer depend on the tag at all. A single condition cannot both keep the tag-based suppression and remove it, so blindly applying both patches leaves contradictory logic that fails one side's tests.
suggestion.shared_region: src/components/views/rooms/RoomTile.tsx — the private get showContextMenu() getter (base: `return this.props.tag !== DefaultTagID.Invite;`), consumed by renderGeneralMenu()/onContextMenu()/renderNotificationsMenu(); secondary same-line collisions in src/components/views/rooms/RoomHeader.tsx renderName() (`if (this.props.enableRoomOptionsMenu)` branch) and src/components/views/dialogs/spotlight/RoomResultContextMenus.tsx (unconditional ContextMenuTooltipButton).
suggestion.taskA: Customized deployments need a way to remove the room options menu from the interface. The menu is reachable from room tiles, the room header, and spotlight search results, and every place renders it unconditionally. Add a `RoomOptionsMenu` member to the `UIComponent` enum and gate all three entry points on `shouldShowComponent(UIComponent.RoomOptionsMenu)`: when the customisation reports it disabled, none of the three places may render the menu; when enabled, they must (RoomHeader additionally keeps honoring its `enableRoomOptionsMenu` prop).
suggestion.taskB: Invited rooms in the room list don't show the room options button (the three-dot menu on the tile), so a user who has been invited to a room has no way to open the room menu to leave or forget it. The tile suppresses its context menus for the 'Invited' tag section; remove that suppression so the room options button renders on invited-room tiles (and right-click still opens the menu).
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a classic standalone UX/permissions ticket: the invited section of the room list is a distinct feature area, and 'invited users can't leave from the room list' is a complaint a maintainer would file with zero reference to deployment customisations or the UIComponent system. It is not a piece of A: A's goal is making the menu hideable by a deployment switch; B's goal is making the menu more visible for a specific user situation. The two motivations (hide everywhere vs. show in the invited section) are genuinely opposed, which is exactly what makes the collision real rather than an artificial split.
suggestion.conflict: Both edits target the same boolean that decides whether the tile renders its options button. A's change ANDs a new `shouldShowComponent(UIComponent.RoomOptionsMenu)` condition onto `tag !== DefaultTagID.Invite`; B's change deletes the `tag !== DefaultTagID.Invite` condition (or otherwise forces the button for invited rooms). A's tests mock the customisation to false and assert the button is absent (with the default Untagged tile), while B's tests render the tile with the Invited tag and assert the button is present. A naive merge keeps both edits: the tag check is gone but the customisation gate remains, so B's invited-room test (customisation mocked true) may pass but A's 'hidden when disabled' semantics and B's 'never suppress by tag' semantics cannot both hold in one expression — any single boolean expression chosen by one agent fails the other's assertions (e.g., keeping the tag check fails B; dropping it while A's tests run with the mock false fails A). The same opposition exists in RoomHeader.renderName (A wraps the prop check with the customisation; a 'menu must always be available' B-side edit unwraps it) and in RoomResultContextMenus (A wraps the button in a conditional; B would keep it unconditional).
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: make the tile's options button visibility `shouldShowComponent(UIComponent.RoomOptionsMenu)` (i.e., drop the tag-based suppression entirely) — or equivalently keep the getter but define it so the customisation is the sole gate. Then A's tests pass (mock false => hidden; mock true => shown) and B's tests pass (invited tile with mock true => button present; right-click menu no longer blocked by the tag). Apply the analogous single-gate logic in RoomHeader (prop AND customisation) and RoomResultContextMenus (customisation gate) so all three entry points share one rule.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the gold fail_to_pass tests — RoomResultContextMenus-test.tsx (menu hidden/shown by mocked shouldShowComponent), RoomHeader-test.tsx (enableRoomOptionsMenu x customisation matrix), RoomTile-test.tsx ('does not render the room options context menu when UIComponent customisations disable room options' / 'renders ... when ... enable'). suggestion.shared_region: lib/assist/assist.go — Chat.ProcessComplete (the switch over *model.Message / *model.StreamingMessage / *model.CompletionCommand that extracts usage, lines ~318-408) and its consumer lib/web/assistant.go — runAssistant (lines ~480-507, which computes extraTokens and the usage event from the returned usage). These are the only two files in the repo that read the *TokensUsed field A's patch deletes from lib/ai/model/messages.go, so both A and B are forced to rewrite them.
suggestion.taskA: Fix assistant token accounting: Chat.Complete and Agent.PlanAndExecute must return a real per-exchange token total (a new *model.TokenCount with CountAll() (prompt, completion)), prompt counters must be registered for every model call, streamed completions must be counted with an asynchronous counter (NewAsynchronousTokenCounter + Add per delta + TokenCount() adding perRequest), and the old embedded *TokensUsed fields on Message/StreamingMessage/CompletionCommand must be removed. New file lib/ai/model/tokencount.go with package-level defaultTokenizer (Cl100kBase).
suggestion.taskB: Persist per-message token usage and fix assistant rate limiting: (1) add prompt_tokens and completion_tokens fields to the AssistantMessage proto (api/proto/teleport/assist/v1/assist.proto) and populate them in ProcessComplete for every assistant message kind (text, streamed text, command) so the conversation store records what each exchange actually cost; (2) in lib/web/assistant.go runAssistant, stop charging the global assistantLimiter with the per-message usage (usedTokens.Prompt + usedTokens.Completion - lookaheadTokens) because the web layer already consumed the lookahead tokens — charging again double-counts, and in the current code the embedded usage is never populated so the limiter effectively never sees real cost. B is written against the base code where ProcessComplete returns *model.TokensUsed taken from message.TokensUsed.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B has its own motivation unrelated to how counting works: billing/audit data (usage persisted per message in the conversation store) and a real base-code bug (double-charging the rate limiter, and the usage event in runAssistant reporting zeros because the embedded counter is never populated). A maintainer could file 'store token usage with each assistant message and stop the double rate-limit charge' without ever touching the counting redesign; conversely A is about making the counts correct across multi-call/streamed exchanges. The overlap is structural, not motivational: both must touch the same extraction point because that is the only place per-message usage is available.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches are authored against the base commit. A's patch deletes *TokensUsed from the three message structs (lib/ai/model/messages.go) and changes Chat.Complete to return (any, *model.TokenCount, error); for the repo to compile, A's author must rewrite ProcessComplete/runAssistant to use the new TokenCount. B's patch keeps the old field and adds code that reads message.TokensUsed.Prompt/.Completion to fill the new proto fields and remove the limiter charge. Naively merging (A's hunks to chat.go/agent.go/messages.go + B's hunks to assist.go/assistant.go) yields assist.go referencing the deleted TokensUsed field and the old 2-value Complete() return — a compile error, so the combined suite fails.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: in ProcessComplete, destructure the new three-value Complete() call, get (prompt, completion) := tokenCount.CountAll(), and store those into the new AssistantMessage proto fields for every message kind; in runAssistant, drop the extraTokens/ReserveN double-charge (keep the lookahead AllowN) and build the usage event from the same CountAll() totals. A's tests (accurate counts, 3-value Complete) and B's tests (persisted fields populated, limiter charged once) both pass against this single version.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: lib/ai/model/tokencount_test.go (TestAsynchronousTokenCounter_TokenCount, TestAsynchronousTokenCounter_Finished) and the updated lib/ai/chat_test.go (TestChat_PromptTokens with new expected totals, TestChat_Complete with 3-value Complete). B's set: new tests in lib/assist/assist_test.go asserting ProcessComplete persists prompt/completion token counts into the stored AssistantMessage proto for text, streaming, and command kinds, plus a lib/web/assistant_test.go case asserting the rate limiter is not charged a second time after the lookahead. Combined suite: run both packages' tests against the merged tree — the naive merge fails to compile (B's code references the field A deleted), so all tests fail; the reconciled version compiles and passes both sets.

notes: Verified at base commit: the only readers of the *TokensUsed field that A's patch deletes are lib/assist/assist.go (ProcessComplete, 3 switch cases) and lib/web/assistant.go (runAssistant, extraTokens + usage event) — which makes the shared region for the contradictory seed structurally forced rather than invented. B's ticket has genuine base-code motivation: runAssistant charges the global assistantLimiter with usedTokens.Prompt+usedTokens.Completion-lookaheadTokens, but in base code the embedded counter is never populated (the completion builder is commented out with a race-condition TODO in agent.go plan()), so the charge is always 0 and the AssistCompletionEvent usage event always reports zeros — a real double-count/zero-report bug independent of A's counting redesign. One caveat keeping confidence at 4 not 5: B's 'populate from message.TokensUsed' fix is a workaround for the same underlying inaccuracy A addresses, so a strict reviewer could argue B only fully makes sense once A exists; the ticket text should emphasize persistence and the rate-limiter double-charge to stay independent. The complementary family fails the 'A alone fails the integration test' bar, so it is recorded as not viable.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A changes the expression parser so that a plain string like "foo" is accepted as a valid (literal) expression instead of being rejected. To do that, A also touches the helper that walks the parsed expression tree: it adds a guard so that only string-tokens are unquoted (because a plain number or character would otherwise crash the unquote step). Task B is an independent bug report: role definitions that contain a non-string literal inside the template brackets (for example a bare number or a character) crash the parser, because the same helper unconditionally tries to unquote every literal token. B's fix is to guard the unquote step so that non-string tokens are passed through as-is. Both A and B therefore must edit the exact same few lines of the same helper function (the BasicLit case in the AST walk). A's edit says 'only unquote strings'; B's edit says 'skip unquoting for non-strings'. These are two different rewrites of the same block. If you naively concatenate both patches you get two conflicting versions of the same case label in the same switch, which does not compile. A single reconciled change — check the token kind, unquote only strings, pass everything else through — satisfies both tickets at once.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/utils/parse/parse.go, function walk, the `case *ast.BasicLit:` block (lines ~237-242). A's gold patch rewrites this block to guard strconv.Unquote behind `n.Kind == token.STRING`; B's fix must rewrite the same block to stop unquoting non-string literal tokens.
suggestion.taskA: String literals are not accepted as valid expressions. Currently a plain string value (e.g. "foo") passed to the role-variable parser is rejected instead of being understood on its own, forcing callers to special-case it. Fix: the parser should accept inputs that contain no template brackets as a valid literal expression, classify them under a new exported LiteralNamespace, keep the original text unchanged, and make Interpolate return that text as the single result without consulting traits. Inputs that contain brackets but do not parse must still return a BadParameter error, and all previously valid templated inputs must keep parsing exactly as before.
suggestion.taskB: Role variable parser crashes on non-string literal tokens. When a role definition contains a template expression whose body is a bare number or a character (for example {{123}} or {{'a'}}), the parser's AST walk calls strconv.Unquote on the token's raw text, which fails for anything that is not a double-quoted string, and the whole role is rejected with an obscure error. Fix: in the AST walk, only unquote tokens that are actually string literals; for numeric and character literals, use the token's raw text directly so that such expressions parse successfully and interpolate to their literal value.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone ticket filed by a different developer who hit a crash while authoring a role with a numeric or character literal in a template. It has its own motivation (fixing a parser crash on a specific input class), its own reproduction (a role containing {{123}}), and its own expected behavior (the expression parses and resolves to the literal number). It never mentions literal namespaces, plain-string acceptance, or Interpolate's trait-free path — all of which are A's concerns. B would be filed and fixed even if A never existed, because the unquote-on-non-string bug is present in the base code independently of any literal-namespace feature.
suggestion.conflict: Both A and B must rewrite the same `case *ast.BasicLit:` block inside walk(). A's version introduces a `token.STRING` guard around strconv.Unquote; B's version introduces a guard that skips unquoting for non-string kinds. These are two different edits to the same lines. Naively merging (concatenating or auto-merging) the two patches produces either a duplicate case label in the same switch (compile error) or one patch's guard silently overwriting the other's, so the combined test suite cannot pass on the naive merge.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: A single coherent edit to the BasicLit case: if the token kind is STRING, unquote it (stripping the double quotes); otherwise (numeric, char, etc.) use the token's raw text as-is. This is exactly A's guard, and it simultaneously fixes B's crash because non-string tokens are no longer passed to strconv.Unquote. The rest of A's changes (LiteralNamespace constant, Variable accepting plain strings, Interpolate short-circuit for literals) are orthogonal to B and carry over unchanged.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestRoleVariable (including the new 'string literal' subtest) and TestInterpolate (including the new 'literal expression' subtest) in lib/utils/parse/parse_test.go. B's set: new subtests in TestRoleVariable / TestInterpolate that feed non-string literal tokens (e.g. a numeric or character body) and assert the expression parses and interpolates to the raw literal value. Combined suite: run both sets against the merged code. On the base commit, A's literal subtests fail (plain strings rejected) and B's non-string subtests fail (unquote crash). A's own patch passes A's set; B's own patch passes B's set. The naive merge of the two patches fails to compile (conflicting BasicLit case), so the combined suite fails. The reconciled single edit passes the full combined suite.

notes: The strongest and most honest pairing for this task is the contradictory family, centered on the `case *ast.BasicLit:` block in walk() in lib/utils/parse/parse.go. A's gold patch already rewrites that block (adding the token.STRING guard), which is the seam B's independent crash-fix must also rewrite. The collision is a genuine same-lines conflict that a naive merge breaks (duplicate switch case / compile error), and a single reconciled edit (unquote only string tokens, pass others through) satisfies both. I verified the base code: strconv.Unquote is called unconditionally on n.Value for every BasicLit, so numeric/character token bodies do crash today, independent of A. The complementary family is weak: the only consumers of Variable/Expression (role.go, user.go) are themselves rewritten by A's patch, so any B built on top of A's new LiteralNamespace reads as a decomposition of A rather than an independent ticket. I marked complementary not viable rather than force an artificial fit. Confidence on contradictory is 4 (strong, real same-region collision with a clean reconciliation), not 5, because B's test inputs (numeric/char literal bodies) are a slightly contrived corner of the expression grammar and the authoring step must ensure B's subtests genuinely fail on the base commit and pass on B's standalone patch.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A adds a 'start position' feature: every streaming call gains an offset parameter, and because transcoded audio is cached on disk, the cache key (a small string built from file ID, modification time, bitrate and format in streamJob.Key()) must also include the offset so two requests for the same file at different start points don't collide. Task B is a separate bug report: when an admin edits the ffmpeg command of a transcoding profile in settings, previously cached transcoded files keep being served, because the same cache key does not include the command; the fix is to add the command to streamJob.Key() as well. Both tickets therefore force a rewrite of the exact same one-line Key() function and the same struct/job construction in core/media_streamer.go, but with different key formats. A merged result that keeps only A's key serves stale audio when the command changes (fails B's test); one that keeps only B's key serves the wrong start position for different offsets (fails A's tests); naively concatenating both patches defines Key() twice and does not compile.
suggestion.shared_region: core/media_streamer.go — the streamJob struct, its Key() method, and the streamJob literal built inside DoStream (A adds an offset field + '%d' to the key; B adds a command field + command to the same key)
suggestion.taskA: Add support for a time offset in streaming and transcoding: NewStream/DoStream/Transcode gain a trailing integer offset (seconds); createFFmpegCommand substitutes a %t placeholder or inserts '-ss <offset>' after the input path when the template lacks %t (no -ss when offset is 0); the offset is propagated unchanged to the transcoder; the transcoding cache key includes the offset; subsonic /stream accepts a timeOffset param and advertises the transcodeOffset OpenSubsonic extension; all other call sites pass 0.
suggestion.taskB: Transcoding cache is not invalidated when a transcoding command is edited: the transcoding profiles (name, target format, bitrate, ffmpeg command) are user-editable at runtime, but the on-disk transcoding cache key is only <mediaFileID>.<updatedAt>.<bitRate>.<format>. After an admin changes, say, the mp3 ffmpeg command, Navidrome keeps serving the previously cached file encoded with the old command until the cache is evicted or the source file changes. The cache key must incorporate the transcoding command (or the transcoding profile's ID) so that editing a command transparently produces fresh cache entries. No behavior change is requested for playback start position; requests always start at the beginning.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a cache-correctness bug about admin-editable transcoding profiles, motivated by a user complaint ('I changed the transcoding command in Settings but the old encoding is still being served'). It says nothing about offsets, seeking, or the subsonic API; it would be filed by a different developer from observing stale cache behavior. It is not 'the part of A that A didn't do' — A's gold patch incidentally touches Key() only to add the offset dimension, while B's whole motivation is the missing command dimension.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches rewrite the same function (func (j *streamJob) Key() string) with incompatible format strings — A: '%s.%s.%d.%s.%d' (offset appended), B: e.g. '%s.%s.%d.%s.%s' (command appended) — and both extend the same streamJob struct and the same job literal in DoStream. Auto-merging yields either a duplicate Key() method (compile failure) or one side's Key() winning, in which case the loser's tests fail: with only A's key, two jobs differing solely in command share a key (B's test fails); with only B's key, offset is not part of the key (A's offset/cache tests fail).
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: streamJob gains both offset int and command string fields; DoStream sets both (command from the transcoding profile looked up for the job); Key() includes both dimensions, e.g. fmt.Sprintf("%s.%s.%d.%s.%d.%s", id, updatedAt, bitRate, format, offset, command) (or a short hash of the command). All of A's offset tests and B's command-invalidation tests then pass together.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set (existing fail_to_pass): TestFFmpeg (createFFmpegCommand %t substitution and -ss insertion, offset 0 unchanged), TestCore (NewStream passes a non-zero offset through to the transcoder's Transcode call; cache/seekable behavior), TestArtwork (compiles and runs against the new 5-arg Transcode signature via the harness mock). B's set: a new spec in the core package (internal test file, e.g. stream_job_test.go in package core) asserting that two streamJobs for the same media file, format and bitrate but different transcoding commands produce different Key() values, and that DoStream keys the cache job with the current command. Combined suite: run both ginkgo suites against the merged core package; everything passes only if Key() contains BOTH the offset and the command dimensions.

notes: Repo state verified at base commit: createFFmpegCommand has 3 args (no %t handling), streamJob.Key() is '%s.%s.%d.%s' (no offset, no command), Transcode/NewStream/DoStream lack offset params, opensubsonic.go advertises no extensions, and timeOffset appears nowhere. A's gold patch bundles the subsonic API param reading + extension advertisement, so any B touching server/subsonic/stream.go's timeOffset handling is a decomposition of A, not independent. A weaker contradictory alternative exists in consts/consts.go: a ticket to 'add a vorbis/ogg default transcoding profile' edits the same DefaultTranscodings var A modifies, but the edits are on different lines (A rewrites three command strings, B appends a fourth entry) and auto-merge would succeed, so it does not meet the mutex bar. The streamJob.Key() collision is the strongest real structure: same function, same struct, same job literal, mutually exclusive key formats, and B has a fully independent motivation (stale cache after editing transcoding commands). Caveat for authoring: B's tests should live in an internal core-package test file (streamJob is unexported) and must not depend on the harness-maintained mocks that A's test patch updates (tests/mock_ffmpeg.go, core/archiver_test.go's mockMediaStreamer).

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A fixes the cover-art service so that when a request names a music file (an 'mf-' style ID), the file's own embedded cover is served instead of pretending it was an album. Task B is a separate, real feature: Subsonic clients also ask the same cover-art endpoint for artist images ('ar-' style IDs), which the service today does not understand at all. Both tasks must rewrite the exact same dispatch section inside the artwork service's main lookup function: A turns it into a branch that says 'album ID -> album art, media-file ID -> file art, anything else -> placeholder', while B adds 'artist ID -> artist image' into that same section. Written independently against the original code, the two edits land on the same lines and cannot simply be glued together: A's catch-all 'otherwise placeholder' branch silently swallows artist IDs, and B's artist branch gets orphaned or overwritten by A's restructuring. A single reconciled version with all three branches (album, media file, artist) plus the placeholder fallback satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: core/artwork.go, func (a *artwork) get() — the dispatch block after model.ParseArtworkID (base lines ~55-74, where the album lookup and extractImage call live). A restructures this block into a switch on artId.Kind; B must insert its artist-ID handling into this same block. (B additionally extends model/artwork_id.go — Kind constants and ParseArtworkID — which A does not touch.)
suggestion.taskA: Embedded media-file cover art is ignored: artwork requests that name a media file are resolved as album lookups, so a track with its own embedded cover shows a placeholder or an unrelated album's cover, and non-not-found lookup failures surface as errors instead of falling back to the placeholder. Make the artwork service dispatch on the ID kind (album vs media file), serve the media file's embedded art with fallback to its album's art, and always fall back to the placeholder on failure; expose MediaFile.AlbumCoverArtID() for the fallback.
suggestion.taskB: The getCoverArt endpoint does not serve artist images: Subsonic clients request artist covers through the same endpoint using artist-prefixed artwork IDs, but the artwork service only understands album IDs, so artist artwork requests come back as a placeholder or an error. Add artist artwork support: accept artist-prefixed artwork IDs, look up the artist's stored image (external metadata image URL), and serve it, falling back to the placeholder when the artist has no image or is not found.
suggestion.independence_rationale: Artist images via getCoverArt is a distinct Subsonic API-compatibility feature motivated by artist pages and third-party clients (DSub, Substream, etc. request artist covers through this endpoint). It says nothing about media files or embedded cover art; a maintainer would file it independently of the track-cover bug. It is not a step toward A's goal — A is about per-track embedded art, B is about a different entity (artists) reaching the same endpoint. (Upstream Navidrome in fact later shipped artist artwork support as its own change, which corroborates that this is a believable standalone ticket.)
suggestion.conflict: Both solutions rewrite the same dispatch block in artwork.get(). A's version replaces the album-only logic with a switch whose default case returns the placeholder for any non-album/non-mediafile kind; B's version (authored against the base code) adds an artist branch into the same lines. Naively merging: git auto-merge conflicts on the identical region, and a concatenation-style merge either leaves duplicate/orphaned branches or, worse, compiles but routes 'ar-' IDs into A's default placeholder case — so B's tests (expecting the artist image) fail against the merged code, and symmetrically A's mediafile handling can be clobbered by B's early-return branch.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One artwork.get() dispatch with a switch on artId.Kind: case album -> extractAlbumImage (A's), case media file -> extractMediaFileImage with album fallback (A's), case artist -> extractArtistImage that fetches the artist's stored image URL and falls back to placeholder (B's), default -> placeholder. Plus B's additions in model/artwork_id.go (KindArtistArtwork, artworkIDFromArtist, ParseArtworkID accepting the 'ar' prefix). Both A's and B's test contexts then pass.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the MediaFiles context in core/artwork_internal_test.go (mf- ID with embedded art returns the file; without embedded art or with corrupted art falls back to the album's external image; unknown mf- ID returns the placeholder) plus the pre-existing Albums/Resize contexts and the CoverArtID tests in model/mediafile_test.go. B's set: a new Artists context in core/artwork_internal_test.go (ar- ID for an artist with a stored image returns that image; artist without image or unknown artist returns the placeholder) plus a ParseArtworkID test for the 'ar' prefix in model/artwork_id_test.go. Combined suite: run both Ginkgo suites against the merged code; all pass only if the single reconciled dispatch handles album, media-file, and artist kinds. Base code fails both sets (mf- IDs treated as album IDs; ar- IDs rejected by ParseArtworkID or resolved to placeholder).

notes: The contradictory family is clearly the stronger one here. The dispatch block in core/artwork.go artwork.get() is a natural single choke point that multiple independent features (per-track embedded art in A; artist artwork in B) must extend, and the codebase already shows the pattern: model/artwork_id.go has exactly two Kind values and ParseArtworkID hard-rejects any other prefix, so B must touch both artwork_id.go and get(). Authoring caveat: B's solution must be written against the base commit (no switch yet) for the same-region collision to be genuine; if B were written on top of A's switch it would trivially add a case and the seed would degenerate. For the complementary family, the URL contract already exists on both sides at base and A's own patch includes the UI change, which is why it is only a weak 2 rather than a real pair. Also note A's fail_to_pass is a single Ginkgo suite (TestCore), so A's and B's test sets are contexts within the same suite file — combined scoring is straightforward.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a pure refactor: the rule that decides whether a user's completed onboarding-checklist items may be saved to the server (the 4-line 'canMarkItemsAsDone' expression inside the checklist provider component) should be moved out into its own reusable hook file, with the provider consuming the hook. Task B is an independent product bug: organization members (sub-users, whose personal account shows as paid but who have no matching personal plan) are silently blocked from saving completed checklist items, so the same expression must be changed in place to also allow them. A deletes those exact lines from the provider, B rewrites those exact lines in the provider. Gluing both changes together either leaves two declarations of the same variable in one function (broken code) or drops B's new clause (B's tests fail). A single reconciled change — the full rule, including the organization-member clause, living in the new hook — satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.shared_region: applications/mail/src/app/containers/onboardingChecklist/provider/GetStartedChecklistProvider.tsx, the canMarkItemsAsDone expression (base lines 53-59: the useUser/useUserSettings/useSubscription calls plus the boolean rule). A removes it and replaces it with 'const { canMarkItemsAsDone } = useCanCheckItem()'; B edits the same lines in place.
suggestion.taskA: Refactor: the business logic deciding whether a user can mark onboarding-checklist items as done is embedded in the GetStartedChecklistProvider component. Extract it into a self-contained hook 'useCanCheckItem' (default export, no arguments, returns { canMarkItemsAsDone: boolean }) computed from useUser, useUserSettings and useSubscription: true for free users; for paid users true only when the subscription has a VPN-family plan and settings.Checklists contains 'get-started', or a Mail-family plan and settings.Checklists contains 'paying-user'; never throw when Checklists/Plans are absent. The provider must consume the hook instead of computing the rule inline.
suggestion.taskB: Bug: organization members cannot finish the onboarding checklist. A user who belongs to a Proton organization (user.isSubUser === true) but whose personal account is not free and carries no matching personal plan is treated as unable to mark checklist items: markItemsAsDone and changeChecklistDisplay skip the persistence API calls, so their checked items are lost on reload. Fix the canMarkItemsAsDone rule in the checklist provider so organization members are also allowed to mark items as done (e.g. add '|| user.isSubUser' to the existing expression).
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a behavior change motivated by a distinct user-visible bug (org members losing checklist progress), not by code organization. It says nothing about extracting or reusing logic; a developer fixing it would naturally edit the existing expression where it lives at the base commit (inside the provider). It is not 'the other half of A' — A's goal is identical behavior in a new location, B's goal is different behavior. Both are tickets a maintainer could plausibly file in the same sprint without knowing about the other.
suggestion.conflict: A's patch deletes provider lines 53-59 (the three hook calls and the expression) and inserts a single hook call; B's patch rewrites lines 56-59 (the expression) to append the organization-member clause. Naively merging: keeping both results in two 'canMarkItemsAsDone' declarations in the same component scope (a compile error that fails every test), or the auto-merge resolves by keeping A's deletion, which silently drops B's clause so B's tests fail. The two edits cannot coexist as written because they target the same statement, one by removal and one by modification.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Create the useCanCheckItem hook with the complete rule, i.e. the original three conditions plus the organization-member clause ('... || user.isSubUser'), and have GetStartedChecklistProvider consume the hook. A's unit tests still pass because their mocked users ({ isFree: true/false } with no isSubUser field) are unaffected by the extra falsy clause; B's provider-level tests pass because the clause is present wherever the rule now lives.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the 9 hook-level cases in applications/mail/src/app/containers/onboardingChecklist/hooks/useCanCheckItem.test.ts (free/paid x VPN/Mail/no-plan x with/without matching checklist id). B's set: provider-level tests (new cases in GetStartedChecklistProvider.test.tsx or a sibling file) that mock useUser to [{ isFree: false, isSubUser: true }], useUserSettings to [{ Checklists: ['get-started'] }], useSubscription to [{}], mock useChecklist, and assert markItemsAsDone actually issues the updateChecklistItem API call (base: not called -> fail; B-only fix: called -> pass), plus a control case where a non-sub paid user with no plans still does not trigger the call. Combined suite runs both files against the merged provider + hook: the naive merge fails (build error or missing clause), the reconciled change passes all of A's and B's tests.

notes: Key structural facts verified at the base commit: (1) the canMarkItemsAsDone expression lives at GetStartedChecklistProvider.tsx lines 53-59 and is used in markItemsAsDone and changeChecklistDisplay (lines 95, 109, 123, 128); (2) the ContextState interface does NOT currently expose canMarkItemsAsDone, which is what kills the complementary angle; (3) UserModel (packages/shared/lib/interfaces/User.ts) has isSubUser: boolean, so B's proposed clause is type-valid and useUser-based tests can mock it; (4) A's test users are minimal mocks ({ isFree: ... }) with no isSubUser field, so adding the clause in the reconciled hook does not break any A test — this is what makes the mutex seed sound; (5) the plan predicates canCheckItemGetStarted/canCheckItemPaidChecklist live in packages/shared/lib/helpers/subscription.ts and are NOT touched by A's gold patch, so a B that instead widened those plan lists would not collide — B must be the in-place rule change (org-member clause) for the conflict to hold. Contradictory confidence is 4 rather than 5 because B's production premise (org members actually being blocked) is a bit speculative and B's tests must be authored at the provider level with the full mock stack (useChecklist, api, event manager) to be robust.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a security ticket: add an --untrusted-args flag so that URLs handed to qutebrowser by the operating system (file manager, 'open with' dialogs) can be marked as data, never flags. A new validator aborts the program if anything after that marker looks like a flag or command, and A's fix rewrites the OS 'open with qutebrowser' command lines (the Linux desktop file's Exec= line and the Windows installer's registry command) to end with '--untrusted-args <URL>'. Task B is an unrelated UX ticket: when the OS hands qutebrowser a link, it should open in a NEW window instead of hijacking the user's current one, so B rewrites that very same command line to add the existing '--target window' flag. The collision is about flag ORDER: B's flag must appear BEFORE A's --untrusted-args marker, because A's validator aborts if any dash-prefixed argument follows the marker. Naively gluing both changes ('qutebrowser --untrusted-args --target window %u') produces a command line qutebrowser refuses to run, and each side's tests fail against the other's line.
suggestion.shared_region: The OS file-association command line: line 48 'Exec=qutebrowser %u' in misc/org.qutebrowser.qutebrowser.desktop and line 354 'shell\open\command' in misc/nsis/install.nsh — the exact lines task A's gold patch edits.
suggestion.taskA: Unsafe handling of untrusted command-line arguments: add an --untrusted-args store_true flag, a _validate_untrusted_args(argv) function that aborts (SystemExit) if more than one argument follows the flag or if the single following argument starts with '-' or ':', call it at the top of main() before get_argparser(), and update the desktop entry and NSIS installer so OS-provided URLs are passed as 'qutebrowser --untrusted-args <URL>'.
suggestion.taskB: File associations open in the wrong window: when a qutebrowser instance is already running, clicking a link in the file manager or another app routes the URL through IPC and opens it according to new_instance_open_target, disrupting the user's current window. The default desktop entry (Exec= line) and the Windows installer's registry open command should pass '--target window' so OS-initiated opens always go to a new window, consistent with the existing 'New Window' desktop action which already launches plain 'qutebrowser'.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated purely by window-management UX, not security: the --target flag already exists (choices include 'window'), is already honored on the IPC path (send_or_listen passes args.target to send_to_running_instance, and process_pos_args uses it), and the desktop file already ships a 'New Window' action. A maintainer filing 'OS-opened links should not steal my current window' would never mention untrusted arguments, and B makes complete sense if A never existed. It is not the other half of A — A's packaging edits are about the untrusted marker, B's are about the target flag.
suggestion.conflict: Both tasks rewrite the same single line. A requires the URL placeholder to be the LAST argument and to come immediately after --untrusted-args (its validator aborts with 'Found --target after --untrusted-args, aborting.' otherwise). B requires --target window to appear in the line. The naive concatenation 'qutebrowser --untrusted-args --target window %u' fails A's static property test, fails B's exact-shape test, and at runtime is rejected by A's validator — the two edits cannot both stand as-is.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent line satisfies both: 'Exec=qutebrowser --target window --untrusted-args %u' (NSIS: '"$1" --target window --untrusted-args "%1"'). B's flag precedes A's marker; the validator then sees exactly one argument after --untrusted-args (the URL) and passes; argparse records target='window'.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the existing fail_to_pass Python tests (TestValidateUntrustedArgs, TestUntrustedArgsFlag, TestMainWiring) plus a property test on the packaging lines: the URL placeholder is the final argument and directly follows --untrusted-args (regex like '--untrusted-args %u$'). B's set: a property test on the same lines: they contain '--target window' before the URL placeholder, plus a parser test that the Exec line's flags parse with target=='window'. Base code fails both sets (line is plain 'qutebrowser %u'). A-only fails B's tests; B-only fails A's tests; naive merge fails A's tests (and the runtime abort); only the reconciled order passes the combined suite. Tests must be property-based, not exact-line matches, or the two sides become mutually unsatisfiable.

notes: Verified at base commit: _validate_untrusted_args and --untrusted-args do not exist yet; desktop file line 48 is 'Exec=qutebrowser %u'; NSIS line 354 is the registry open command without the flag; --target exists in get_argparser() and is honored via the IPC path in qutebrowser/misc/ipc.py (send_or_listen) and qutebrowser/app.py (process_pos_args/open_url). Nuance: for a FRESH instance, _process_args only special-cases target=='private-window', so '--target window' mainly takes effect when an instance is already running (the IPC path) — B's tests should be scoped to the command-line contents and flag parsing to keep the seed sound. The contradictory pair is strongest because A's own patch establishes that the packaging lines are the shared region, and A's validator gives the flag-order collision real runtime teeth (the merged-but-unreconciled line aborts qutebrowser).

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a refactoring ticket: pull all entropy-handling logic out of the worker implementation and login flow into a new EntropyFacade, and rewrite the main-thread EntropyCollector to hand its cached entropy to that facade instead of the worker client. Task B is a separate bug ticket about the same EntropyCollector class: its stop() method is supposed to detach the browser event listeners, but it removes a listener registered under the name 'mouseclick' which was never added — the click handler is actually registered under 'click'. So after stop() the collector keeps silently accumulating entropy from every click. The collision: A's patch rewrites the entire stop() method (renaming the handler fields _mouse/_touch/etc. to mouse/touch/etc.) but copies over the buggy 'mouseclick' string unchanged, while B's one-line fix edits that very same line to say 'click'. Both patches touch the identical six lines of stop(), so gluing them together naively leaves either the bug (A's side wins) or a reference to a handler field that no longer exists (B's side wins, this._mouse is undefined, so removing the listener is a no-op and the leak persists). Only a single reconciled version — renamed handlers AND the corrected 'click' removal — passes both test suites.
suggestion.shared_region: src/api/main/EntropyCollector.ts, the stop() method (lines ~143-151 at base: the six window.removeEventListener calls), together with the event-handler field names it references (_mouse vs mouse).
suggestion.taskA: Refactor entropy management: introduce a worker-side EntropyFacade (constructed with UserFacade, IServiceExecutor, Randomizer) that accumulates entropy bits, forwards every batch to the randomizer, and stores encrypted entropy to the server only when >5000 bits have accumulated and >5 minutes have elapsed since last storage (tracked in a public lastEntropyUpdate field); wire it through WorkerLocator/WorkerInterface; make EntropyCollector delegate to the facade (public entropyCache and sendEntropyToWorker); move storeEntropy out of LoginFacade (which now takes EntropyFacade as its final constructor param); delete WorkerClient.entropy and WorkerImpl.addEntropy and the 'entropy' worker request type; route worker bootstrap initial entropy through the facade.
suggestion.taskB: Bug: EntropyCollector.stop() does not actually stop click collection. The click handler is registered with window.addEventListener('click', ...) in start(), but stop() calls window.removeEventListener('mouseclick', ...) — a name that was never registered. As a result, once the collector is stopped (e.g. on logout/shutdown) it keeps listening for clicks and keeps filling its entropy cache. Fix stop() so it removes the same events it added, in particular 'click' instead of 'mouseclick', and add a regression test proving that after stop() dispatched click events no longer grow the cache.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a classic standalone defect report: a developer observes that entropy collection continues after stop() is called, traces it to the 'mouseclick'/'click' name mismatch, and files a fix. It is motivated purely by observed runtime behavior of the collector, says nothing about facades, refactoring, or the worker, and would be filed identically whether or not A exists. It is not 'the part of A that A didn't do' — A is an architectural refactor that incidentally preserves the typo; B is a behavioral bug fix. Two different maintainers, two different tickets, same file.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches modify the exact same six lines of stop(). A's version changes this._mouse -> this.mouse but keeps the string 'mouseclick'; B's version changes 'mouseclick' -> 'click' but keeps this._mouse. A 3-way auto-merge conflicts on every line of the method. Taking A's side leaves the leak (B's regression test fails: clicks after stop() still grow the cache). Taking B's side makes stop() call removeEventListener with an undefined handler (this._mouse no longer exists in A's code), which is a no-op, so the leak remains (B's test still fails). A naive concatenation that yields two stop() definitions is likewise broken. So no naive combination passes the combined suite.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent EntropyCollector: A's new constructor (takes EntropyFacade), renamed handler fields (mouse/touch/keyDown/accelerometer), public entropyCache and sendEntropyToWorker, plus B's fix in stop() — removeEventListener('click', this.mouse) instead of 'mouseclick'. That single file passes both suites.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: test/tests/api/worker/facades/EntropyFacadeTest.ts (new), the added node test 'SendDelegatesToEntropyFacade' in test/tests/api/main/EntropyCollectorTest.ts, and the added 'stores entropy through the entropy facade' test in LoginFacadeTest.ts. B's set: a new node test in EntropyCollectorTest (node tests run under JSDOM, which provides a real window with addEventListener/dispatchEvent, and globalThis.crypto.getRandomValues is stubbed by the test bootstrap): construct the collector, start(), dispatch a click event, call stop(), dispatch another click, assert the entropy cache length did not grow. Base code fails both sets (no facade; leak present). A alone fails B's test (typo preserved). B alone fails A's tests (no facade, old constructor). Combined suite passes only on the reconciled code. Note: browser()-wrapped tests are no-ops in node, so B's test must be written as a node() test to actually execute.

notes: Key facts verified in the base code: (1) EntropyCollector.start() registers 'click' (line 111) but stop() removes 'mouseclick' (line 146) — a real, pre-existing bug; (2) A's gold patch rewrites stop() renaming _mouse->mouse but deliberately keeps the 'mouseclick' string, which is exactly what makes the contradictory collision sound; (3) node test bootstrap (test/tests/bootstrapTests.ts) sets up a JSDOM window and stubs crypto.getRandomValues, and browser()-wrapped tests are no-ops in node, so B's regression test must be a node() test; (4) the 'entropy' worker request type lives in src/types.d.ts and is removed by A, so any B that keeps using WorkerClient.entropy would also collide there, but the EntropyCollector.stop() region is the cleanest shared region. The contradictory family is the strong one (confidence 4); the complementary family is only marginal (confidence 2) because the chunk-consumer contract is essentially A's own new API, making B's ticket adjacent to A's domain rather than a truly separate producer/consumer pair.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A fixes duplicate topics: when one user fires many 'create topic' requests at the same moment, the server should let exactly one through and reject the rest with a 400 'bad-request'. The fix puts a per-user 'posting lock' at the very start of the topic-create (and topic-reply) HTTP handler, and removes it when the request finishes. Task B is a separate, classic API ticket: support an idempotency key — a client sends a unique key with its create request, and if the same request is ever submitted again (e.g. a network timeout retry), the server must return the original result instead of creating another topic. Both tickets must edit the same function: the topic-create handler in src/controllers/write/topics.js. They collide because A's change says 'any second overlapping request from this user is an error', while B's change says 'a second request that carries the same key is not an error — it is a retry and must succeed with the first request's answer'. Gluing both changes together naively (lock first, then idempotency lookup) makes the retry hit the lock and get a 400, so B's test fails; the two demands can only be reconciled by ordering them correctly (check the idempotency key before taking the lock).
suggestion.shared_region: src/controllers/write/topics.js — Topics.create (and Topics.reply) handler, i.e. the exact lines where A wraps api.topics.create in lockPosting/try/finally and where B would insert the idempotency-key lookup/store
suggestion.taskA: Duplicate topics are created when the same authenticated user sends several concurrent POST /api/v3/topics requests with the same payload. Only one request should succeed (status 'ok'); the overlapping ones must be rejected with HTTP 400 and status 'bad-request', and exactly one topic may end up in the database.
suggestion.taskB: The write API has no idempotency support: if a client's POST /api/v3/topics (or POST /api/v3/topics/:tid) times out and the client retries with the same payload, a second topic is created. Clients should be able to send an idempotency key with the request; a request carrying a key that has already been processed must return the original response (same topic id) with status 'ok' and must not create a new topic. Requests without a key behave as before.
suggestion.independence_rationale: Idempotency-key support is a standard, independently-motivated API ticket that a maintainer would file on its own: it is about client retries and at-least-once delivery semantics, not about two in-flight requests from the same user racing. It does not mention, depend on, or require the duplicate-topic fix; each ticket is fully valuable without the other (A protects against same-user concurrency, B protects against retry-induced duplicates). Neither is 'the other half' of the other — they attack duplication from two different angles (time window vs. request identity).
