suggestion.conflict: A's solution makes the handler acquire a per-user lock at the top and throw a 400 'already-posting' for any overlapping request; B's solution makes the handler recognize a repeated idempotency key and answer it successfully with the stored first response. In a naive merge, B's retried request still collides with A's lock (the first request holds the lock while the retry arrives, or the lock field is checked before the idempotency key), so the retry gets 'bad-request' instead of the original 'ok' response — B's test fails, and A's blanket rejection contradicts B's 'same key must be accepted' rule in the same lines of the same function.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent handler: (1) if the request carries an idempotency key and a stored response for that key exists, return the stored response immediately without touching the lock; (2) otherwise acquire A's per-user posting lock (reject with 400 if already held); (3) create the topic; (4) if a key was supplied, store the response under that key; (5) release the lock in a finally block. This keeps A's guarantee (one in-flight create per user) and B's guarantee (a keyed retry never duplicates).
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the fail_to_pass tests from test/user.js — 'should only post 1 topic out of 10' (10 concurrent unkeyed POSTs → exactly 1 'ok', 9 'bad-request') plus the unread-count tests that assert exactly one extra topic exists. B's set: a new test that POSTs /api/v3/topics with idempotency key K, then POSTs again (sequentially, so no lock overlap) with the same key K and asserts status 'ok' with the identical topic id and that the topic count did not increase. Combined suite: base code fails both sets; A-only and B-only each pass their own set; the naive merge (lock before key-check) fails B's test; the reconciled ordering passes everything.

notes: Exploration findings: A's gold patch edits only src/controllers/write/topics.js (Topics.create/Topics.reply + new lockPosting helper) and adds one string to public/language/en-GB/error.json. The codebase already uses the same db.incrObjectField('locks', ...) pattern in src/user/create.js (username/email registration lock) and src/api/users.js (export lock), which makes the idempotency-key task B a believable, pattern-consistent standalone ticket that lands in the exact same handler A rewrites. The contradictory pair is real but needs authoring work: B's test must use sequential (not concurrent) keyed retries so the only failure mode is A's lock, and the reconciliation (key-check before lock) is a genuine semantic ordering, not a cosmetic merge. The fail_to_pass list also includes two unread-count tests (3→4) that simply account for the one extra topic the new A-test creates; they are part of A's suite, not evidence for B. Complementary family is weak: A adds no contract for another task to implement against, and the post-queue path (which A's lock deliberately does not cover, since queued posts return 202) would only support a decomposition-flavored B ('also dedupe queued posts'), so I marked it not viable.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A hardens the 'list recent chats' API method: it must reject calls that carry no pagination info at all (no start, no stop, no page) with a clear invalid-data error, instead of crashing. Task B is the v4 cleanup of the same method: the code still contains a block that accepts the old, deprecated pagination style (page number + perPage) and silently converts it into start/stop, printing a warning that says these parameters 'will be removed in v4'. B's ticket is to finish that removal. Both tickets must edit the very same few lines of the same function — A wants to keep the old 'page' parameter alive (so a page-only call is treated as valid and must NOT be rejected), while B wants to delete the code that makes 'page' mean anything. Glue the two changes together naively and the function either still honors the deprecated parameters (B's tests fail) or rejects page-only calls (A's tests fail); only a single reconciled edit — validation that accepts page as 'data present' plus deletion of the conversion block — satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: src/api/chats.js, chatsAPI.list — the deprecation block at base lines 40-44 ('if (!start && !stop && page) { winston.warn(...deprecated...); start = ...; stop = ...; }') and the function signature line 39. A inserts its 'if (!start && !stop && !page) throw invalid-data' guard directly above/around this block and must keep 'page' in the guard; B deletes the block itself.
suggestion.taskA: Original ticket: chats/users API endpoints do not consistently validate missing or malformed input. api.chats.getRawMessage must fail with [[error:invalid-data]] when mid or roomId is missing; api.chats.list must fail with [[error:invalid-data]] when the payload is omitted or none of start/stop/page is supplied (never a runtime destructuring error); api.users.getPrivateRoomId must fail with [[error:invalid-data]] when uid is missing. Valid calls must return correct data, recent-chat teasers must be escaped, and user status must round-trip (e.g. 'dnd').
suggestion.taskB: v4 cleanup ticket: the chat list API still honors the deprecated 'page'/'perPage' pagination style. The deprecation warning in src/api/chats.js literally says 'The deprecated parameters will be removed in v4'. Finish the removal: api.chats.list should accept only start/stop, delete the winston.warn deprecation block and its page->start/stop conversion, and callers passing page/perPage should no longer get them silently converted (the web controller src/controllers/write/chats.js and the socket shim src/socket.io/modules.js already send start/stop, so nothing internal depends on the old path).
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated entirely by the deprecation cycle already present in the code (the warning string, the v4 note at the top of socket.io/modules.js, and the fact that both in-repo callers already use start/stop). A maintainer planning v4 would file 'remove deprecated pagination params from api.chats.list' without ever touching the validation-hardening ticket A. B's goal (removing a deprecated input path) is orthogonal to A's goal (failing fast on missing input); B is not a step toward A and A is not a step toward B.
suggestion.conflict: The two edits occupy the same lines and make opposite demands about the 'page' parameter. A's guard must be '!start && !stop && !page' — i.e. page-only input is valid and must not throw — which only makes sense while page is still a recognized pagination field. B deletes the only code that gives page meaning. Naive merge (A's guard prepended + B's block deleted) still passes A's listed tests but breaks B's; the more likely naive auto-merge (A's guard plus the deprecation block left in place, or duplicated/overlapping hunks) breaks B's tests because page-only calls are still converted and honored. Either way the combined suite fails until someone reconciles.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Single edit to chatsAPI.list: signature '(caller, { uid = caller.uid, start, stop, page, perPage } = {})'; keep the guard 'if (!start && !stop && !page) throw new Error("[[error:invalid-data]]")' (page counts as supplied data, so A's page-related tests hold); delete the entire winston.warn deprecation block (B's goal). A page-only call then validates and falls through to messaging.getRecentChats with undefined start/stop (a full-range read, no crash, no conversion), and a start/stop call behaves exactly as before.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the four fail_to_pass tests in test/messaging.js (invalid-data for getRawMessage with undefined/{} and with mid-but-no-roomId; invalid-data for list with undefined, {start:null}, {start:0,uid:null}; invalid-data for getPrivateRoomId with undefined payload; plus the status/teaser/private-room positive tests). B's set: new tests asserting api.chats.list(caller, {start, stop}) returns the expected rooms slice, and that api.chats.list(caller, {page: 2, perPage: 20}) does NOT apply the old conversion (no winston deprecation path, page ignored) while still returning a valid rooms array. Combined suite: base code fails both sets (no validation for A; deprecated block still honored for B); A-alone passes A's tests but fails B's (page still converted); B-alone passes B's tests but fails A's (no invalid-data guard); only the reconciled function passes everything.

notes: Base-commit facts verified: src/api/chats.js line 39-47 contains chatsAPI.list with the winston.warn deprecation block for page/perPage ('will be removed in v4'); both in-repo callers (src/controllers/write/chats.js Chats.list, src/socket.io/modules.js SocketModules.chats.getRecentChats) already pass start/stop, so removing the deprecated path is a real, self-motivated v4 cleanup ticket. The collision is real but narrow: it hinges on A's guard needing '!page' (page = valid input) while B deletes page's meaning; the reconciled function keeps the guard and drops the block. Confidence capped at 3 because B's test set must be authored carefully (assert page is ignored, not that it errors) and the deprecation block is small. The complementary family is weak: A changes no interface and all consumers pre-exist, so any B there reads as decomposition.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a bug report: when a regular user edits their topic, a system tag that an admin added earlier silently disappears, because the tag-validation code treats every submitted tag as 'newly added' and rejects any that is a system tag. Task A's fix makes the validator aware of the topic's existing tags so that keeping a system tag during an edit is allowed. Task B is a different complaint from a moderator's point of view: a regular user can deliberately strip a system tag off a topic just by editing, and the forum should reject that edit with a clear error instead of silently letting it happen. Both fixes must rewrite the same system-tag check inside the same validation function, and both must change the same edit call site to pass the topic id in — so two agents working independently collide on the same lines.
suggestion.shared_region: src/topics/tags.js, Topics.validateTags (lines ~65-84: the function signature, the Promise.all that fetches category data/privileges, and the systemTags check at lines 80-83), plus the call site at src/posts/edit.js line 132 (await topics.validateTags(...))
suggestion.taskA: Bug: 'System tags disappear when regular user edits their post.' Steps: configure system tags; user creates a topic with normal tags; admin adds a system tag; user edits the topic (reordering/adding normal tags only). Expected: the system tag is still present after the edit. Actual: it is removed, because validation rejects the edit or the tag is dropped. The fix must make tag validation compare submitted tags against the topic's current tags on edit (treating current tags as empty on create) so existing system tags are not treated as newly added.
suggestion.taskB: Bug/feature: 'Regular users can remove system tags from topics by editing.' A moderator reports that a regular user edited a topic and deleted the 'moved' system tag that the staff had applied, with no error and no trace. Request: when a non-privileged user's edit would remove a tag listed in the system-tags setting, reject the edit with a dedicated error message (e.g. 'You can not remove this system tag'), while privileged users keep full control. This is a deliberate-removal guard, distinct from A's accidental-loss preservation.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a plausible standalone ticket: it is filed from a different persona (moderator protecting staff-applied tags) and demands a different observable behavior (an edit that removes a system tag must FAIL with an error), whereas A's reporter wants an edit that keeps the system tag to SUCCEED. Neither ticket mentions the other; a maintainer could file B on its own against the base code (where removal is silently possible) and A on its own (where preservation is broken). Caveat: the official gold patch happens to implement both behaviors, which is why B is not a 4-5 confidence independent pair — B's solution must be authored as its own minimal patch (add tid awareness + removedTags check, leaving the base 'all submitted tags are new' check untouched) rather than taken from A's diff.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches rewrite the same lines of Topics.validateTags: the signature (adding a tid parameter), the Promise.all block (loading the topic's current tags), and the systemTags check. A's version changes the check to only inspect newly-added tags; B's version adds a check over removed tags. Naively gluing the two changes together duplicates declarations (two `const systemTags`, two current-tag loads, two signature edits) or leaves two incompatible versions of the check in one function, producing broken code that fails the combined suite. The src/posts/edit.js call site is also edited by both to pass tid.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent validateTags(tags, cid, uid, tid = null): load current tags when tid is given (empty on create), compute addedTags = submitted minus current and removedTags = current minus submitted, keep minTags/maxTags checks, throw cant-use-system-tag for non-privileged users adding system tags, and throw cant-remove-system-tag for non-privileged users removing them. Pass tid from posts/edit.js. This is exactly the shape of the gold patch and satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the fail_to_pass test 'Topic's tags should not error if regular user edits topic after admin adds system tags' (admin adds system tag, regular user edits keeping it, edit succeeds, tag preserved) plus the existing system-tag tests (regular user cannot add system tag on create; admin can). B's set: a new test where an admin adds a system tag to a topic, then a regular user edits the topic with a tag list that omits it, and the edit must reject with the cant-remove-system-tag error (and a privileged user's removal must succeed). Combined suite: run both against the merged code — base fails both; A-only passes A but not B (removal still silently succeeds); B-only passes B but not A (preserving edit still errors); naive merge breaks; only the reconciled function passes everything.

notes: Key observation: the official gold patch already contains both behaviors (preserve-on-edit AND reject-removal via cant-remove-system-tag, plus a dangling SocketTopics.canRemoveTag with no client caller). This makes the contradictory pair the natural fit but caps confidence at 3, because B's solution must be authored independently (minimal removedTags check without adopting A's addedTags semantics) for the naive-merge-fails condition to hold. The textual collision is real and localized to Topics.validateTags (src/topics/tags.js lines 65-84) and the validateTags call in src/posts/edit.js line 132. Complementary is weak: no second consumer of the new tid parameter exists (create and queue paths are create-only), and the client-side consumer of canRemoveTag is absent from the repo. Base-code sanity verified: validateTags currently throws cant-use-system-tag for ANY submitted system tag by non-privileged users (so A's test fails), and has no removal check at all (so B's test fails).

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A asks that the 'does this name belong to a user or a group?' check (meta.userOrGroupExists) accept a whole list of names at once and answer one yes/no per name, in order. Task B is a separate, real bug: the same check says 'no' for the built-in pseudo-groups 'guests' and 'spiders', even though the rest of the forum treats them as real groups (membership, privileges, and the Groups.exists() function all recognize them). Because of that, a new user can register with the username 'guests' or 'spiders', colliding with a group name. Both tickets force edits to the exact same function body in src/meta/index.js: A rewrites its input-validation and name-normalization lines to handle lists, while B has to insert an extra 'is this one of the built-in pseudo-groups?' check into those same lines. Two developers editing the same ~10 lines for different reasons will produce two versions that cannot simply be stacked: the B-only version still breaks list input, and the A-only version still misses the pseudo-groups, so a naive merge fails at least one side's tests.
suggestion.shared_region: Meta.userOrGroupExists in src/meta/index.js (lines 29-41 at base: the falsy-input validation, the slugify normalization line, and the return line). Task A rewrites all of these for array support; Task B must modify the same normalization/return region to add the ephemeral-group ('guests'/'spiders') check.
suggestion.taskA: Support array input in meta.userOrGroupExists: a single slug still resolves to a boolean; an array of slugs resolves to an array of booleans, one per input, in input order; each element is normalized to canonical slug form and checked against both the user and group namespaces; any falsy element (or falsy single input) rejects with the error message '[[error:invalid-data]]'.
suggestion.taskB: meta.userOrGroupExists returns false for the built-in pseudo-groups 'guests' and 'spiders', but these are real groups everywhere else: Groups.exists('guests') is true, Groups.isMember(0, 'guests') is true, and privileges are granted to them by name. Consequence: User.uniqueUsername() (which relies on meta.userOrGroupExists) happily hands out the username 'guests' or 'spiders', colliding with a group name. Fix: userOrGroupExists must report true for slugs that are members of Groups.ephemeralGroups, in addition to existing users and stored groups.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by a genuine inconsistency that exists at the base commit and is unrelated to batch lookups: Groups.exists() (src/groups/index.js lines 245-256) explicitly ORs in Groups.ephemeralGroups, while Groups.existsBySlug() and therefore meta.userOrGroupExists() do not. A maintainer filing 'username registration can collide with the guests/spiders group names' would never mention array support; the two tickets come from different bug reports (batch API ergonomics vs. a name-collision bug) and different symptoms.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches rewrite the same 4-6 lines of Meta.userOrGroupExists. A's version replaces 'if (!slug) throw' and 'slug = slugify(slug)' with array-aware validation ('(isArray && slug.some(...)) || (!isArray && !slug)') and 'slug = isArray ? slug.map(s => slugify(s, false)) : slugify(slug)'. B's version keeps the single-slug shape but must add an ephemeral check, e.g. 'slug = slugify(slug); if (Groups.ephemeralGroups.includes(slug)) return true;' or fold it into the return. Gluing the two changes together either leaves B's ephemeral check operating on a (possibly array) slug with the wrong shape, double-normalizes, or breaks A's array return path — the combined suite then fails on either A's array assertions or B's ephemeral assertions. They cannot both stand as written.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent implementation: detect array input; reject on any falsy element (or falsy single) with '[[error:invalid-data]]'; normalize each element with slugify(s, false); await user.existsBySlug and groups.existsBySlug (both array-capable); compute per-slug existence as userExists[i] || groupExists[i] || Groups.ephemeralGroups.includes(s); return the boolean array for array input, or a single boolean (with the same ephemeral check) for single input. This passes A's tests and B's tests together.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the fail_to_pass test 'test/user.js | User socket methods should return true/false if user/group exists or not' (single-slug true/false, mixed array results, order preservation, rejects on ['' , undefined]). B's set: a new test in test/groups.js or test/user.js asserting await meta.userOrGroupExists('guests') === true, await meta.userOrGroupExists('spiders') === true, and that User.uniqueUsername({username: 'guests'}) resolves to null (name already taken). Base code fails both sets (no array support; ephemeral slugs report false). A's gold patch passes A's set only; B's standalone fix passes B's set only. A naive merge of the two independent patches fails the combined suite; the reconciled single change passes all of it.

notes: Key structural facts verified at base commit be86d8ef: (1) Meta.userOrGroupExists (src/meta/index.js:29-41) is single-slug only and throws '[[error:invalid-data]]' on falsy input; (2) User.existsBySlug (src/user/index.js:52-55) is single-slug only, while its sibling Groups.existsBySlug (src/groups/index.js:258-263) already supports arrays — the codebase has an established 'accept string or array' idiom (see User.exists, Groups.exists), which is what makes A's ticket idiomatic; (3) Groups.exists() (src/groups/index.js:245-256) ORs in Groups.ephemeralGroups = ['guests','spiders'], but Groups.existsBySlug() does not, and 'guests'/'spiders' are never stored in groups:createtime or groupslug:groupname (install only creates verified/unverified/banned users groups, Global Moderators, and the admin's groups), so meta.userOrGroupExists('guests') is genuinely false at base — a real, independently-fileable bug; (4) User.uniqueUsername (src/user/create.js:182-194) depends on meta.userOrGroupExists, giving B a concrete user-visible symptom (username 'guests' registrable). Contradictory confidence is 3 rather than higher because the collision is 'same function edited for two different reasons' rather than 'two mutually exclusive behaviors on the same line' — the naive-merge failure is semantic (array path vs. ephemeral check in the same normalization/return lines) and a lazy auto-merge could in principle produce code that happens to pass, so the authoring step should pin B's fix to the slugify/return lines of Meta.userOrGroupExists specifically. The complementary family does not hold: A's array plumbing is self-contained and its only consumer is A itself.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A rewrites the WebFinger endpoint so that a query for the site's own hostname resolves to the 'instance actor': it inserts a special case right after the user lookup and replaces the single flat response object with two branches (one for a real user, one for the instance). An independent task B would ask for the WebFinger response to also include the subject's public key (as Mastodon does, and as NodeBB's own internal WebFinger client already expects to read from the response body). B's edit adds a field to that same flat response object that A deletes and splits into branches. Two agents working blindly produce a file where the key is added to an object that no longer exists (or the object is declared twice), which is broken; only someone who reconciles the two — keeping A's branching and putting the public key in both branches — gets a working endpoint that satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.shared_region: src/controllers/well-known.js, Controller.webfinger — the uid-resolution block (lines ~26-29) and especially the response-object construction (lines ~31-49), which A restructures into if/else branches while B adds a publicKey field to the original flat object
suggestion.taskA: Proper WebFinger Response for Instance Actor: /.well-known/webfinger must resolve a resource whose slug equals the instance hostname to the instance actor (uid 0), returning 200 with subject acct:{slug}@{host}, aliases containing the base site URL, and a self link {rel:'self', type:'application/activity+json', href:<base URL>}; the Application actor's preferredUsername must equal the hostname. Non-existent user slugs still 404, malformed resources still 400.
suggestion.taskB: WebFinger responses should include the subject's public key: the /.well-known/webfinger endpoint currently returns only subject, aliases, and links. The ActivityPub ecosystem (e.g. Mastodon) includes the subject's publicKey (id, owner, publicKeyPem) in the WebFinger document so peers can verify signatures without a second fetch. NodeBB's own WebFinger client (activitypub.helpers.query) already destructures publicKey from the response body and caches it, but it is always undefined today. Add the resolved subject's public key to the WebFinger response.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by WebFinger spec compliance and by a real consumer already present in the codebase (src/activitypub/helpers.js line 60: `const { publicKey } = body;` cached in webfingerCache). It says nothing about the instance actor, about hostnames, or about A's discovery goal — it applies to every WebFinger response, user or instance. A maintainer would file it as 'our WebFinger documents are missing publicKey that our own federation client expects'.
suggestion.conflict: A's patch replaces the entire flat `const response = { subject, aliases, links }` literal with a conditionally-built object (user branch vs instance branch) and inserts `if (slug === hostname) uid = 0` into the resolution block. B's patch adds `publicKey: ...` inside the original flat literal (and needs `activitypub.getPublicKey(uid)` in scope). Naively gluing the two changes yields either a duplicate `const response` declaration, a publicKey line attached to a deleted object, or a missing publicKey in one branch — the combined suite fails.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent Controller.webfinger: resolve uid (hostname slug -> 0, missing user -> 404), then build the response with subject always, aliases/links chosen by branch as A specifies, and `publicKey: await activitypub.getPublicKey(uid || 0)` present in both branches (uid 0 keys already exist via activitypub.getPublicKey(0)).
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the two fail_to_pass tests in test/activitypub.js ('Instance Actor endpoint should return a valid ActivityPub Actor JSON-LD payload' asserting preferredUsername === hostname, and 'should also have a valid WebFinger response tied to preferredUsername') plus the pre-existing WebFinger user/404/400/403 tests. B's set: new tests asserting a user WebFinger body contains publicKey with id/owner/publicKeyPem equal to activitypub.getPublicKey(uid), and that the instance WebFinger body contains the uid-0 key. Combined suite runs both against the merged code: base fails both sets; A-alone and B-alone each pass only their own set; the naive merge fails (broken object/duplicate declaration or missing key in a branch); the reconciled version passes everything.

notes: Key facts verified at base commit: (1) src/controllers/well-known.js builds one flat response object (lines 31-49) and returns 404 for any slug without a user — A restructures exactly this region, making it the natural shared region for the contradictory seed. (2) src/activitypub/helpers.js line 60 already reads `const { publicKey } = body;` from WebFinger responses and caches it, giving the contradictory task B a genuine in-codebase consumer hook rather than an invented one. (3) helpers.resolveLocalUid (line 87) and inbox.follow (line 38-43) reject uid 0 (`if (!localUid) throw`), so the complementary consumer-side ticket B is real and currently broken for the instance actor. (4) Caveat for the complementary pair: B's ticket is adjacent to A's overall federation goal, though it operates on the receive side in files A never touches; if a stricter independence bar is applied, the contradictory pair (publicKey in WebFinger) is the cleaner split since B's motivation is spec compliance + the existing client code. (5) The test file test/activitypub.js has an empty 'Helpers .query()' describe block, a natural home for B's tests. (6) meta.config.site_title referenced in A's test patch is not set anywhere in src at this commit — tests rely on the `|| 'NodeBB'` fallback, which is fine but worth knowing when authoring.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A changes how 'copy privileges from category X to category Y' decides WHICH privileges to copy: today the admin UI sends a numeric column range (e.g. 'copy columns 6 through 15') and the server slices the privilege list by position; A replaces that with a privilege-type string (e.g. 'copy only viewing privileges') and rewrites the function body that computes the list to copy. An independent Task B reports that when an admin copies a GROUP's privileges between categories, the individual per-user overrides set in the source category are silently dropped, and fixes the same function so that, in addition to the group's privileges, the corresponding per-user privileges are copied too. Both rewrites happen in the same if/else block of the same function, and they cannot both stand: one replaces the position-based list computation with a type-based one, the other builds its extra user-privilege list off the position-based group list, so gluing the two patches together yields code where either the type filter is ignored (numeric slice of a string) or the user propagation is lost.
suggestion.shared_region: src/categories/create.js — Categories.copyPrivilegesFrom (the `if (group) {...} else {...}` block that derives `privsToCopy` and dispatches to copyPrivileges/copyPrivilegesByGroup), reached from src/socket.io/admin/categories.js
suggestion.taskA: Privileges do not declare their type, so nothing that exposes them can tell one kind from another: the privilege maps carry no type, the ACP responses and rendered cells have no type information, and copying privileges between categories is driven by fragile numeric column ranges over the privilege list, so adding or reordering a privilege silently changes what a copy covers. Fix: declare a type (viewing/posting/moderation/other/admin) for every privilege, expose getType/getPrivilegesByFilter, add labelData and per-entry types to the privilege list payloads, render a data-type attribute in the privilege cells, and make copyPrivilegesFrom accept a privilege-type string filter instead of a numeric range.
suggestion.taskB: Copying a group's category privileges to another category drops individual user-level overrides: an admin grants/revokes per-user privileges in the source category, uses 'copy group privileges from category', and the destination category only receives the group grants — the user exceptions are lost and users end up with different effective permissions than in the source. Fix copyPrivilegesFrom so that when a specific group is copied, the matching per-user privileges for that same set of privileges are copied as well (grant where the source user had it, rescind where the source user did not), mirroring what the group-level copy does.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a data-loss bug report about the group-copy workflow's handling of user overrides — a completely different symptom (missing user grants after a copy) from A's (position-based filter fragility and missing type metadata). A maintainer triaging 'user exceptions lost after copy group privileges' would never mention privilege types or the ACP table rendering; the ticket stands on its own and its fix (propagating user-level privileges during group copy) has value even if A's type system never existed.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches rewrite the same if/else block in Categories.copyPrivilegesFrom. A's version derives the list via privileges.categories.getPrivilegesByFilter(filter) where filter is a type string, and maps it to groups:-prefixed names when a group is given. B's version keeps the position-based getGroupPrivilegeList().slice(...filter) (filter is a numeric range) and additionally derives a user-level list from it to copy alongside. Naively merged, the function either slices a string (TypeError/empty list) or applies B's user propagation to A's type-filtered list with B's numeric-range assumption — A's 'copy only matching type' test and B's 'user overrides are copied' test cannot both pass on the naive combination.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent copyPrivilegesFrom: compute the base list with getPrivilegesByFilter(typeFilter) (all privileges when falsy), map to groups:-prefixed names when a group is targeted, and — for the group case — also copy the corresponding bare (user) privilege names using the same give/rescind-by-group machinery, so type filtering and user-override propagation compose.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: test/privileges.js (type declarations, getPrivilegesByFilter, labelData/types payloads, 'should copy only privileges whose type matches the filter when copying between categories') plus test/template-helpers.js 'should spawn privilege states'. B's set: a new test in test/categories.js style — grant group + individual user privileges in fromCid, call socketCategories.copyPrivilegesFrom with a group, assert the user's matching privileges now exist in toCid (and non-matching user privileges do not). Combined suite passes only on the reconciled function; base fails both sets; each solution alone passes only its own set.

notes: Explored at base commit c1f873b. Key facts: (1) copyPrivilegesFrom in src/categories/create.js (lines 216-239) is the one server function whose body A rewrites (filter semantics) and which is also the natural home of an independent 'user overrides lost on group copy' fix — this is the strongest contradictory region. (2) An alternative contradictory B — 'add a new core category privilege (e.g. topics:pin)' — also collides with A on the _privilegeMap in src/privileges/categories.js and on the data-filter buttons in src/views/admin/partials/privileges/{category,global}.tpl (A changes them from numeric ranges to type strings; B must shift the ranges), BUT it is UNSOUND: A's fail_to_pass tests hard-code the exact 16-privilege insertion order and labelData[13].type, so any reconciled code containing a 17th core privilege fails A's own tests; the two suites are mutually exclusive, not reconcilable. (3) The 'other' filter button only renders when columnCountUserOther > 0, so plugin-registered privileges already fall in the 19-99 range — a plugin-privilege B would not need to touch the shared lines, weakening the collision. (4) Complementary is weak: the only consumers of A's new payload fields are A's own template/client edits. (5) Caveat for the contradictory seed: A's copy-filter test must be authored so it does not assert the absence of user-level grants on the destination, or it will clash with B's propagation; the reconciliation sketch handles this by scoping B's user propagation to the type-filtered list.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A asks to add two new operations to the posts API: one that returns a post's raw text and one that returns a permission-adjusted post summary, both refusing access (returning null) when the caller cannot read the topic or when the post is deleted. While doing so, A's official solution also restructures the existing 'get a post' function in the same file: it moves the 'post does not exist' check to after the permission check and reorders the lines that stamp the voter's up/down-vote state onto the post and that strip the poster's IP address from the result for non-moderators. Task B is a separate, real bug: the existing 'get a post' endpoint leaks the poster's IP address to ordinary users whenever the post is deleted — the IP-stripping line runs unconditionally, while the 'deleted post' masking only happens for users who are not the poster, not for moderators/admins. B's fix must change that same IP-stripping line (and/or the deleted-post branch) inside the same function. Both agents therefore edit the same ~10 lines of the same function: A reorders the early-return and the vote/IP lines, B rewrites the condition on the IP line. Glued together without reconciliation, the result is broken (the deleted-post branch and the IP condition disagree about which fields to mask, or the reordering drops one of the changes), while a single merged change — keep A's restructure AND make the IP strip conditional on the caller being an admin/mod — satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: src/api/posts.js, function postsAPI.get (base-commit lines ~20-43, specifically the early-return block, the Object.assign(post, voted) line, the post.ip = ... line, and the post.deleted masking branch)
suggestion.taskA: Provide privilege-aware raw and summary post retrieval through the posts API: expose postsAPI.getRaw(caller, {pid}) and postsAPI.getSummary(caller, {pid}) as public operations on the exported posts API. getRaw must return null when the caller lacks topic read access and null when the post is deleted unless the caller is an admin or moderator, otherwise the raw content; getSummary must return the privilege-adjusted summary object (pid matching, non-empty content) or null when topic read access is denied. Wire both into the REST layer with 404 responses when inaccessible.
suggestion.taskB: Security bug: GET /api/v3/posts/:pid leaks the poster's IP address. The post-fetch code strips the IP field only in the deleted-post masking branch, so (a) any logged-in user with read access to the topic can see the poster's IP on a deleted post, and (b) the IP is exposed to non-moderators in cases where the post is masked. Fix postsAPI.get so the IP field is included only when the caller is an administrator or moderator, regardless of the post's deleted state.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a classic security-hardening ticket a maintainer would file on its own: 'IP address of deleted posts visible to regular users'. It targets the pre-existing postsAPI.get endpoint (already shipped and documented in public/openapi/write.yaml) and has nothing to do with raw-content or summary retrieval. It is not a step toward A's goal — A's ticket never mentions the IP leak, and B's ticket never mentions raw/summary operations. The overlap is incidental: both happen to live in the same function because A's gold patch restructures that same function (moving the !post early return and the Object.assign(post, voted) line) while B must rewrite the post.ip condition on the very line A also touches.
suggestion.conflict: A's patch reorders the top of postsAPI.get (null-check post after privilege check, move Object.assign(post, voted) below the privilege gate) and keeps 'post.ip = userPrivilege.isAdminOrMod ? post.ip : undefined' on its original line; B's patch must change that same post.ip line's condition (e.g. strip IP whenever the post is deleted and the caller is not admin/mod) and likely restructure the deleted branch. Two independent diffs on the same 5-10 lines: a naive concatenation/auto-merge either drops A's reordering (leaving B's condition applied to the old structure, where the deleted-post masking branch and the IP condition now disagree about what a non-admin sees) or keeps both lines in an inconsistent order, so the combined behavior (vote state on inaccessible posts, IP visibility on deleted posts, null vs object return) fails at least one side's tests.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent postsAPI.get: fetch privileges/post/voted in parallel; return null if post missing OR caller lacks read/topics:read; then Object.assign(post, voted); post.ip = userPrivilege.isAdminOrMod ? post.ip : undefined; if post.deleted and caller is not admin/mod/self, mask content with '[[topic:post_is_deleted]]'. This is exactly what A's gold patch produces, and it already contains B's fix (IP only for admin/mod), so a single reconciled change passes both suites.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the six fail_to_pass tests in test/posts.js ('Post's socket methods' describe block) calling apiPosts.getRaw/apiPosts.getSummary for guest, voter, and global-mod callers, plus the existing 'should get post' test. B's set: new tests in test/posts.js that delete a post and assert postsAPI.get({uid: voterUid}) returns an object whose ip is undefined, while postsAPI.get({uid: globalModUid}) (with view_deleted) still returns the ip and the real content. Combined suite runs both against the merged src/api/posts.js: base code fails both (A's methods missing; B's IP present on deleted posts), A alone fails B's ip assertion, B alone fails A's null/reorder-dependent expectations only if B's diff also touched the restructured lines — the collision is scored by requiring all of A's and B's tests to pass simultaneously, which only the reconciled function achieves.

notes: Verified at base commit f0d989e: postsAPI.get (src/api/posts.js lines 20-43) does leak post.ip — getPostData returns the ip field and the only stripping is 'post.ip = userPrivilege.isAdminOrMod ? post.ip : undefined' which is unconditional, while the deleted-content masking branch excludes admins/mods, so a non-admin with read access sees the IP of a deleted post. A's gold patch restructures exactly those lines (moves !post early-return after privilege check, relocates Object.assign(post, voted)), which is what makes the contradictory pairing real rather than invented. Two caveats keeping confidence at 3: (1) a lazy B-solution that only edits the single post.ip line could auto-merge cleanly with A's restructure, so the 'naive merge fails' property depends on B's diff touching the reordering/deleted-branch region, which the bug description naturally induces; (2) A's fail_to_pass tests exercise getRaw/getSummary directly and do not pin postsAPI.get's internal ordering, so A's restructure is not strictly forced by its tests — the collision is on the shared region, not on test-forced lines. The complementary family is weak: the client migration and socket-method removal are inside A's own patch, so any B built from them is a decomposition. test/api.js's OpenAPI route-coverage test is a real, independently-motivated B candidate (document GET /posts/{pid}/raw and /posts/{pid}/summary in public/openapi/write.yaml) but it is a documentation follow-up to A's routes, not a true interface contract, so it was not scored as complementary.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A fixes the YAML dump filters so that a vault-encrypted value is either emitted as a '!vault' ciphertext tag (when dump_vault_tags is true) or raises an error (when false), and it explicitly requires that dumping with dump_vault_tags=None (the old implicit behavior) produces NO warnings or deprecation messages of any kind. An independently-motivated task B would be the ticket the maintainers already planned: 'emit a deprecation warning when dump_vault_tags is left at its default None, because implicit ciphertext dumping is going away' — the commented-out deprecation call is literally sitting in the base code waiting to be enabled. Both tickets must edit the same function in the YAML dumper that decides what to do with a vault value, and their demands are opposite: A's test suite asserts zero deprecation output for the None case, while B's test suite asserts a deprecation warning for exactly that case. Gluing both changes together fails A's no-warning assertion; only a reconciled change (warn only for the decryptable-value sub-case, still never for undecryptable values that raise) satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/ansible/_internal/_yaml/_dumper.py — AnsibleDumper.represent_ansible_tagged_object / get_node_from_ciphertext (the dump_vault_tags=None branch containing the commented-out Display().deprecated call)
suggestion.taskA: Fix YAML filter trust propagation and vault handling: from_yaml/from_yaml_all must preserve trust and origin annotations (use AnsibleInstrumentedLoader, pass the tagged string unmodified, offset only the line number); to_yaml/to_nice_yaml must accept templated containers and dump undecryptable/decryptable vault values per dump_vault_tags (ciphertext !vault scalar when truthy, AnsibleTemplateError containing 'undecryptable' when falsy), handle VaultExceptionMarker, raise AnsibleUndefinedVariable for undefined vars, and emit no warnings or deprecations for any dump_vault_tags value including None.
suggestion.taskB: Deprecate implicit YAML vault dumping: when to_yaml/to_nice_yaml (or the AnsibleDumper directly) is used without explicitly passing dump_vault_tags (i.e. it is None) and a vaulted value is actually serialized as ciphertext, emit a deprecation warning telling the user to set dump_vault_tags explicitly. This is the follow-up the codebase already stubbed with a commented-out Display().deprecated call and a 'deprecated: description=...' marker; a maintainer would file it as its own ticket once the implicit behavior's fate was decided.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is not a piece of A: A is about correctness of trust/origin/vault serialization and explicitly keeps the None case warning-free for compatibility; B is a user-facing deprecation policy ticket about the default parameter value. The base code contains direct evidence (the commented-out deprecation block and the DTFIX comment) that this was a planned, separately-tracked change. A developer working on deprecation hygiene would file B without knowing about A's trust/origin fix.
suggestion.conflict: Both edits land in the same dump_vault_tags=None branch of represent_ansible_tagged_object. A's solution must keep that branch silent (its test asserts emits_warnings(warning_pattern=[], deprecation_pattern=[]) for dump_vault_tags=None), while B's solution must add a deprecation warning there (its test asserts the warning fires). Naively merging A's refactor with B's enabled warning makes A's no-deprecation assertion fail; merging B onto the unmodified base also fails A's vault round-trip tests, so the two changes cannot simply coexist.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's get_node_from_ciphertext structure and add B's warning only in the sub-case where dump_vault_tags is None AND the value is a decryptable vault (the implicit behavior actually being deprecated), while the undecryptable path still raises AnsibleTemplateError without any warning. Adjust the combined suite so A's no-warning assertion applies to the undecryptable/None case and B's warning assertion applies to the decryptable/None case — one coherent behavior that satisfies both tickets' user-visible goals.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: test/units/_internal/_yaml/test_dumper.py (test_yaml_dump parametrized over dump_vault_tags True/False/None with emits_warnings expecting no deprecations, test_yaml_dump_undecryptable_without_vault_tags, test_yaml_dump_undefined, test_yaml_dump_iterables) and test/units/plugins/filter/test_core.py (test_from_yaml_trust, test_from_yaml_origin). B's set: new unit tests asserting that dumping a decryptable EncryptedString with dump_vault_tags=None emits the deprecation warning, and that passing True/False does not. Combined suite: run both against the merged dumper; it passes only if the warning is scoped as in the reconciliation (A's strict no-warning case stays clean, B's warning case fires).

notes: Base commit confirms the natural collision site: _dumper.py has a commented-out Display().deprecated call for dump_vault_tags=None with a 'deprecated: description=...' marker, and A's requirements explicitly demand 'no warnings and no deprecation messages of any kind, for every dump_vault_tags value including None' — so the contradictory pairing is real but requires scoping the warning to the decryptable sub-case (and a softened A assertion) to be fully sound, hence confidence 3 rather than 4-5. The complementary pairing's weakness: B's fix (registering a '!vault' constructor) is in _constructor.py, which A also edits (construct_yaml_str), but the edits are in different functions so the pair works as a contract, not a collision; the round-trip integration test is clean. A's gold patch also renames ITERABLE_SCALARS_NOT_TO_ITERATE_FIXME and adds TypeGuard annotations in module_utils/_internal — cosmetic, not seed-relevant. Integration test changes in A (templating target using dump_vault_tags=False) are consistent with the dump-side behavior only.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a security fix: files that Ansible's atomic_move() creates are coming out readable by every local user, so A tightens the built-in default permission from 0666 to 0600 and makes sure newly-created files get that restrictive mode. Task B is a separate, independently-filed bug: when atomic_move() is replacing a file that already exists but the current user is not allowed to read that file's metadata (the operating system returns a 'permission denied' error when inspecting it), atomic_move() silently skips setting any permissions at all, so the replaced file keeps whatever loose permissions the temporary copy had. The test file even carries a FIXME asking 'should atomic_move() set a default permission value when it cannot retrieve the existing file's permissions?'. B's fix therefore adds an explicit permission-setting call inside that exact error-handling branch. Both A and B must therefore decide what permission to apply in the same region of atomic_move() (the branch that runs when inspecting the existing destination fails), and they pick different, incompatible values: A's world says the safe default is 0600, while B's natural fix hard-codes 0644. If you just glue the two changes together, that branch applies 0644, so the security test that expects 0600 fails.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/ansible/module_utils/basic.py, AnsibleModule.atomic_move() — specifically the `except OSError as e: if e.errno != errno.EPERM: raise` fallback branch (lines ~2349-2351) that runs when the destination exists but cannot be stat'ed, and the permission value applied there. A's change is the _DEFAULT_PERM constant (0o0600) that defines the correct value for this region; B's change is an explicit os.chmod call added inside this same region.
suggestion.taskA: Files created by atomic_move() end up world-readable (mode 0644 under umask 022) because the default permission constant is 0666. Tighten _DEFAULT_PERM in module_utils/common/file.py to 0600 and ensure newly-created destination files are chmod'd to DEFAULT_PERM & ~umask, so no file is ever left group/other-readable by default (CVE-2020-1736).
suggestion.taskB: atomic_move() silently leaves a file with wrong (inherited/temporary) permissions when the destination already exists but the running user cannot stat it (os.stat raises EPERM). Today the EPERM is swallowed and no permission is applied at all, so the replaced file keeps the loose mode of the temp file. atomic_move() should apply a sensible default permission in that stat-failure path instead of doing nothing (this is the gap flagged by the existing FIXME comment in test_atomic_move.py::test_existing_file_stat_perms_failure).
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is not a piece of A. A is about the value of the default permission and the new-file path; B is about a distinct, pre-existing defect — the EPERM/stat-failure path applying no permission at all — which the codebase already acknowledges with a FIXME in the test file. A security/robustness maintainer would file 'atomic_move leaves files with incorrect permissions when it cannot read the existing file's metadata' without ever referencing the CVE or the 0666->0600 constant change. The two tickets happen to converge on the same function because that function is where all of atomic_move's permission decisions live.
suggestion.conflict: In the stat-failure (EPERM) region, A's resolved state says the permission that must be applied is the tightened default (0600, via _DEFAULT_PERM), while B's natural fix hard-codes a permissive value (0644) in that same branch. A single branch cannot chmod the file to both 0600 and 0644. Naively merging both patches leaves B's explicit 0644 chmod in place, so A's security test asserting 0600 for that scenario fails; conversely a merge that only honors A's constant leaves B's 'apply a default on stat failure' behavior untested/unsatisfied at the value B asked for.

The two versions of the same function cannot both stand in one file, so two agents working blindly collide, but a single reconciled function (all four checks, consistent bounds) satisfies both tickets' tests at once.

A creates the file with validate_parameters(module, timeout, count) checking only timeout and count; B rewrites the same function to also check ttl (1-255) and size (0-10000) and to use the documented timeout upper bound.
suggestion.taskA: Add an icx_ping module for Ruckus ICX 7000 switches: accept dest (required), count, timeout, ttl, size, source, vrf, and state (present/absent); build the device ping command with non-None options in the order vrf, dest, count, timeout, ttl, size, source; execute it via the shared run_commands() helper and report ConnectionError failures; parse the ICX reply (Success line, or Sending-line fallback with 0% success, 0 rx, real tx, zero RTTs); compute packet_loss as (100 - success)% and return commands, packet_loss, packets_tx, packets_rx, rtt; fail with 'Ping failed unexpectedly' (state=present, 100% loss) or 'Ping succeeded unexpectedly' (state=absent, any success), carrying the full results dict in the failure; never report changed on success.
suggestion.taskB: icx_ping rejects nothing for out-of-range ttl or size, and its enforced timeout limit disagrees with its own documentation. The module doc says timeout is valid from 1 to 4294967296, ttl from 1 to 255, and size from 0 to 10000, but the code only validates timeout (against 1-4294967294) and count. Fix: before any command is sent, validate all four numeric options and fail with clear messages — 'bad value for ttl - valid range (1-255)' for ttl outside 1-255 and 'bad value for size - valid range (0-10000)' for size outside 0-10000 — and make the enforced timeout bound match the documented one (4294967296). A ping request with ttl=300 or size=10001 must fail fast without ever touching the device.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B reads as a classic documentation-vs-behavior bug ticket: a user follows the module's documented option ranges, the module silently sends an invalid command to the switch (or the enforced bound contradicts the docs), and a maintainer files 'validation is incomplete/inconsistent'. It is motivated entirely by the documented contract of the option ranges, not by anything in A's goal description (A's stated success criteria are about parsing, state assertions, and the commands key). B does not ask for ping functionality, parsing, or state checking — only for the validation step to honor the documented ranges. The one caveat that keeps this at confidence 3 rather than higher: B presumes the module already exists, so in a real-world timeline B would be filed after A's merge, not truly at the same commit; the 'same commit' framing is only consistent if we treat A's creation as the base state B's bug report is written against.
suggestion.conflict: Both tickets' solutions define different contents for the same function in the same file. A's validate_parameters(module, timeout, count) contains exactly two range checks (timeout 1-4294967294, count 1-4294967294) and no ttl/size handling; B's version must contain four checks (timeout 1-4294967296, count, ttl 1-255, size 0-10000). Naively merging collides: B's patch is written against A's file, so it cannot even apply to the base commit (file missing) — a hard merge conflict; and if B's edits are merely concatenated alongside A's, the function still lacks the ttl/size checks (or keeps A's contradictory timeout bound), so B's tests fail. suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One validate_parameters() that validates all four numeric options before any command is executed: timeout in 1-4294967296 (matching the DOCUMENTATION), count in 1-4294967294, ttl in 1-255, size in 0-10000, each failing with its 'bad value for <opt> - valid range (...)' message. This single function passes A's tests (timeout/count invalid cases still fail with the same messages; valid values still proceed) and B's tests (ttl=300 and size=10001 now fail fast with the documented ranges, and timeout=4294967296 is accepted per the docs).
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set = the 9 fail_to_pass tests in test/units/modules/network/icx/test_icx_ping.py (expected success/failure, unexpected success/failure, command-building, and the invalid timeout/count/ttl/size cases). Combined suite = both files run against the merged module: it passes only if the reconciled validate_parameters covers all four options with consistent bounds — A-only code fails B's ttl/size tests, B-only code fails A's parsing/state tests, and a naive concatenation of the two function bodies fails B's tests (or the merge fails to apply at all).

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is about isolating worker processes from the parent's terminal: it rewrites the worker's startup so the worker no longer saves/duplicates the parent's stdin, and it makes the worker detach from standard input/output/error when it begins running. An independent Task B is about process-group cleanup: when a worker is killed (Ctrl-C or a terminate signal), the kill must be propagated to the whole group of processes the worker created, not just the worker itself, or leftover subprocesses survive. Both tickets must edit the exact same method, WorkerProcess.start() in lib/ansible/executor/process/worker.py. A's edit deletes the stdin-saving lines from start(); B's edit adds signal-handler registration lines to start(). Gluing the two changes together yields a start() that both registers the new signal handlers AND still calls the _save_stdin() method that A deleted, so the merged code crashes (NameError/AttributeError) and A's tests fail. One coherent start() — signal handlers registered, stdin-saving removed — satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.shared_region: WorkerProcess.start() in lib/ansible/executor/process/worker.py (base lines ~93-108), the method that runs just before the fork. A removes the self._save_stdin() call and the try/finally that closes self._new_stdin; B adds signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM/SIGINT, handler) registrations (with a handler that kills the worker's process group) to the same method.
suggestion.taskA: Isolate worker processes by detaching inherited standard I/O: workers must not inherit the parent's stdin/stdout/stderr, must run in their own session/process group, and all output must go through the controlled display queue. (The original SWE-bench-Pro ticket: keyword-only annotated WorkerProcess constructor with cliargs, _detach() using setsid/dup2/StringIO/fdopen, run() ordering, TaskExecutor/TaskQueueManager/connection signature changes.)
suggestion.taskB: Terminating a worker process (Ctrl-C during a play, or SIGTERM to the worker) leaves the worker's child subprocesses alive, because the signal only reaches the worker itself and not the process group the worker spawned. Register SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers in WorkerProcess.start() so that when the worker is terminated, the signal is propagated to its entire process group (killpg on the worker's pid), guaranteeing no orphaned subprocesses survive a killed worker.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a classic, self-contained process-hygiene ticket: 'killing a forked worker orphans its children'. It is motivated by signal/process-group semantics, not by stdio isolation. It reads naturally as a ticket a different developer would file after observing leftover ssh/subprocesses after Ctrl-C. It does not mention detaching stdio, cliargs, or any of A's goals; its only connection to A is that both happen to need to touch the pre-fork hook start().
suggestion.conflict: A's patch rewrites start() to delete _save_stdin() (and the method itself) and to drop the try/finally close, while B's patch (written against the base) rewrites start() to keep _save_stdin() and add signal.signal(SIGTERM/SIGINT, self._term) registrations. A naive merge/auto-merge of the two versions of start() produces a method that registers the handlers but still calls the now-deleted self._save_stdin(), so instantiating-and-starting a worker raises AttributeError; A's constructor/detach/run tests and any test that starts a worker fail. The two versions of the same method cannot both stand.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: A single start() that (1) does NOT save/restore stdin (A's requirement), (2) calls super().start() under display._lock, and (3) registers SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers that propagate the signal to the worker's process group (B's requirement). This is exactly the shape of the gold solution's start(), which already contains the _term/killpg handler — evidence the codebase itself reconciled these two concerns in one method. A reconciler keeps the handler registration and drops the _save_stdin call.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the fail_to_pass tests in test/units/executor/test_worker.py (TestWorkerProcessConstructor, TestWorkerProcessDetach, TestWorkerProcessRun, TestTaskQueueManagerStdioInheritance) plus test/units/executor/test_task_executor.py. B's set (new, authored against base): a test that constructs a WorkerProcess, patches signal.signal, calls start(), and asserts SIGTERM and SIGINT handlers were registered whose behavior kills the worker's process group (e.g. os.killpg called with the worker pid and the received signum). Base fails both sets (no handlers; no detach/keyword-only ctor). A's solution passes A's set and also happens to pass B's set (its start() registers the handlers); B's solution passes B's set. Naively merged code fails A's set (start() references deleted _save_stdin / duplicate or broken method), so only the reconciled single start() passes the combined suite. Authoring caveat: B's test must construct WorkerProcess with keyword arguments (or a tolerant helper) so it also works against A's keyword-only constructor, otherwise the combined suite is unsatisfiable.

notes: Key structural facts verified at base commit 3684b48: (1) WorkerProcess.start() (worker.py lines 93-108) currently calls self._save_stdin() and closes self._new_stdin in a finally; A deletes both the call and the method. (2) The base code has NO signal handlers anywhere in worker.py, so a process-group-termination ticket (B) is genuinely unaddressed at base and fails its test there. (3) The gold patch itself registers signal.signal(SIGTERM/SIGINT, self._term) in start() with a killpg-based _term — i.e., the real fix already bundles A's stdio isolation with B's signal propagation in the same method, which is exactly why this region is a natural mutex collision point. (5) Connection plugins (ssh/winrm/psrp/local) all use *args/**kwargs constructors, so A's 'tolerate extra positional new_stdin' requirement is already satisfied at base; the complementary angle via the connection signature is therefore empty. suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A adds an opt-in 'manifest' (MANIFEST.in-style) file-selection mode to `ansible-galaxy collection build`. To do that it restructures the file-selection function `_build_files_manifest` in lib/ansible/galaxy/collection/__init__.py: the old single 4-argument function containing a directory-walk is deleted and replaced by a 5-argument dispatcher plus two new sub-functions (the old walk moved into `_build_files_manifest_walk`, and a new distlib-based selector). Task B is a separate, independently-motivated bug ticket: when a collection directory contains a *file* symlink whose target lies outside the collection, the build silently follows it and copies the outside file's contents into the tarball (and records the outside file's checksum in FILES.json), while *directory* symlinks pointing outside are already skipped with a warning. B asks for the same skip-plus-warning behavior for file symlinks, which requires editing the file branch of that same walk. The collision: B's patch modifies lines inside the old monolithic function, while A's patch deletes/moves that function body. Naively combining the two changes either drops B's guard (so B's test fails) or keeps the old function shape (so A's tests fail); only a single reconciled change — A's new structure with B's symlink guard placed inside the moved walk — passes both test suites.
suggestion.shared_region: The file branch of the directory walk in `_build_files_manifest` (lib/ansible/galaxy/collection/__init__.py, base lines ~1077-1090, the `else:` branch with the comment 'Handling of file symlinks occur in _build_collection_tar'), which A's gold patch relocates into the new `_build_files_manifest_walk` function.
suggestion.taskA: Original ticket, restated: `ansible-galaxy collection build` only supports `build_ignore` for selecting files. Add support for a `manifest` block in galaxy.yml with MANIFEST.in-style `directives` and `omit_default_directives`, processed via the optional `distlib` library: `_build_files_manifest` gains a fifth dict parameter; empty dict keeps the legacy walk; non-empty dict with non-empty `build_ignore` raises 'mutually exclusive'; missing distlib raises a clear error; default directives wrap user directives; selected files get sha256 entries; plus a `ManifestControl` dataclass with defaults and strict unknown-key rejection.
suggestion.taskB: Separate ticket: `ansible-galaxy collection build` follows file symlinks that point outside the collection. A symlink inside the collection directory whose target resolves outside is dereferenced at tar time (os.path.realpath in `_build_collection_tar`), so the external file's contents are copied into the built tarball and its checksum is recorded in FILES.json, even though the file is not part of the collection. Directory symlinks pointing outside are already skipped with a warning ('Skipping ... as it is a symbolic link to a directory outside the collection'), but file symlinks are not, creating an inconsistent and information-leaking behavior. The build should skip file symlinks whose target resolves outside the collection directory, emit a warning, and continue to preserve symlinks whose target resolves inside the collection.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated purely by the existing asymmetric symlink handling visible in the base code (the directory guard at lines 1061-1067 exists; the file branch explicitly defers symlink handling to tar time, where realpath dereferences the link). A developer auditing symlink safety or reviewing a report that 'building my collection leaked a file from outside the repo into the tarball' would file this without any knowledge of manifest/distlib work. It never mentions `manifest`, `distlib`, or `build_ignore` changes, and it has value on its own (hardening the build).
suggestion.conflict: A's patch rewrites the same function: it replaces the 4-arg monolithic `_build_files_manifest` with a dispatcher and moves the walk body into `_build_files_manifest_walk`. B's patch edits the file branch inside the old monolith. The two hunks overlap in the same code region: an auto-merge conflicts; if A's version wins, B's guard is lost and B's end-to-end test still sees the outside file in the artifact; if B's version is kept, A's tests fail because the function has no fifth parameter and no manifest behavior. Naively concatenating both changes yields two definitions of `_build_files_manifest` (Python binds the last) or a patch that fails to apply — either way the combined suite fails.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's restructure (5-arg dispatcher, `_build_files_manifest_walk`, distlib path, ManifestControl) and insert B's guard into the file branch of `_build_files_manifest_walk`: if the entry is a symlink, resolve its target with os.path.realpath, and if `_is_child_path(target, top_level_dir)` is False, display a warning ('Skipping ... as it is a symbolic link to a file outside the collection') and continue; otherwise record it as before. Symlinks inside the collection are still preserved as single entries, so A's `test_build_copy_symlink_target_inside_collection` and B's new test both pass.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the 15 fail_to_pass unit tests in test/units/galaxy/test_collection.py (manifest/distlib behavior, ManifestControl dataclass, and the legacy-walk tests updated to the new 5-arg signature). B's set: one new test, e.g. `test_build_file_symlink_target_outside_collection`, written against the stable public entry point `build_collection` (NOT the private 4-arg function, so it survives A's signature change): create a collection, place a file outside it, symlink to it from inside, build, then assert the symlinked name is absent from FILES.json, the outside file's contents are not in the tarball, and a warning was displayed. Soundness: base fails A's tests (no 5th param/manifest) and fails B's test (outside contents included); A alone passes A's tests but still fails B's; B alone passes B's test but fails A's; the naive merge fails the combined suite; the reconciled change passes all of A's + B's tests together.

notes: Key structural facts from the base commit: (1) `_build_files_manifest` is a 4-arg monolith whose walk already guards directory symlinks pointing outside (lines 1061-1067) but not file symlinks — the file branch comment says symlink handling happens in `_build_collection_tar`, which uses os.path.realpath and thus dereferences outside file symlinks into the artifact. This asymmetry is the real, pre-existing hook for the contradictory task B. (2) The base galaxy.yml schema file ends at `build_ignore` with no `manifest` key, so A's (truncated) gold patch must add `manifest` to collections_galaxy_meta.yml or `build_collection`/`install_src` would KeyError on `collection_meta['manifest']` — that schema piece is a decomposition of A, which is why the complementary family is weak. (3) The contradictory collision is structural (A moves the code B edits) rather than semantic (two incompatible behaviors for the same input), which is why confidence is 3 not 4-5; the authoring step must write B's test through the stable `build_collection` entry point so it remains valid after A's signature change, and must ensure B's guard is placed in `_build_files_manifest_walk` in the reconciled solution. (4) A's own fail_to_pass list includes legacy-walk tests (e.g. test_build_ignore_patterns) that were updated to the new 5-arg call, confirming A rewrites exactly the region B needs.

B's fix also changes the GalaxyAPI constructor (adding a timeout parameter and storing it) and the same _call_galaxy method (passing self.timeout to the open_url call instead of the literal 20). Both patches therefore edit the exact same constructor signature line, the same few body lines right after it, and the same hunk of _call_galaxy. Glued together naively the signature line is duplicated/broken (syntax error) or one ticket's parameter is silently dropped, so both test suites fail; a single reconciled constructor accepting all four new options and one _call_galaxy that both caches and honors the timeout passes everything.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/ansible/galaxy/api.py: GalaxyAPI.__init__ (signature line 'def __init__(self, galaxy, name, url, ..., available_api_versions=None):' and the body lines immediately after it where A inserts the cache-dir/cache-load block) and GalaxyAPI._call_galaxy (signature line where A appends cache=False, and the body hunk containing 'open_url(..., timeout=20, ...)' where B substitutes self.timeout)

Add a response cache: a GALAXY_CACHE_DIR setting, a shared api.json store (version 1, 0o600, dir 0o700, world-writable stores ignored with a warning), no_cache/clear_response_cache options on GalaxyAPI, a get_cache_id(url) host:port key helper, and cache read/write logic in _call_galaxy, plus --no-cache/--clear-response-cache CLI flags on collection install/download.
suggestion.taskB: ansible-galaxy makes every HTTP request with a hard-coded 20 second timeout (GalaxyAPI._call_galaxy calls open_url(..., timeout=20)). Users with slow corporate proxies time out, and requests to unreachable internal Galaxy servers hang for 20s each. Make the Galaxy HTTP timeout configurable: add a timeout parameter to GalaxyAPI (default 20, so existing behavior is unchanged) and use it in _call_galaxy's open_url call, exposed via a --timeout CLI option on the collection subcommands.
suggestion.independence_rationale: Timeout configurability is a classic standalone usability ticket with its own motivation (hard-coded latency in the HTTP layer), its own user-visible symptom, and its own fix (a parameter plumbed to open_url). It says nothing about caching, metadata, or api.json; a maintainer would file it without knowing task A exists. It is not 'the other half of A' — A's cache works perfectly with the default timeout, and B's timeout works perfectly without any cache.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches rewrite the same physical lines: the GalaxyAPI.__init__ signature (A appends ', clear_response_cache=False, no_cache=True', B appends ', timeout=20'), the constructor body (A inserts the makedirs/cache-clear/cache-load block at the same spot B inserts self.timeout = timeout), and the _call_galaxy signature/body (A appends cache=False and inserts the cache-read block immediately above the open_url call; B edits that open_url call). Both feature sets coexist because they are orthogonal behaviors on the same method.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the existing fail_to_pass tests in test/units/galaxy/test_api.py (test_cache_id[*], test_missing_cache_dir, test_existing_cache, test_cache_invalid_cache_content[*], test_world_writable_cache, test_no_cache, test_clear_cache, test_clear_cache_with_no_cache). suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a bug ticket: users whose kinit is a custom tool (e.g. a corporate wrapper that takes its own flags) can't pass extra arguments to it, because the WinRM plugin only ever builds the kinit command as 'kinit [-f] principal' and the -f flag is hardcoded. A's fix adds a new host variable (ansible_winrm_kinit_args) whose space-separated value replaces all default kinit arguments. Task B is a separate feature ticket: some users' Kerberos tickets expire during long playbooks, and the standard kinit flag -R requests a renewable ticket, so B asks the plugin to support a new host variable (ansible_winrm_kerberos_renewable) that adds -R to the kinit call. Both tasks must edit the exact same few lines in the winrm connection plugin where the kinit command line is assembled: A deletes the small 'kinit_flags' list and replaces it with logic that prefers kinit_args over the delegation flag, while B appends to that same list. If the two changes are glued together naively, one of them breaks the other (the list A deleted is the one B writes to, or the precedence A introduced contradicts B's requirement that -R always appear).
suggestion.shared_region: lib/ansible/plugins/connection/winrm.py, Connection._kerb_auth() — the kinit command-line construction block (base lines ~294-302: the kinit_flags list, the -f delegation append, and kinit_cmdline = [self._kinit_cmd] / extend / append(principal)). A rewrites this block (deletes kinit_flags, adds kinit_args precedence); B extends the same block (adds -R to kinit_flags when the new renewable var is set).
suggestion.taskA: BUG: ansible_winrm_kinit_cmd fails for custom kinit tools on WinRM Kerberos auth (regression vs 2.5). suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent block in _kerb_auth: build a defaults list (append -f if ansible_winrm_kerberos_delegation, append -R if ansible_winrm_kerberos_renewable, fixed order); if kinit_args is set, shlex.split it and use those tokens INSTEAD of the defaults (kinit_args wins, mirroring A's existing delegation rule); then cmdline = [kinit_cmd] + args + [principal], shared by both the pexpect and subprocess paths.
