suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A says: when the browser's local database (IndexedDB) is suddenly closed under the app, the session is unrecoverable — so stop the client, and either silently reload the page (for guest users) or pop up an error dialog with a Reload button (for logged-in users). An independent task B, coming from a developer with the opposite UX philosophy, says: for logged-in users, a closed database shouldn't kill the session — the app should quietly swap in an in-memory store, restart the client, and keep working (with a warning that data won't persist), and must NOT reload the page. Both tickets hook into the exact same spot: the place in MatrixClientPeg where the client's store is started up, where each one registers its own handler for the store's 'closed' event. If two agents blindly merge, both handlers fire on the same event: one stops the client and reloads the page, the other stops the client and restarts it in memory — the app both reloads and keeps running, and B's tests (which assert no reload and a restarted in-memory client) fail. A single reconciled handler can satisfy both: guests reload immediately (A's test), logged-in users get the memory-store fallback AND the explanatory dialog (A's test only checks that a dialog is shown, B's test only checks no reload + memory store), so the combined suite can pass.
suggestion.shared_region: src/MatrixClientPeg.ts — MatrixClientPegClass.assign() (the lines immediately after the store.startup() fallback loop, where A attaches this.matrixClient.store.on?.("closed", ...)) plus the class body where each task adds its 'closed'-event handler method. Both tasks must register a reaction to the same store 'closed' event at the same wiring point.
suggestion.taskA: IndexedDB store closes unexpectedly: the app freezes with no feedback. Detect the store's 'closed' event, stop the Matrix client, reload the app for guest users, and for logged-in users show a standard error dialog (via the modal system, localized, with a Reload button) that reloads through the platform abstraction when confirmed.
suggestion.taskB: Session loss when the browser evicts IndexedDB: logged-in users currently lose their whole session (page reload) when the local database is evicted by the browser (storage pressure, clearing data). Instead of a hard reload, the client should degrade gracefully: when the backing store closes, replace it with the in-memory store (the same fallback already used when IndexedDB fails at startup), restart the client, and warn the user that data will no longer persist. No page reload should happen for logged-in users.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by a real, separate complaint (forced page reload / lost session when the browser evicts IndexedDB) and a different recovery philosophy (degrade to in-memory, keep the session alive) — the codebase already contains the building blocks for that philosophy (MemoryStore fallback in assign(), the lowBandwidth setting, storage-consistency checks in StorageManager). B is not 'the other half of A': A's goal is user feedback + reload; B's goal is avoiding reload entirely. They are two competing answers to the same underlying event, exactly the kind of tickets two maintainers with different opinions would file independently.
suggestion.conflict: Both changes attach handlers to the same 'closed' event at the same wiring point in assign(). A's handler: stopClient, then reload (guest) or stopClient + error dialog + reload (logged-in). B's handler: stopClient, swap in MemoryStore, restartClient, explicitly no reload. Naively merged, both listeners run: the app reloads (violating B's no-reload expectation) while also trying to restart in memory (violating A's 'unrecoverable, must reload' premise). B's test asserting 'reload not called / client restarted on memory store' fails against the merged code, and A's 'unrecoverable state' semantics are broken by the concurrent restart.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One handler in assign()'s wiring: on 'closed' → stopClient; if guest → PlatformPeg.reload() (satisfies A's guest test); if logged-in → swap matrixClient.store to a MemoryStore, restart the client, and show the ErrorDialog as an informational warning that the database closed and data no longer persists (satisfies A's 'modal shown' test, which only asserts Modal.createDialog was called, and B's 'no reload + memory store + restarted' test). A single coherent change passes the combined suite.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the two new tests in test/MatrixClientPeg-test.ts ('should reload when store database closes for a guest user' — asserts PlatformPeg reload called; 'should show error modal when store database closes' — asserts Modal.createDialog called) plus the existing .start tests that must keep passing. B's set: a new test in the same file — non-guest session, emit 'closed' on the store, assert reload was NOT called, matrixClient.store is now a MemoryStore, and startClient was called again. Combined suite: both test files' assertions run against the merged MatrixClientPeg; naive merge fails (B's no-reload assertion broken by A's listener), reconciled handler passes all.

notes: node_modules is not checked out, so matrix-js-sdk's store 'closed' event semantics could not be verified directly; the gold patch and its tests (store.on = emitter.on; emitter.emit('closed')) confirm the event exists on the store at this commit. The contradictory seed is behavioral (two listeners on one event with incompatible recovery strategies) rather than a textual line conflict, and it only becomes sound if B is explicitly scoped to logged-in (non-guest) sessions — if B also covered guests, A's 'guest reloads' test and B's 'no reload' test would be irreconcilable and the seed would be invalid. A's non-guest test is deliberately weak (only asserts the dialog was opened, not that a reload followed), which is what makes reconciliation possible. Complementary is weak: all of A's dependencies (PlatformPeg.reload, ErrorDialog, Modal, i18n) pre-exist, so there is no missing contract for a second task to provide. Overall: a moderate (confidence 3) contradictory candidate; the authoring step should write B's tests to assert no-reload + memory-store swap for non-guests only.

Increase the amplitude sampling rate in the recorder worklet (e.g. to 10 samples/second) and update the recording-side sanity check so the amplitudes array accumulates at the new rate, giving thumbnails enough data points for short clips.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A makes filesystem-backed flag state carry a real per-namespace version: it threads an ETag through the object-storage file types, records a version for each namespace when a snapshot is built, and implements the store's GetVersion so it returns that version (or an error for a namespace that was never loaded). A different developer, working from a test-failure report, files Task B: the shared test double (StoreMock) that stands in for every store is recording the wrong arguments for its GetVersion method — it only logs the request context and drops the namespace it was asked about, so any test that wants to assert 'the version was requested for namespace X' cannot be written, and the mock does not honestly reflect the real GetVersion(ctx, namespace) signature. Both tasks are forced to rewrite the body of the very same function, StoreMock.GetVersion, in incompatible ways: A needs the mock to record the namespace (so its new version test can set up and verify per-namespace expectations), while B's minimal fix, taken on its own, keeps the recording context-only. Glued together naively, the mock's recording line can only hold one of the two argument lists, so one task's tests break against the other's change. A single reconciled edit — record both the context and the namespace — satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: internal/common/store_mock.go, func (m *StoreMock) GetVersion — the single line 'args := m.Called(ctx)' that both tasks must rewrite (A to pass ns, B to make the recording match the real interface).
suggestion.taskA: Namespaces loaded from filesystem/object storage carry no version. A snapshot built from files reports an empty version for every namespace, and GetVersion on the declarative store is an unimplemented stub that always returns ('', nil), so callers cannot tell an unversioned namespace from one that was never loaded, and cannot detect that the underlying state changed. Make file metadata expose a version identifier (ETag), derive a per-document and per-namespace version when building snapshots from filesystem, git, OCI and object storage, and implement GetVersion on the snapshot and the declarative store so it returns the stored version for a loaded namespace and an error for one that was not.
suggestion.taskB: The shared store test double does not faithfully record GetVersion calls. StoreMock.GetVersion is the one method in the mock that records only the context and silently discards the namespace request it is handed, even though every other method in the mock records all of its arguments and the real interface is GetVersion(ctx, namespace). Tests that want to assert which namespace a version was requested for cannot be expressed, and the mock diverges from the interface it claims to implement. Fix the mock so it records the namespace alongside the context and returns the version/error configured for that namespace.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B reads as a routine test-infrastructure hygiene ticket: 'our mock drops an argument on one method, make it record it like all the others.' It is motivated by the mock's inconsistency with its interface and with its sibling methods, not by any need for filesystem versions to exist. A developer fixing a flaky or under-specified test would file exactly this without knowing about the snapshot-versioning work. It is not 'the half of A that A didn't do' — A is about producing real versions from storage; B is about a shared recording helper. The only overlap is the mechanical necessity that both edits land in the same 5-line function.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches rewrite the same statement, the mock's call-recording line for GetVersion. A's version requires the namespace to be recorded (its new store test sets an expectation keyed on the namespace and asserts the returned version); B's standalone, minimal interpretation keeps recording context-only to match what it believes the method should capture. A naive merge leaves one argument list in place, so the mock records either (ctx) or (ctx, ns) but not the form the other task's test expects — testify then fails to match the expectation and the combined suite breaks.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep a single GetVersion on the mock that records both arguments — args := m.Called(ctx, ns) — and returns args.String(0), args.Error(1). This is exactly A's form, and it also satisfies B's requirement that the namespace be recorded and that the configured per-namespace version/error be returned. One coherent line replaces both competing edits.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set is its fail_to_pass tests: TestFSWithoutIndex (snapshot GetVersion returns a non-empty version for a loaded namespace and an error for an unknown one), TestGetVersion (declarative Store.GetVersion delegates to the read-only store and returns its version), TestNewFile and TestFileInfo (object-storage file/fileinfo expose the ETag). B's set is a new mock test, e.g. TestStoreMockGetVersionRecordsNamespace, which sets storeMock.On('GetVersion', mock.Anything, <ns>).Return('v', nil), calls GetVersion, and asserts the namespace was recorded and 'v' returned. The combined suite runs both against the merged code: it passes only if the mock records (ctx, ns) — the reconciled form — because A's TestGetVersion needs the namespace-keyed expectation to match and B's test needs the namespace to be recorded. The base fails both sets (stub GetVersion, context-only mock); each task's own solution passes its own set; the naive glue (whichever single recording line survives) fails the other's set.

notes: Strongest real structure is the contradictory mock collision in internal/common/store_mock.go GetVersion: it is the one place two independently-motivated tickets (produce real versions vs. fix the shared test double's argument recording) must rewrite the same line incompatibly, and a single reconciled edit (record ctx and ns) satisfies both. It is a narrow, mechanical conflict (hence confidence 3, not higher) but it is genuine and already present in the code, not invented. A secondary, weaker collision exists in internal/storage/fs/object/store.go build(): A adds a fifth etag argument to the NewFile call, while an independent 'stop rebuilding the object-store snapshot on every poll when the bucket is unchanged' ticket (mirroring the OCI store's IfNoMatch/digest short-circuit) would restructure the same build/update region; the two are reconcilable but the overlap is looser than the mock one. The complementary family is essentially absent because the consumer of GetVersion (the evaluation ETag/304 endpoint) and a working producer (the SQL store) both already exist at the base commit, so A's value is standalone and there is no independent second ticket to pair with it without decomposition.

Glued together, the code no longer compiles (A's constructor references a field B removed) or the two rewrites of the same lines cannot both stand, so the combined test suite fails. One coherent change — keep the joined string for legacy consumers, add the array, and add the operator fields — satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: internal/server/audit/types.go — the `Rule` struct (lines 134-141) + `NewRule` (lines 143-157), and the `RolloutSegment` struct (lines 173-176) + `NewRollout` (lines 178-200). Both A and B must rewrite these same struct definitions and constructor bodies.

suggestion.conflict: A's patch keeps `Rule.SegmentKey string` and rewrites `NewRule` to set it to the comma-joined value (and add `SegmentOperator`); B's patch deletes `Rule.SegmentKey` and adds `Rule.SegmentKeys []string` (same for `RolloutSegment.Key` vs `Keys`). suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A asks Flipt to let operators choose how application metrics are shipped out (a new 'metrics' config section with an exporter choice of prometheus or otlp, plus a function that builds the chosen exporter). Task B, filed by a different developer, asks for a different but adjacent capability: letting operators move or reconfigure the metrics endpoint port, which also requires introducing a 'metrics' section in the same configuration system. Both tickets independently invent the very same new config file and the very same new field on the top-level config struct, but with different contents. If two agents work blindly, the repository ends up with two incompatible definitions of the same config section and duplicate struct fields, so the code no longer compiles; only someone who merges the two field sets into one coherent 'metrics' section makes both sets of tests pass.
suggestion.shared_region: internal/config/config.go (the Config struct's new 'Metrics' field and the Default() function's new 'Metrics' entry) plus the newly created file internal/config/metrics.go (both A and B create this file defining type MetricsConfig, with different fields), and the metrics section of config/flipt.schema.cue / config/flipt.schema.json

suggestion.taskB: Make the port of the /metrics HTTP endpoint configurable: add a 'metrics' section to the Flipt configuration exposing a 'port' key (defaulting to the current behavior, i.e. served on the main HTTP port), and have the HTTP server in internal/cmd/http.go serve the /metrics endpoint on the configured port. Motivation: in containerized deployments the metrics endpoint on the main HTTP port conflicts with sidecars/load-balancer health checks and operators want to pin it to a dedicated port.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is about where the metrics endpoint is served (an HTTP server concern in internal/cmd/http.go, which A never touches), while A is about how metric data is exported (an OTel concern in internal/metrics). A maintainer could file 'let me configure the /metrics port' without any knowledge of exporter work; the tickets share only the fact that Flipt's config system has no 'metrics' section yet, so both naturally introduce one. B's acceptance criteria (port key deserializes, server listens on it) say nothing about exporters, OTLP, or GetExporter.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches create internal/config/metrics.go with different definitions of type MetricsConfig (A: Enabled/Exporter/OTLP; B: Port) and both add a 'Metrics MetricsConfig' field to the Config struct in internal/config/config.go at the same position, plus a 'Metrics:' entry in Default() and a 'metrics' block in the CUE/JSON schemas. Naively gluing the two changes yields duplicate type definitions and duplicate struct fields (or one file overwriting the other), so the package fails to compile and both A's tests (TestLoad metrics cases, TestGetxporter) and B's tests (port deserialization, server-on-port) fail.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep a single internal/config/metrics.go whose MetricsConfig carries the union of fields (Enabled, Exporter, OTLP from A plus Port from B), one 'Metrics' field on Config, one Default() entry (Port defaulting to 0 meaning 'use main HTTP port', Enabled true, Exporter prometheus), one 'metrics' schema block covering both keys, and wire http.go to honor Port while metrics.go honors Exporter. A single agent (or two that talk) produces this; the combined suite then passes.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the TestLoad cases for metrics (disabled.yml, otlp.yml, defaults) in internal/config/config_test.go plus TestGetxporter in internal/metrics/metrics_test.go. B's set: a TestLoad case asserting metrics.port deserializes into cfg.Metrics.Port with the right default, plus a test that NewHTTPServer mounts /metrics on the configured port (httptest or a cmd-level test). Combined suite: run both packages' tests against the merged tree; it fails on the naive merge (compile errors from duplicate MetricsConfig/field) and passes only on the reconciled union struct.

notes: Base commit verified: internal/metrics/metrics.go creates the Prometheus exporter in init() and has no GetExporter; internal/config has no metrics.go and Config has no Metrics field; internal/cmd/http.go mounts /metrics unconditionally on the main HTTP port; internal/cmd/grpc.go calls tracing.GetExporter but nothing for metrics — confirming the gold patch leaves runtime wiring undone, which is why the complementary B (wiring) exists but carries decomposition risk. An alternative contradictory B (also plausible, slightly weaker on testability): 'add OTel resource attributes (service.name/service.version) to the metrics provider' — it would edit the same init()/provider-construction region of internal/metrics/metrics.go that A replaces, and naively gluing B's modified init() with A's GetExporter would create the Prometheus exporter twice (duplicate-registration failure of A's tests); reconciliation moves the resource into GetExporter. The config-section collision (both tickets inventing internal/config/metrics.go) is the cleaner, more defensible mutex because the conflict is structural (duplicate type/field) and both sides' tests are straightforward. CUE/JSON schema edits in A's gold patch also reformat the adjacent #tracing block, which would add trivial line-level merge noise for any B touching the schema files. Overall: contradictory at confidence 3 (real, natural collision, but reconciliation is a simple field union and B's server-level test needs care); complementary at confidence 2 (genuine producer/consumer shape, but B is essentially 'finish A's feature').

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A says: when an operator writes a cookie-domain setting that accidentally contains a web address prefix and a port number (like 'http://localhost:8080'), the server should clean it up automatically at startup, keeping only the bare host name ('localhost'), and the cleaned value should replace what was configured. Task B is a separate, equally plausible ticket: 'browser login cookies are rejected when the configured domain is localhost or contains junk, because the code that sets the cookie hands the browser an invalid domain'. B's developer fixes the problem at the cookie-setting code instead: the config value is left exactly as the operator wrote it, and the cookie logic strips the junk (and omits the domain attribute for localhost) right before sending the cookie. Both fixes target the same pipeline: the config-validation function in internal/config/authentication.go (where A inserts its cleanup) and the cookie blocks in internal/server/auth/method/oidc/http.go (where B inserts its cleanup). They cannot both be the canonical fix point: if A's startup cleanup runs, the cookie code in B's world never sees the messy value B's tests assert on, and B's test that checks 'the configured value is preserved verbatim' fails. If only B's cookie-side cleanup exists, A's test that checks 'the configured value was rewritten to the bare host' fails. A single reconciled change (normalize once at config load, cookie code just uses the clean value) satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: The session-domain pipeline: (*AuthenticationConfig).validate() in internal/config/authentication.go (the sessionEnabled block where A adds getHostname normalization) together with the cookie-construction blocks in internal/server/auth/method/oidc/http.go (Handler's state cookie and ForwardResponseOption's token cookie, where B adds cookie-site domain sanitization). Both tasks' fixes land in this one data path for the same field, AuthenticationSession.Domain.
suggestion.taskA: OIDC login breaks when authentication.session.domain is configured with a scheme and port (e.g. 'http://localhost:8080') because browsers reject cookie Domain values containing scheme/port. Fix: when a session-compatible auth method is enabled, validate() must normalize Session.Domain via a getHostname helper (strip scheme and port, keep only host) and overwrite the field; errors must propagate. Also the OIDC callback URL builder must strip a single trailing slash from the host so the redirect URI has no double slash.
suggestion.taskB: Session cookies are not set for localhost deployments: the OIDC middleware copies the configured session domain verbatim into the state and token cookies, and (a) domains that carry a scheme or port are rejected by browsers, and (b) 'localhost' is not a valid cookie domain per the RFC (needs two dots), so the Domain attribute must be omitted for it. Fix at the cookie-setting site in internal/server/auth/method/oidc/http.go: sanitize the domain there (strip scheme/port, drop the attribute for localhost) while the loaded configuration value is preserved exactly as the operator wrote it (the config is also used for display/other purposes and must not be mutated).
suggestion.independence_rationale: B reads as its own ticket because it is motivated by observed browser behavior (Set-Cookie rejected) and by the cookie RFC's localhost rule — a different developer debugging 'login cookies don't stick on localhost' would naturally reach for the cookie-construction code in http.go, which is where the Domain attribute is actually emitted. It never mentions config normalization; its explicit requirement that the raw configured value be preserved is a legitimate design stance (don't mutate user config at load time; sanitize at the point of use). The same bug class was in fact fixed in two places across flipt's history (config-side normalization vs cookie-side localhost handling), which supports that these are two independently-filed approaches to one symptom.
suggestion.conflict: A's fix rewrites AuthenticationSession.Domain at load time; B's fix and its test assume the domain still carries the scheme/port (or is the raw 'localhost') when the cookie code runs, and B's test asserts the loaded config equals the raw value. Naively merging: A's normalization runs first, so B's cookie-site sanitizer is dead code for the tested inputs, and B's test case expecting the preserved raw config value fails; conversely a B-only merge fails A's TestLoad case expecting Domain=='localhost'. The two changes encode incompatible invariants about the same field in the same code path.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's load-time normalization in validate() (getHostname strips scheme+port and overwrites Session.Domain), and in http.go simply use m.Config.Domain as-is for the cookie, omitting the Domain attribute only when it equals 'localhost' (B's RFC concern). B's cookie-site stripping becomes unnecessary because the value is already clean; B's test must be re-based to assert cookie behavior (no scheme/port in Set-Cookie, no Domain attribute for localhost) rather than raw-config preservation. One coherent change satisfies both test intents.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestLoad (config package, new YAML case 'strip session domain scheme/port' expecting Domain=='localhost') and TestCallbackURL (oidc package, trailing-slash cases). B's set: a new TestLoad-style case asserting the configured domain is preserved verbatim (e.g. 'http://localhost:8080' stays as written) plus an http-middleware test (httptest) asserting the emitted state/token cookies have no scheme/port in Domain and omit Domain for localhost. Base code fails both sets. A alone passes A's set but fails B's preservation assertion; B alone passes B's set but fails A's normalization assertion. Combined suite passes only on the reconciled change (normalize at load; cookie code consumes the clean value with the localhost omission).

notes: Key structural facts verified at base commit: (1) validate() only checks Session.Domain is non-empty; no normalization exists. (2) callbackURL(host, provider) in server.go concatenates without slash handling; providerFor feeds it pConfig.RedirectAddress, which is also used as the OAuth redirect_uri, so the double-slash bug breaks the provider round-trip. (3) Both cookie sites in http.go copy m.Config.Domain verbatim; the token cookie in ForwardResponseOption was NOT fixed by A's gold patch (only the state cookie got the localhost omission), which is what makes the cookie-site ticket (B) a believable independent follow-up. The contradictory pairing is the strongest: two canonical fix points (load-time vs use-time) for the same field in the same pipeline, with directly opposed invariants about whether the config value is mutated. It is a 3, not a 4/5, because B's opposing invariant (raw config preserved) must be asserted in B's tests for the naive merge to fail; if B only asserted cookie output, the merged code would pass both and the pair degenerates into duplicate fixes. Complementary is weak (2) because A's gold patch already spans both sides of the only available contract, so any B on the consumer side is largely 'the other half of A'.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a real flipt ticket: deleting a segment that is still referenced by flag rules or rollouts silently succeeds and breaks those flags; the fix must make the delete fail with the exact error 'segment "<ns>/<key>" is in use' on every SQL backend. The natural way (and the way the repo does it) is to flip the database foreign keys on the rule_segments and rollout_segment_references tables from 'delete cascade' to 'delete restrict', plus new migration files and error-mapping code in each backend's store. Task B is the sibling ticket for variants: deleting a variant that is still referenced by a rule's distribution also silently succeeds and breaks the flag; the same developer pattern would flip the rules/distributions foreign keys to 'restrict', add its own migration files, and add its own error mapping. The two collide because they both must (1) add the next-numbered migration in the same four migration directories and (2) edit the same per-backend store files where the delete methods and their database-error-to-API-error mapping live. Worse, B's 'restrict' constraint on the rule side of rule_segments blocks deleting a rule while it still references a segment — which is exactly the step A's own test performs (delete the rule, then delete the segment must succeed). Gluing both changes together therefore breaks A's test; only a solution that keeps both restricts but makes the rule/variant delete paths explicitly clean up their child rows first satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.shared_region: config/migrations/{postgres,mysql,cockroachdb,sqlite3}/ (next migration number in each of the four sequences, both tasks ALTER the same rule_segments/rollout_segment_references/distributions foreign keys) and internal/storage/sql/{postgres,mysql,sqlite}/*.go (adjacent Delete* methods and their constraint-error mapping, e.g. postgres.go lines ~133-235) plus internal/storage/sql/common/segment.go DeleteSegment (lines 376-393) and common/flag.go DeleteVariant (lines 603+)
suggestion.taskA: Deleting a segment that is still used by flag rules or rollouts succeeds today and silently breaks those flags. Block the deletion: each SQL backend's DeleteSegment must fail with the exact error 'segment "<namespace>/<segmentKey>" is in use' while any rule or rollout references the segment, succeed once all references are removed, and behave identically across PostgreSQL, MySQL, CockroachDB and SQLite/LibSQL for both variant and boolean flags.
suggestion.taskB: Deleting a variant that is still used by a flag rule (its distribution) succeeds today and silently breaks the rule. Block the deletion: DeleteVariant must fail with a clear 'variant in use' error while any rule distribution references the variant, and succeed once the referencing rule is removed, with identical behavior across all SQL backends. (The repo even contains a skipped test, TestDeleteVariant_ExistingRule, documenting this exact gap — strong evidence this ticket would be filed independently.)
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is about variants and rules, a different entity with its own user-visible bug, its own skipped test placeholder (TestDeleteVariant_ExistingRule in flag_test.go), and its own foreign keys (rules->variants via distributions). It never mentions segments or A's error message; a maintainer would file it as the mirror-image of A's ticket for a different resource. It is not 'the part of A that A didn't do' — A is complete without it.
suggestion.conflict: Both tasks must add the next migration in the same four numbered migration directories (filename collision, and both ALTER overlapping foreign keys on rule_segments) and both edit the same per-backend store files in the same region. Behaviorally, B's natural 'ON DELETE RESTRICT' on the rule side of rule_segments makes DeleteRule fail while rule_segments rows exist; A's test requires DeleteRule to succeed in exactly that state (create rule -> segment delete blocked -> delete rule -> segment delete succeeds). Naively merging A's and B's changes therefore fails A's test (and symmetrically B's flow if A's migration ordering breaks B's expectations).
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep both sets of RESTRICT constraints (or enforce the checks in Go), and change the delete paths to be explicit rather than cascade-dependent: DeleteRule removes its rule_segments rows (and DeleteVariant removes its distributions rows) inside its transaction before deleting the parent row. Then A's in-use segment error, B's in-use variant error, and both 'delete the referencing object first, then the delete succeeds' flows all hold in one coherent change.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: DBTestSuite segment tests, chiefly the rewritten TestDeleteSegment_ExistingRule (variant-flag and boolean-flag subtests asserting the exact 'segment "ns/key" is in use' error, then success after removing the rule/rollout) plus TestDeleteSegment/TestDeleteSegmentNamespace. B's set: the un-skipped TestDeleteVariant_ExistingRule asserting the variant-in-use error and success after deleting the rule. Combined suite = the whole DBTestSuite run over all backends: it passes only if the collision is reconciled (explicit child-row cleanup + both in-use guards), and fails on the naive merge because the rule deletion required by A's test is blocked by B's restrict constraint.

notes: Repo is flipt at ~v1.50 (base commit 19fe7a3e, pre-fix). Key evidence: (1) the FKs on rule_segments/rollout_segment_references are ON DELETE CASCADE in all four backends' migration 11 (postgres/11, mysql/9, cockroachdb/8, sqlite3/11); A's gold patch adds the next-numbered migration (16/15/13/15) flipping them to RESTRICT. (2) common.Store.DeleteSegment (segment.go:376) is a plain DELETE with no reference check; per-backend stores (postgres.go, mysql.go, sqlite.go) only override Create*/Update* for error mapping — the in-use error mapping for DeleteSegment lives in the gold patch's truncated portion. (3) A skipped mirror test TestDeleteVariant_ExistingRule (flag_test.go:1597) makes the contradictory B ticket feel authentic rather than invented. (4) Contradictory soundness caveat: the behavioral conflict depends on B's author choosing the same migration/RESTRICT approach as A (which the repo's history supports); if B implements the guard purely in Go, the collision shrinks to the shared migration numbers and store-file regions, so I rate 3 not 4. (5) Complementary is weaker (2): the server already passes errors through and the UI lives in a separate TS module, so the only clean Go-side consumer is the gRPC error-status mapping, and B's value is somewhat derivative of A.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A renames Flipt's tracing-destination setting from 'backend' to 'exporter' (and the Go type from TracingBackend to TracingExporter) and adds OTLP as a third allowed destination. An independent Task B would ask to add a different new tracing destination (e.g. SkyWalking) with its own config section, extending the existing 'backend' setting. Both tickets must edit the same struct and enum in internal/config/tracing.go, the same viper defaults map, and the same 'tracing' section of config/flipt.schema.json. A renames the selector field/type while B adds a new value to the old name, so naively gluing the two patches together leaves code referencing a type and field that no longer exist (compile error), and B's 'backend: skywalking' YAML key would no longer decode into the renamed field.
suggestion.shared_region: internal/config/tracing.go (TracingConfig struct, TracingBackend/TracingExporter enum + string maps, setDefaults) and the tracing section of config/flipt.schema.json (the same enum line ['jaeger','zipkin'] is rewritten by both A and B); also the decode-hook registration in internal/config/config.go
suggestion.taskA: Rename tracing.backend to tracing.exporter, allow jaeger/zipkin/otlp, add a tracing.otlp.endpoint default of localhost:4317, keep the deprecated tracing.jaeger.enabled working with a warning that references tracing.exporter, and update the JSON schema and sample configs.
suggestion.taskB: Add SkyWalking as a supported tracing destination: a new value on the tracing backend enum, a tracing.skywalking config section (host/port), a 'backend: skywalking' YAML case in TestLoad, and a skywalking entry in the JSON schema's tracing enum/properties.
suggestion.independence_rationale: Requests for additional tracing backends are a normal, recurring category of ticket in observability software and are motivated purely by a user's existing infrastructure (SkyWalking deployments), with no knowledge of or need for the backend->exporter rename or OTLP. It reads as its own feature request against the base code, not as a step toward A.
suggestion.conflict: A deletes/renames TracingBackend to TracingExporter and the Backend field to Exporter (mapstructure tag 'backend' -> 'exporter'); B's solution adds TracingSkyWalking to the TracingBackend enum, a SkyWalking field to TracingConfig, and a 'backend: skywalking' test fixture. Merged naively: B's constants/fields reference the removed type (compile failure), both patches rewrite the same schema enum line differently, and B's 'backend:' YAML no longer decodes after A's tag rename, so B's TestLoad case fails while A's deprecation-message and exporter cases define incompatible expectations for the same lines.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: rename to TracingExporter/Exporter, include both new values (otlp and skywalking) in the enum and string maps, add both otlp and skywalking sections to TracingConfig, setDefaults, and the JSON schema (enum ['jaeger','zipkin','otlp','skywalking']), and update B's fixture to use the 'exporter:' key. Optionally keep 'type TracingBackend = TracingExporter' as a deprecated alias so B's base-written tests still compile; the reconciled code passes both suites.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestTracingExporter, TestLoad (exporter/deprecation cases), TestJSONSchema, TestCacheBackend (from fail_to_pass). B's set: B's own TestLoad case for 'backend: skywalking', an extended enum String/MarshalJSON test, TestJSONSchema. Combined suite runs both against the merged tree: base fails both; A-alone passes A's; B-alone passes B's; naive merge fails (compile error and/or B's decode case); the reconciled rename-plus-both-destinations change passes everything.

notes: Key structural facts verified at base commit: TracingConfig{Enabled, Backend TracingBackend, Jaeger, Zipkin} in internal/config/tracing.go; the only non-test consumer of cfg.Tracing.Backend is the switch in internal/cmd/grpc.go (lines 139-173), so A's rename necessarily touches grpc.go and likely adds the OTLP runtime case there — this kills the complementary angle as a decomposition. go.mod has no otlptrace dependency, so A's patch must also add one (in the truncated portion). The contradictory angle is the best fit: any ticket that adds a new tracing destination value collides with A's rename of the selector field/type and rewrites the same schema enum line; SkyWalking is the example, but the same logic applies to any new destination. Confidence capped at 3 because B's tests written against the base reference the TracingBackend symbol A deletes (needs a deprecated alias or test adaptation for the combined suite to compile), and B's runtime side would need a new exporter dependency that the repo doesn't have.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A reworks the shared polling helper so it owns its own lifecycle: the poller is built with a context and an update callback, runs a no-argument polling loop on its internal context, and gains a Close() that cancels that context and blocks until the background polling task has fully finished. Task B is a separate, independently-motivated ticket: because several Flipt instances typically poll the same git/S3/Azure/OCI backend on identical fixed schedules, they all hit the backend at the same instant (thundering herd); B asks for a randomized jitter to be added to each polling interval. Both tasks must rewrite the very same polling loop in internal/storage/fs/poll.go (the Poller.Poll method and its ticker setup). A's version of the loop is a parameterless method driven by an internal context; B's version is the old method with a randomized ticker. Glued together they are two incompatible definitions of the same loop, so the combined test suite fails until someone writes one loop that both derives its ticker from interval+jitter AND honors the internal context/Close semantics.
suggestion.shared_region: internal/storage/fs/poll.go — the Poller struct, NewPoller, and especially the Poller.Poll method body (the ticker setup and the for/select loop). A restructures it for lifecycle (internal context, cancel, Close that waits); B modifies the same loop's timing (adds jitter to the interval).
suggestion.taskA: Polling goroutines in the declarative storage backends (git, local, S3, Azure Blob, OCI) have no lifecycle management: after a SnapshotStore is created, its background poller keeps running forever. Make the shared Poller manage its own context and cancellation, expose Close() (io.Closer) that cancels the context and blocks until the polling goroutine has terminated, and have every SnapshotStore delegate its Close() to the poller so shutdown is deterministic.
suggestion.taskB: Declarative storage polling hammers the backend in lockstep: every Flipt instance configured against the same git repo / S3 bucket / OCI registry polls on the exact same fixed interval (30s/60s), so all instances issue fetches at the same moment, creating periodic load spikes on the remote. Add randomized jitter to the polling interval in the shared poller so successive checks are spread out, while keeping the configured interval as the mean/upper bound.
suggestion.independence_rationale: Jittering a polling interval is a standard, self-contained reliability ticket that a maintainer would file without any knowledge of the lifecycle work: its motivation is remote-backend load synchronization, its scope is the poller's timing, and it is testable purely by observing the deltas between successive update invocations. It does not mention Close, shutdown, or goroutine leaks, and it would be filed against the base code exactly as-is (where Poll already takes ctx and update). It is not 'the other half' of A — A is about when polling stops, B is about when it ticks.
suggestion.conflict: Both solutions rewrite the same method body. A's Poll becomes a parameterless loop over the poller's internal context (ticker built from p.interval only, plus a Close that cancels and waits on the goroutine). B's Poll keeps the old signature but changes the ticker construction to interval+jitter. Naively merging the two patches yields either a duplicate/competing definition of the loop or a loop that has jitter but no internal-context/Close semantics (or Close semantics but a fixed interval): the package fails to build, or A's lifecycle tests and B's jitter test cannot both pass against the glued code.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent Poller: NewPoller(logger, ctx, update, opts...) derives an internal cancellable context and stores the update func; Poll() (no args) builds its ticker from the configured interval plus a per-tick random jitter and loops on the internal context; Close() cancels the internal context and blocks until the loop returns. This single loop satisfies A's wait-for-termination/idempotent/no-update-after-close tests and B's variable-interval test simultaneously.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the new internal/storage/fs/poll_test.go (TestPollerCloseWaitsForGoroutine, TestPollerCloseIdempotent, TestPollerNoUpdateAfterClose) plus the store tests that now call source.Close() in t.Cleanup (local/git/s3/azblob/oci store tests). B's set: a poller test that records the timestamps of successive update invocations (e.g., 4+ ticks at a small interval) and asserts the deltas are not all identical and each falls within [0, interval+jitterCap]; it uses the base Poll(ctx, update) signature so it compiles and passes on base+B. On the base commit both sets fail (no Close/wait semantics; constant intervals). A alone passes A's set but fails B's jitter test; B alone passes B's set but fails A's lifecycle tests. Only the reconciled single-loop implementation passes the combined suite.

notes: Base commit confirmed: internal/storage/fs/poll.go has Poller{logger, interval, notify func(modified bool)}, NewPoller(logger, opts...), and Poll(ctx, update func(context.Context)(bool,error)) — no context ownership, no Close. All five stores (git, local, s3, azblob, oci) fire `go storagefs.NewPoller(...).Poll(ctx, s.update)` in their constructors with no way to stop them; the SnapshotStore interface is only View+Stringer; the gRPC server's onShutdown stack covers listener/db/tracing/cache/audit but not the declarative store. The contradictory family is the stronger of the two: the jitter ticket is a genuinely independent, commonly-filed reliability change that collides on the exact lines A restructures (the Poll loop/ticker). Its soundness rests on B's test using the base Poll signature so it compiles against base+B, and on the naive merge producing a non-compiling or semantically-inconsistent duplicate of the loop. A slightly weaker alternative B in the same region: 'run an initial update immediately on poller start instead of waiting for the first tick' — also independent, also collides on the same loop, but less distinctive. The complementary family is really one feature (store Close + server teardown) split at the interface boundary, so it is scored low; A's standalone testability is what keeps it above 'pure decomposition'.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A (the original ticket) moves flag caching down into the storage layer and lets clients opt out of the cache via a 'no-store' request header. To do that, it rewrites the two small helper functions (set/get) inside the cached storage wrapper so they take an extra parameter saying how to encode the value, and splits them into JSON and protobuf variants. An independent Task B — 'the evaluation path still hits the database for rollouts and distributions on every evaluation even when the cache is enabled; cache those two reads too' — is a believable separate performance ticket. B's new code is written against the current helpers and calls them with the old three-argument form. If both agents merge blindly, B's new methods call a helper whose signature A just changed, so the combined code does not even compile. One person reconciling both would simply have B's new methods call A's new JSON-encoding helper, and everything builds and passes.
suggestion.shared_region: internal/storage/cache/cache.go — the unexported set/get helpers (A changes their signatures into setJSON/getJSON/setProto/getProto with a marshal/unmarshal function parameter) plus the cache-key const block; B's new GetEvaluationRollouts/GetEvaluationDistributions methods on the same Store call those same helpers
suggestion.taskA: Flag lookups are cached only in the gRPC interceptor and clients cannot opt out of cached values: move flag caching into the cached storage Store (protobuf-encoded, key s:f:<ns>:<key>), rename the request-level interceptor to EvaluationCacheUnaryInterceptor (dropping the flag/invalidation cases), and honor Cache-Control: no-store by marking the request context so the storage cache skips writes.
suggestion.taskB: With caching enabled, the evaluator still issues a database query for GetEvaluationRollouts and GetEvaluationDistributions on every single evaluation — only GetEvaluationRules is cached by the storage cache layer. Add caching for those two reads in the same cached Store, using the existing JSON encoding and the same s:… key convention, so enabling the cache actually reduces database load on the full evaluation path.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is scoped to two different storage methods (rollouts and distributions) with its own measurable problem (DB load per evaluation) and its own tests; it does not mention no-store, flags, or the interceptor at all. A maintainer chasing 'cache is on but the DB is still hot' would naturally file it after or alongside A. It is a sibling ticket in the same subsystem, not a step of A: A's ticket is specifically about flag reads and the client opt-out, and B would still make sense if A's no-store/flag parts never happened (B only collides because both touch the shared helpers).
suggestion.conflict: A's solution removes the 3-argument set(ctx,key,value)/get(ctx,key,value) and replaces them with 4-argument versions taking an encode/decode function (setJSON/getJSON/setProto/getProto). B's solution, written independently against the base commit, adds GetEvaluationRollouts/GetEvaluationDistributions that call s.set(ctx, key, rollouts) and s.get(ctx, key, &rollouts) with the old 3-argument form. Naively merging (git auto-merge keeps both hunks since they are in different regions of the file) yields code that fails to compile: not enough arguments in B's calls. Even a hand 'fix' that routes B through setProto would be wrong, since rollouts/distributions are plain structs, not protobuf messages.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's helper refactor and write B's two new methods against it: cacheHit := s.getJSON(ctx, key, &rollouts) on read and s.setJSON(ctx, key, rollouts) on miss, with keys like s:er-r:<ns>:<flag> / s:ed:<ruleID>. Both tickets' behaviors then coexist in one file.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the given fail_to_pass tests (TestCacheControlUnaryInterceptor, TestCacheControlHeaderKey, TestEvaluationCacheUnaryInterceptor_*, TestGetFlagCached, TestGetJSONHandleGetError, TestGetJSONHandleUnmarshalError, TestSetJSONHandleMarshalError, TestSetSkipsWhenDoNotStore). B's set: new tests in internal/storage/cache/cache_test.go modeled on the existing TestGetEvaluationRulesCached (e.g. TestGetEvaluationRolloutsCached, TestGetEvaluationDistributionsCached) using the existing cacheSpy: assert the underlying store mock is not called on hit, and that the spy recorded the expected key and JSON payload on miss. Base commit fails both sets (B's methods don't exist as overrides, so the spy records nothing); each solution passes its own set; the naive merge fails to compile (fails everything); the reconciled code passes the combined suite.

notes: Primary risk for the contradictory pair: B lives in the same subsystem as A, so a strict reviewer could call it 'the part of A that A didn't do' — mitigated by scoping B to rollouts/distributions (different methods, different motivation) rather than to flag caching. A second, weaker contradictory B was considered: an independent 'honor Cache-Control: no-cache' ticket that would create its own CacheControlUnaryInterceptor/constants in internal/server/middleware/grpc/middleware.go, colliding with A's identically-named symbols — real duplicate-definition conflict, but weaker independence since no-store and no-cache are two directives of the same header and would likely be filed together. For the complementary pair, note that sdk/go files are marked 'Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT', so B must be implemented as a small hand-written file (e.g. sdk/go/cache.go) — plausible but worth flagging to the authoring step. The complementary integration test requires the live-server dagger harness (cache suite), which already exists and was extended by A's test patch (FLIPT_CACHE_TTL=500ms), so it is feasible. Base-commit facts verified: internal/storage/cache/cache.go has only GetEvaluationRules cached with 3-arg set/get; the interceptor has GetFlag/UpdateFlag/DeleteFlag/variant invalidation cases that A removes; runtime.MetadataPrefix is 'x-'; the SDK has no header/metadata helper beyond the auth token.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a refactor/bugfix ticket: the code that decides whether the running build is a real release and whether a newer version exists is written inline in the CLI's main file, and it wrongly treats pre-release builds (versions ending in -rc, e.g. 1.0.0-rc1) as proper releases. A asks for that logic to move into a new reusable internal/release package with testable functions, and for rc/dev/snapshot versions to be classified correctly. Task B is a separate, real operations ticket: when Flipt starts, it phones home to the GitHub API to check for updates using an HTTP client created with no timeout, so if GitHub is unreachable or slow the server startup can hang indefinitely; B asks for that update-check client to be given a bounded timeout. Both tickets must touch the exact same few lines in cmd/flipt/main.go — the place where the GitHub client is created and the getLatestRelease function that calls the GitHub API. A's fix deletes those lines (moving the logic into internal/release), while B's fix edits those very lines in place to attach a timed-out HTTP client. Two agents working blindly produce a broken combination: A's patch removes the function B patched, so the timeout never lands anywhere, and the merged code fails B's test (and A's tests fail on the unpatched base). A single reconciled change — the new release package's GitHub checker constructed with a timeout-bounded HTTP client — satisfies both tickets at once.
suggestion.shared_region: cmd/flipt/main.go — the update-check code path: getLatestRelease(ctx) and the github.NewClient(nil) call inside it (lines ~373-381 at base commit). A deletes/moves this into internal/release/check.go's githubReleaseChecker; B must modify the same client construction to add an HTTP timeout.
suggestion.taskA: Release/update checking is not reusable, and '-rc' builds are misclassified as proper releases. Extract release detection and latest-release lookup into a dedicated internal/release package exposing Is(version) (false for dev/snapshot/rc identifiers), an Info result type (CurrentVersion, LatestVersion, UpdateAvailable, LatestVersionURL), and Check(ctx, version) with an injectable latest-release dependency; wire cmd/flipt/main.go to use it and remove the inline isRelease()/getLatestRelease() logic.
suggestion.taskB: Server startup can hang when the update check cannot reach GitHub. The update-availability check performed at startup uses a GitHub API client built from a default HTTP client with no timeout, so a network partition or slow GitHub response blocks Flipt from starting. The ticket: bound the update-check network call — construct the client used by getLatestRelease with an HTTP client that has a finite Timeout (e.g. a few seconds) so startup degrades gracefully instead of hanging.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by an operational reliability bug (unbounded network call at startup) that exists independently of A's refactor and of the rc misclassification: at the base commit the client is github.NewClient(nil) with no timeout, so a maintainer could file 'update check hangs startup when GitHub is unreachable' today, with zero knowledge of the release-package extraction. It is not 'the other half of A' — A is about where the logic lives and how versions are classified; B is about how long the network call is allowed to take. The collision is purely that both happen to need to touch the same client-construction site.
suggestion.conflict: A's solution removes getLatestRelease and the github.NewClient(nil) call from cmd/flipt/main.go (moving them into internal/release/check.go as githubReleaseChecker, still with github.NewClient(nil)). B's solution edits getLatestRelease in cmd/flipt/main.go to use a client with a timeout. Naively merging: A's deletion wins and B's hunk has nothing to apply to (or, if concatenated, leaves a duplicate/orphaned getLatestRelease that no longer compiles or is dead code). In either case the merged code has no timeout on the update-check client, so B's test asserting the client's HTTP timeout fails; on the base, A's tests fail because internal/release does not exist.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: create internal/release with Is/Info/Check and a githubReleaseChecker whose client is built as github.NewClient(&http.Client{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}) (or equivalent), and update cmd/flipt/main.go to call release.Check and drop the inline isRelease()/getLatestRelease(). This satisfies A (reusable package, rc/dev/snapshot classified as non-releases) and B (update-check call is time-bounded) simultaneously.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestCheck and TestIs in internal/release/check_test.go (mock releaseChecker; verify Info population and version classification). B's set: a new test in package main (cmd/flipt), e.g. TestUpdateCheckClientTimeout, which asserts the GitHub client used for the update check has a non-zero HTTPClient.Timeout (e.g. 5s) — written so it compiles both pre- and post-A by referencing the client construction site. Combined suite: base fails both (no release package; no timeout); A-only fails B's timeout test; B-only fails A's tests; naive merge fails B's timeout test (A deleted the function B patched); the reconciled code (timeout on githubReleaseChecker's client) passes A's and B's tests together.

notes: Base-commit facts that ground the assessment: cmd/flipt/main.go has no test files at all (cmd/flipt/*_test.go does not exist), so B's timeout test would be the first in package main — feasible but a new test home. The unbounded client is real: github.NewClient(nil) at main.go:374, and the check runs synchronously inside run() before the servers start (main.go:241-274), so a hung GitHub call does delay startup — B's motivation is genuine. The conflict is structural (A deletes the exact lines B edits) rather than semantic (both changes are ultimately compatible), which is why confidence is 3 not higher: a reconciler can satisfy both, and B's intent could in principle be re-applied to A's new githubReleaseChecker, but a naive merge of the two independent patches leaves the timeout unapplied and fails the combined suite. Also worth recording: A's gold patch additionally changes telemetry gating (disables telemetry for non-release versions and moves the info.Flipt construction after that check) — that part is a behavior change a separate ticket could also target, but it is clearly part of A's own diff, so it was not used as B. The go.mod change in A's patch (promoting google.golang.org/genproto to a direct dependency) is incidental to the new package's imports.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A asks: when Vuls checks an Oracle Linux or Amazon Linux vulnerability database entry that has no architecture recorded, stop silently guessing and raise an error saying the OVAL database is old and must be re-fetched. Task B (independent ticket) asks: Vuls currently matches a vulnerability entry against a package even when the entry names a different CPU architecture (e.g. an aarch64 entry matched on an x86_64 host), which causes false positives; make the architecture match strict — an entry that names an architecture only applies if it exactly equals the installed architecture, and entries with a named architecture must be skipped when the installed architecture is unknown. Both tickets land on the exact same two lines of the same function (the architecture check inside isOvalDefAffected in oval/util.go, base lines 299-301). A's official fix deliberately leaves that line's lenient behavior untouched (an entry with empty architecture still matches anything), while B's fix rewrites that line into a strict rule. Two agents editing the same lines independently produce either duplicated/conflicting arch logic or one side's behavior silently overriding the other's, so a naive merge fails at least one side's tests; a single reconciled edit (strict arch matching for everyone, plus the Oracle/Amazon empty-arch error) satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: oval/util.go, function isOvalDefAffected, the arch-matching lines (base lines 299-301: `if ovalPack.Arch != "" && req.arch != ovalPack.Arch { continue }`), plus A's signature change of the same function and its two callers getDefsByPackNameFromOvalDB / getDefsByPackNameViaHTTP
suggestion.taskA: Display an error for missing arch in OVAL DB for Oracle and Amazon Linux: when evaluating OVAL definitions for Oracle/Amazon, if the matching package entry has an empty arch field, return an error stating the OVAL DB is outdated and needs re-fetching (text contains 'OVAL DB for <family> is old'); callers getDefsByPackNameFromOvalDB (return immediately, wrap with 'Failed to exec isOvalAffected') and getDefsByPackNameViaHTTP (skip the definition, collect errors, wrap with 'Failed to detect OVAL') must surface it. Edits confined to oval/util.go; other families unaffected.
suggestion.taskB: OVAL matching ignores the architecture of the installed package: an OVAL entry that names a specific arch (e.g. aarch64) is currently matched against an x86_64 host only when the arches differ it is skipped, but an entry with an empty arch matches every host, and hosts with unknown arch still match arch-specific entries in some paths. Make arch matching strict in isOvalDefAffected: if the OVAL entry names an arch, it must exactly equal the installed package arch or the entry is skipped; if the installed arch is unknown (empty), skip any entry that names an arch. Applies to all distros, no new error return, no change to callers.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a classic false-positive/false-negative accuracy ticket about arch-specific OVAL entries (multi-arch distros like Oracle Linux 8/9 aarch64 and Amazon 2023 aarch64 make this a real, commonly-filed vuln-scanner complaint). It is motivated by wrong match results, not by database staleness, and it never mentions the missing-arch error, the 'OVAL DB is old' message, or A's callers. A maintainer could file it on its own; it is not 'the other half of A' — A is about erroring on incomplete data, B is about tightening the matching rule on complete data. The two only collide because both must touch the same arch-check lines in isOvalDefAffected.
suggestion.conflict: A's required solution keeps the lenient base line intact (per A's requirements: 'if arch is present and differs -> not affected; if equal -> evaluate; version parse failure must not become the missing-arch error' — i.e. the existing `ovalPack.Arch != "" && req.arch != ovalPack.Arch` continue stays, and an empty-entry-arch still matches for non-Oracle/Amazon families). B's solution replaces that same line with a strict rule (named arch must equal installed arch; unknown installed arch skips named-arch entries). Naively merging both diffs yields two contradictory arch checks in the same loop body (e.g. B's strict continue plus A's lenient continue, or a duplicated switch block), which is either dead/conflicting logic or, when one side's line wins, breaks the other side's tests: B's test 'Oracle entry with arch aarch64 vs x86_64 host -> not affected, no error' fails under A-only code because A's lenient line still skips it only by accident while A's 'RedHat empty-arch entry still matches' and B's 'unknown installed arch skips named-arch entry' cases directly contradict each other on the same lines. The combined suite therefore cannot pass with a naive concatenation.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent edit in isOvalDefAffected: (1) add the error return to the signature; (2) for Oracle/Amazon, if the matching entry's arch is empty, return the 'OVAL DB for <family> is old' error; (3) for all families, apply B's strict rule — entry names an arch and it differs from (or installed arch is unknown) -> skip; (4) keep the ksplice/modularity/kernel-major filters and version comparison unchanged; (5) update both callers to handle the new error exactly as A requires. This single change passes A's three tests and B's strict-matching tests together.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestIsOvalDefAffected (wantErr cases for Oracle/Amazon empty arch, same-arch/different-arch/no-error cases), TestGetDefsByPackNameFromOvalDBArchError, TestGetDefsByPackNameViaHTTPArchError (both use the mock DB / httptest server added by A's test patch). B's set: new table cases in TestIsOvalDefAffected asserting strict arch behavior (named arch vs different installed arch -> not affected; named arch vs empty installed arch -> not affected; empty entry arch on RedHat/CentOS -> still affected; empty entry arch on Oracle/Amazon -> error). Combined suite = both test files merged into oval/util_test.go, run against the merged oval/util.go. Base code fails both sets (no error return exists; lenient arch matching). suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A asks that when a scanned RPM line has a source filename that doesn't follow the normal pattern (e.g. elasticsearch-8.17.0-1-src.rpm), the scanner should not crash the whole scan: it should record a warning, keep the binary package, and skip the source package. It also asks that the epoch (the number before a colon) be read from the source filename itself. Task B is a different, independently reportable bug: the source package's version is built by copying the epoch from the binary package's row instead of from the source RPM filename, so when the two epochs differ (a package rebuilt with a new epoch), the source version is reported wrong and vulnerability matching against source-based data misbehaves. Both fixes must rewrite the same few lines inside the same function (the block that parses fields[5] and builds the source package version), and the two rewrites disagree about what that block should do when the filename doesn't parse, so pasting both changes together breaks one of the two test sets.

suggestion.taskA: Original ticket: parsing RPM installed-package lines aborts the entire scan with a fatal error when SOURCERPM does not match <name>-<version>-<release>.<arch>.rpm (e.g. 'elasticsearch 0 8.17.0 1 x86_64 elasticsearch-8.17.0-1-src.rpm (none)'). Expected: append a warning, continue scanning, still emit the binary package, and skip the source package. Additionally, epochs embedded in the source filename (e.g. '1:bar-9-123a.src.rpm') must be parsed correctly so binary and source versions carry the epoch.
suggestion.taskB: Separate ticket: 'Source package version uses the wrong epoch'. When the source RPM filename carries an epoch different from the epoch reported for the binary package (e.g. line 'foo 1 2.0 1 x86_64 foo-2.0-1.src.rpm' where the binary row says epoch 1 but the source rpm is epoch 2), the recorded source version is built from the binary row's epoch field instead of from the source filename, so the source package version is wrong. The source version should be derived from the epoch parsed out of the source RPM filename, not copied from the binary package's epoch column.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by a distinct observable defect (epoch provenance in SrcPackage.Version) with its own reproducer where the binary-row epoch and filename epoch disagree; it never mentions non-standard filenames, warnings, or scan aborts. A maintainer could file it purely from seeing a wrong source version in a scan result. The weakness: in the normal rpm -qa flow the filename epoch equals the binary-row epoch, so B's bug only manifests in the rpm -qf path or epoch-rebuild edge cases, which makes B slightly contrived — hence confidence 3, not higher.

A's change turns the 'splitFileName returned an error' branch into: append to o.warns and return (nil, nil) — i.e. abandon the version-building code below for that line. suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a bug report: vulnerabilities that only carry a severity word (like HIGH from a distro's OVAL data) are converted into a fake CVSS version-2 number, so the tool's headline score, its score filtering, its impact sorting, and its per-severity counts all use the wrong number, and there is no 'Critical' bucket at all. Task B is a separate, plausible ticket: the one-line CVE summary printed in reports and email subjects ('Total: 12 (High:5 Medium:4 Low:2 ?:1)') has no Critical bucket, so a fleet with a 9.8 CVE looks the same as one whose worst CVE is 8.9; users want 'Critical' broken out. Both fixes must rewrite the same two functions in models/vulninfos.go: the per-severity counter (which score to read and which buckets exist) and the summary line formatter (the literal format string). A's version of the counter reads the CVSS3 score first and adds Critical; B's version, written independently against today's code, keeps the existing CVSS2-first reading and only adds a Critical case. The two summary-line format strings cannot both be the final text of the same function, and the two counter implementations disagree on which score decides the bucket, so naively merging both changes leaves one side's tests failing.
suggestion.shared_region: models/vulninfos.go — VulnInfos.CountGroupBySeverity() (lines ~57-76) and VulnInfos.FormatCveSummary() (lines ~79-89); A's gold patch rewrites both, and B's fix must edit the same functions (plus the hardcoded twin summary strings in report/email.go lines ~58-66 for the one-email mode).

A scan whose worst CVE scores 9.8 renders identically in the summary to one whose worst scores 8.9, which misleads triage. Add a Critical bucket (score >= 9.0) to the severity grouping and to the summary line, in both the normal and ignore-unscored variants, and in the e-mail one-line summary.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B reads as its own ticket: it is about the presentation of the summary line and the absence of a Critical bucket, which a maintainer would file from user complaints about reports/subjects without ever touching the CVSS2-vs-CVSS3 scoring confusion that A is about. B is fully implementable and valuable on today's code (add a 9.0+ case to the existing counter and extend the format strings), and it does not require or mention A's re-scoring of severity-derived entries. It is not 'the other half of A': A's core deliverables (Cvss2Scores/Cvss3Scores contents, MaxCvssScore preference, filtering, sorting, Format()) stand on their own, and B's deliverable (summary line with Critical) stands on its own.

Naively gluing both (e.g., A's body plus B's format string, or B's counter plus A's summary) yields either A's tests failing (no Critical bucket / wrong score preference) or B's tests failing (summary text or bucket counts disagree).
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: keep A's CVSS3-first score selection in CountGroupBySeverity, add the Critical bucket (9.0+) there, and emit A's 'Critical:%d' format strings in both variants of FormatCveSummary (and the matching strings in report/email.go). If two agents work blindly, one keeps the tag-mandatory logic and the other removes it, so the merged code either still rejects digest-only images (failing A's tests) or still accepts the malformed tag (failing B's tests). One reconciled version — 'require a name; if a tag is present it must be well-formed; a digest alone is also fine' — satisfies both.

A configured image tag containing an extra colon (e.g. 'nginx:1.14.1:extra' or 'ubuntu:20.04:typo') passes validation and only fails later, confusingly, during the image pull. The contradictory family is the stronger fit: parseInstalledPackages is a real, independently-motivated data-loss region (name-only map key drops multi-arch/multi-version entries) that A's restructure also touches, giving a genuine same-region collision that a single reconciled edit (pointer + kernel dedup + composite key) resolves.
