suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a ticket about the ScanResult helper RemoveRaspbianPackFromResult: it must return a pointer, giving back a filtered copy for Raspberry Pi (Raspbian) systems and the original object for everything else, and every place that calls it (including the Debian CVE-detection routine in gost/debian.go) has to be adapted. Task B is a separate, real bug: in gost/debian.go, when the Debian Security Tracker is queried over HTTP, the code computes a filtered copy of the scan result (with Raspberry-Pi-only packages removed) but then passes the UNfiltered original to the HTTP request builder, so Pi-specific packages are still sent to the tracker and get 404s. B's natural one-line fix changes that same HTTP call line to pass the filtered copy. A's official fix rewrites the entire surrounding function and deletes the filtered-copy variable B's fix depends on, so gluing the two patches together does not compile; a single reconciled change (filter once before both OVAL and gost run, using the new pointer API) satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.shared_region: gost/debian.go, func (deb Debian) DetectUnfixed — specifically the HTTP branch line `responses, err := getAllUnfixedCvesViaHTTP(r, url)` (and the `scanResult` local variable around it), which A's gold patch rewrites/deletes and B's fix must edit; secondarily models/scanresults.go RemoveRaspbianPackFromResult whose callers A must update
suggestion.taskA: RemoveRaspbianPackFromResult in the ScanResult model should return a pointer: for Family=Raspbian it must return a pointer to a new ScanResult with all Raspberry-Pi-specific packages (per IsRaspbianPackage) excluded from both Packages and SrcPackages; for every other family it must return a pointer to the original, unmodified ScanResult. All call sites must be updated to the pointer API.
suggestion.taskB: Bug: when Vuls is configured to fetch Debian Security Tracker data over HTTP (gost-url mode), scanning a Raspberry Pi still sends requests for Pi-specific packages (e.g. libraspberrypi-dev, rpi-eeprom, *-rpi-* packages) that the tracker does not know, producing 404s and wasted requests. The code already computes a filtered copy of the scan result with those packages removed, but the HTTP branch of the Debian gost client ignores it and builds requests from the unfiltered result; the DB branch does use the filtered copy. The package exclusion must apply consistently in both HTTP and DB modes.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a genuine, verifiable bug in the base commit: gost/debian.go lines 57-68 compute `scanResult = r.RemoveRaspbianPackFromResult()` with the comment 'Debian Security Tracker does not support Package for Raspbian, so skip it', yet line 68 calls getAllUnfixedCvesViaHTTP(r, url) with the unfiltered r. A developer who sees 404s while scanning a Pi in HTTP mode would file exactly this ticket without ever touching the pointer-return question in A; its motivation (correct request filtering) is orthogonal to A's motivation (clarifying the helper's return type/aliasing semantics).
suggestion.conflict: A's gold solution rewrites DetectUnfixed: it deletes the `scanResult` local variable entirely, renames DetectUnfixed to DetectCVEs, and replaces the HTTP call with getCvesWithFixStateViaHTTP(r, url, s). B's canonical fix edits the very line A deletes (`getAllUnfixedCvesViaHTTP(r, url)` -> pass the filtered result). Naively merging (git auto-merge or concatenating the patches) yields either a conflict or code referencing the now-undefined `scanResult` / calling a restructured function, i.e. a compile failure, so the combined test suite cannot run.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Adopt A's pointer API and function restructuring, and satisfy B by ensuring the Raspbian-filtered result is what the HTTP request builder sees — either by applying `r = r.RemoveRaspbianPackFromResult()` once in detector.DetectPkgCves before both OVAL and gost run (which is what the gold patch actually does), or by passing the filtered pointer into the HTTP branch inside the restructured gost function. Both A's model test and B's HTTP-filtering test then pass against one coherent change.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestRemoveRaspbianPackFromResult (models/scanresults_test.go) — fails on base because the test dereferences the return value (`r = *r.RemoveRaspbianPackFromResult()`), a compile error against the value-returning base signature. B's set: a new gost-package test (e.g. TestDebianDetectUnfixedHTTPExcludesRaspbianPackages) that runs the Debian client in HTTP mode against an httptest server with a Raspbian ScanResult containing both normal and Pi-specific packages, asserting no request path contains a Pi-specific package name; fails on base because the HTTP branch uses the unfiltered r. Combined suite: run both packages' tests against the merged code — the naive merge fails to build (undefined scanResult / conflicting rewrite of DetectUnfixed), while the reconciled change passes both.

notes: Verified at base commit 43b46cb: (1) models/scanresults.go:294 RemoveRaspbianPackFromResult returns a value ScanResult, so A's test (which dereferences it) fails to compile on base; (2) gost/debian.go:57-68 contains the real inconsistency B targets — filtered `scanResult` computed but HTTP branch passes unfiltered `r`, while the DB branch iterates `scanResult`; (3) A's gold patch deletes the `scanResult` variable and rewrites the exact HTTP line B must change, giving a true same-line collision; (4) gost has no existing _test.go files, so B's test is net-new but straightforward (httptest server + HTTP-mode GostConf). The contradictory pairing is the strong one; the main authoring risk is that B's fix is small and an author could write it in a non-colliding form (e.g. in-place filtering at the top of DetectUnfixed), so B's canonical fix should be pinned to passing the filtered result to the HTTP request builder. Complementary family does not meet the soundness bar.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a refactor: pull the syslog settings out of the main configuration file into their own small package, and as part of that, delete the Windows-only copy of the main configuration file so there is just one configuration file for all operating systems. Task B is an unrelated Windows feature: add a new 'send report to the Windows Event Log' option, which requires adding a new field to the Windows-only copy of the main configuration file (the exact file A deletes) and wiring it into the Windows report command. Both tickets therefore fight over the same struct definition in the same file: A removes the file entirely, B adds a field to it. If both changes are applied blindly, the Windows build either loses the new field (file deleted) or fails to compile (field added to a file that no longer exists / duplicated struct). A single reconciled change keeps the one unified configuration file and adds the new Windows field into it.
suggestion.shared_region: The Config struct definition: config/config.go (non-Windows, line ~53 Syslog field) and config/config_windows.go (Windows, lines 28-62). A changes the Syslog field type in config.go, removes the //go:build !windows tag from config.go, and deletes config_windows.go; B must add a new field to the Config struct in config_windows.go.
suggestion.taskA: Reorganize syslog configuration into a dedicated configuration component: expose a public syslog.Conf struct with a public Validate() method in a new config/syslog package, keep observable validation behavior identical, and make the build pass when the dedicated public type is expected.
suggestion.taskB: Add Windows Event Log reporting: the report command on Windows cannot write results to the Windows Event Log even though every other OS supports syslog. Introduce an EventLog report configuration (enabled flag, log name) in the Windows Config struct, add an -to-eventlog flag to the Windows report command, and wire it to a new EventLog writer, mirroring how the non-Windows side handles syslog.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a platform feature ticket a Windows-support maintainer would file on its own: the Windows report command (subcmds/report_windows.go) deliberately has no -to-syslog and no syslog field, so 'no Windows-native log output' is a real, pre-existing gap independent of any refactor. It never mentions syslog or the config/syslog package; its motivation is feature parity for Windows users.
suggestion.conflict: A's gold solution deletes config/config_windows.go and unifies everything into config/config.go (removing the build tags). B's solution adds a field to the Config struct inside config/config_windows.go. Naively merging both changes either drops B's field (the file is gone, so the Windows build loses the feature and report_windows.go no longer compiles against the unified struct) or produces two conflicting Config definitions. The two edits to the same struct/file cannot both stand.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's unified config/config.go (single Config struct, syslog.Conf field, no build tags, config_windows.go deleted) and add B's EventLog field to that single struct; wire B's -to-eventlog flag in subcmds/report_windows.go to the unified field. One coherent change satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: config/syslog/syslogconf_test.go TestSyslogConfValidate (plus the removal of the old test from config/config_test.go). B's set: a new test asserting the Windows Config struct exposes the EventLog field and that the Windows report command registers the -to-eventlog flag (e.g., a test built with GOOS=windows, or a compile-time assertion). Combined suite: run both against the merged code — it passes only if the unified Config struct contains both the syslog.Conf field and the EventLog field; a naive merge (file deleted or duplicated struct) fails to build or fails B's test.

notes: Base-commit structure that makes the contradictory pair work: config/config.go has //go:build !windows and a Syslog SyslogConf field; config/config_windows.go is a full duplicate of the Config struct for Windows with no Syslog field; config/syslogconf.go is !windows-only; subcmds/report.go is !scanner && !windows while subcmds/report_windows.go exists. A's gold patch deletes config_windows.go and unifies into config.go, so any independent Windows-side ticket that edits the Config struct in config_windows.go collides mechanically. The collision is real but somewhat mechanical (hinges on A deleting the file), and B's 'missing Windows log output' motivation is plausible but invented — hence confidence 3, not higher. Complementary fails the independence bar: the only consumer of the new type is code A itself touched, and A's test is a pure unit test with no cross-ticket contract.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A adds schema-version validation to the Vuls2 database connection function by calling GetMetadata() and checking the version after the database handle is created. An independent Task B (a common ops request) asks the same connection function to log the database's last-download timestamp at debug level so operators can diagnose stale-data issues, which also requires calling GetMetadata() at the same spot. If two developers independently add their GetMetadata() call and follow-up logic at the same insertion point, naively merging their patches produces two separate 'metadata, err := dbc.GetMetadata()' statements in the same scope, which is a compile error in Go. A single reconciled change calls GetMetadata() once and then performs both the schema check (A) and the staleness logging (B).
suggestion.shared_region: detector/vuls2/db.go, function newDBConnection — the block immediately after the db.Config{...}.New() call (base lines 49-53), where both A and B insert a GetMetadata() call and post-metadata logic
suggestion.taskA: Schema version mismatches in the Vuls2 database are not handled explicitly. When the on-disk database has a different schema version than the code expects, shouldDownload must force a re-download (or error if SkipUpdate is set), and newDBConnection must reject the connection with a clear error. Currently the code silently continues with an incompatible database.
suggestion.taskB: Operators cannot tell which Vuls2 database build is loaded when troubleshooting detection results. Add debug-level logging in newDBConnection that prints the database metadata (schema version and last-downloaded timestamp) every time a connection is established, so that 'vuls -vvv' output reveals the DB state without requiring manual inspection of the bolt file.
suggestion.independence_rationale: Task B is a standard observability/debugging ticket that any maintainer would file independently: 'I keep getting support questions about why detection results look wrong and I have no way to see what DB version is loaded from the logs.' It has nothing to do with schema version validation or download logic — it is purely about logging existing metadata. The motivation (operator troubleshooting) is completely separate from A's motivation (correctness of download/skip decisions).
suggestion.conflict: Both A and B insert a 'metadata, err := dbc.GetMetadata()' statement at the same location in newDBConnection (right after the db handle is created). A naive text merge or concatenation of the two patches produces two declarations of the variable 'metadata' in the same scope, which is a Go compile error ('metadata redeclared in this block'). The combined test suite cannot even build, so all tests fail.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Call dbc.GetMetadata() once after the db handle is created. Store the result in a single 'metadata' variable. Then perform A's schema-version check (return error if mismatched) followed by B's debug logging (log schema version and downloaded timestamp). Both checks use the same metadata value, no redeclaration, code compiles, and both A's and B's tests pass.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's test set: the existing Test_shouldDownload table tests (including the two new schema-mismatch subtests from A's test patch) plus any test that exercises newDBConnection's schema rejection. B's test set: a new test (e.g. Test_newDBConnection_logsMetadata) that creates a temp bolt DB with known metadata, calls newDBConnection with a capture logger, and asserts the debug log contains the expected schema version and timestamp. Combined suite: run all tests from both sets against the merged code. The naive merge fails to compile (duplicate 'metadata' declaration), so the entire suite errors out. The reconciled code compiles and all tests in both sets pass.

notes: The contradictory seed is the stronger fit here. The conflict is real but somewhat mechanical (duplicate variable declaration rather than a semantic logic contradiction), which caps confidence at 3. A stronger semantic conflict would require B to change the control flow of newDBConnection in a way that contradicts A's schema check (e.g., B wants to skip GetMetadata entirely for performance when SkipUpdate is set, directly opposing A's need to call it). However, that B would be less independently motivated. The complementary family does not fit well because all relevant code is in one file with no natural interface boundary between two separate features.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a bug fix in roles.go: the role-list validator (Roles.Check) must reject unknown AND duplicate roles, and the role-list comparator (Roles.Equals) must compare as sets (order-insensitive, duplicates ignored, nil == empty). The official fix rewrites ParseRoles to stop validating each piece as it goes and instead validate the whole list once at the end. Task B is a separate, real gap in the same file: the constant RoleRemoteProxy ('RemoteProxy') is declared with a comment but is NOT accepted by the single-role validator (Role.Check), and ParseRoles can never produce it because it normalizes input with a title-case trick that mangles multi-word names ('remote_proxy' becomes 'Remote_proxy', 'RemoteProxy' becomes 'Remoteproxy'). A developer working on remote-cluster support would file B: register the RemoteProxy role and make ParseRoles case-insensitive. Both tasks must rewrite the same validation/parsing code in roles.go, and they pull in opposite directions: A makes parsing/validation stricter (reject duplicates, validate the finished list), B makes it more permissive (accept new role, accept any letter case). Each fix alone breaks the other's tests, so blindly merging the two patches yields code that fails the combined suite.
suggestion.shared_region: roles.go — the role validation/parsing path: ParseRoles (both A's and B's solutions rewrite its loop body) and the Check functions (A rewrites Roles.Check to add duplicate detection; B must edit the adjacent Role.Check switch to register RoleRemoteProxy).
suggestion.taskA: Fix Roles.Check and Roles.Equals in roles.go: Check must return an error when the list contains any unknown role or any duplicated role (nil for empty or all-valid-unique lists); Equals must compare the two lists as sets of distinct roles, ignoring order and repetition, and treat nil and empty as equal. NewRoles and ParseRoles should enforce the same validation.
suggestion.taskB: The built-in role constant RoleRemoteProxy ('RemoteProxy') exists in roles.go but is unusable: Role.Check rejects it as 'not registered', and ParseRoles can never produce it because its title-case normalization turns 'remote_proxy'/'RemoteProxy' into 'Remoteproxy'/'Remote_proxy'. Register RoleRemoteProxy as a valid built-in role and make ParseRoles match role names case-insensitively so tokens/certificates for remote SSH proxies can actually be created (e.g. tctl tokens add with the remote proxy role).
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by the remote-cluster/reverse-tunnel feature, not by the duplicate/equality bug: the constant is already declared with a doc comment ('role for remote SSH proxy in the cluster'), RBAC code in lib/auth/permissions.go already treats 'RemoteProxy' as a role name, and the title-case parsing bug is independently reproducible in the base code (ParseRoles("RemoteProxy") errors today). A maintainer filing B would never mention duplicate rejection or set equality; it reads as 'our new role is dead code because validation rejects it'.
suggestion.conflict: A's solution rewrites ParseRoles to keep the title-case normalization and defer all validation to a Roles.Check that now rejects duplicates; B's solution rewrites the same ParseRoles loop to do case-insensitive mapping to registered roles (and adds RoleRemoteProxy to Role.Check). Under A's code, ParseRoles("remote_proxy") still errors (unregistered mangled name), so B's tests fail; under B's code, Roles{Auth,Auth}.Check() still returns nil (no duplicate detection), so A's tests fail. Naively gluing/merging the two patches collides on the ParseRoles body (textual conflict, or one side's semantics silently wins) and the combined suite fails either way.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent roles.go: ParseRoles splits the input, trims, and maps each piece case-insensitively onto the registered role constants (including the newly registered RoleRemoteProxy); it then calls Roles.Check once, which validates membership via Role.Check and rejects duplicates with a seen-map; Equals stays set-based (asSet comparison, nil/empty equal). This single change passes both tickets' tests.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestRolesCheck and TestRolesEqual from the new roles_test.go (duplicate rejection, unknown rejection, set equality, nil/empty equality). B's set: new tests asserting RoleRemoteProxy.Check() == nil, ParseRoles("remote_proxy,auth") == Roles{RoleRemoteProxy, RoleAuth} with no error, and NewRoles(["RemoteProxy"]) succeeds. Combined suite = both files run against the merged roles.go; base fails both sets, each standalone solution fails the other's set, only the reconciled code passes everything.

notes: Both families hinge on the same task B candidate, whose independence is grounded in a real base-commit gap: RoleRemoteProxy is declared at roles.go:53-54 with a doc comment but absent from the Role.Check switch (lines 157-166), and ParseRoles' strings.Title(strings.ToLower(...)) normalization provably cannot produce it ('RemoteProxy' -> 'Remoteproxy', 'remote_proxy' -> 'Remote_proxy'), so ParseRoles("RemoteProxy") errors in the base. The contradictory pairing is the stronger of the two: A's gold patch rewrites ParseRoles (defers validation to a new duplicate-rejecting Roles.Check) while B must rewrite the same function's loop for case-insensitive matching, and each solution demonstrably fails the other's tests (A's code: ParseRoles("remote_proxy") errors; B's code: Roles{Auth,Auth}.Check() returns nil). Caveats keeping confidence at 3: the overlap is one function plus adjacent Check code (Equals is A-only), so 'naive merge fails' relies on the ParseRoles textual/semantic collision rather than a deep contradiction; and B's ticket naturally spans two small edits (Role.Check switch + ParseRoles), which an author would need to scope carefully. The complementary framing is a stretch (registry as contract) and is reported at confidence 2. No decomposition was needed: B is not 'the other half of A' — A's equality fix and B's role registration are separately motivated.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A fixes a bug where the terminal stays locked (echo off) after a password prompt is interrupted or the program exits: it adds a helper that restores the saved terminal state, calls it when a read is abandoned, and calls it from the reader's Close method, plus a new NotifyExit hook that tsh's main calls before exiting. An independent Task B targets a different, real defect in the same reader: its Close method returns immediately even though a background goroutine is still running and may keep reading from the underlying stdin, so Close does not actually guarantee the reader's resources are released (the code's own comment admits this). B's fix makes Close wait for that background goroutine to finish (when no read is in progress). Both A and B must edit the same Close function in context_reader.go, and A's version of Close calls a helper (maybeRestoreTerm) that only exists in A's patch, so gluing the two independent edits together does not compile or behave correctly.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/utils/prompt/context_reader.go, func (cr *ContextReader) Close() (and, for B, the related processReads/NewContextReader goroutine-lifecycle code in the same file)
suggestion.taskA: Terminal remains locked after exiting tsh login in Bash: interrupting the password prompt with Ctrl-C, or completing a password+MFA login, leaves the shell with input echo disabled. The shared stdin ContextReader must restore the saved terminal state when a password read is abandoned, when the reader transitions from password to clean, and on Close/program exit (via a NotifyExit hook called from tsh main).
suggestion.taskB: ContextReader.Close does not guarantee release of resources: the doc comment says 'ongoing reads cannot be interrupted' and 'Close doesn't guarantee a release of all resources', but even when no read is in progress Close returns while the background reader goroutine is still alive and can keep reading from the underlying stdin. Make Close wait for the background goroutine to exit when it is safe to do so (i.e. no read is currently in progress), so that after Close returns the underlying reader is no longer being used. This is a resource-lifetime/correctness ticket, not a terminal-UX ticket.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by goroutine/resource lifetime and the explicit 'doesn't guarantee a release of all resources' caveat in the Close doc comment — a classic maintainer cleanup ticket that a different developer would file without knowing about the terminal-lock bug. It does not mention terminal state, NotifyExit, or tsh login; it is about Close's contract. It is not 'the other half' of A: A is about restoring terminal state, B is about ensuring the background reader actually stops. Both are independently worth doing even if the other never existed.
suggestion.conflict: Both A and B rewrite the body of Close() in context_reader.go. A's Close inserts a call to cr.maybeRestoreTerm(...) (a new helper A introduces) before marking the reader closed; B's Close adds a wait for the background goroutine (e.g. a sync.WaitGroup done in processReads) under the same lock, before/around the closed transition. Naively merging the two independent patches either (a) leaves A's maybeRestoreTerm call referencing a symbol that B's patch never defined, so the package fails to compile, or (b) if both define their own restore/cleanup inline, produces duplicate, conflicting logic in the same lines. The two edits occupy the same switch/default block in Close and cannot both stand verbatim.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: A single Close() that, under the lock, (1) restores the terminal state via maybeRestoreTerm when in password mode, (2) transitions to readerStateClosed and closes the closed channel, and (3) if no read is in progress (state was idle/closed), waits on the processReads WaitGroup so the goroutine is guaranteed gone before Close returns. processReads signals the WaitGroup on exit; NewContextReader adds it. This satisfies A's terminal-restore requirement and B's resource-release requirement in one coherent function.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestContextReader, TestContextReader_ReadPassword, TestNotifyExit_restoresTerminal (terminal restore on abandoned read, on close, on NotifyExit). B's set: a new test, e.g. TestContextReader_CloseWaitsForGoroutine, that closes a reader with no pending read and asserts the background goroutine has exited / the underlying reader is no longer read after Close returns (fails on base because Close returns before the goroutine stops). Combined suite: run A's and B's tests together against the merged code. It passes only if Close both restores the terminal (A) and waits for the goroutine when safe (B); a naive merge fails to compile (missing maybeRestoreTerm) or fails B's wait assertion / A's restore assertion.

notes: The strongest real structure here is the contradictory family on ContextReader.Close: A (gold patch) edits Close to restore terminal state via a new maybeRestoreTerm helper, and an independently-motivated B (Close should actually wait for the background reader goroutine when no read is in progress, per the code's own 'doesn't guarantee a release of all resources' comment) edits the same Close function and the processReads/NewContextReader goroutine lifecycle. The collision is concrete: A's Close references maybeRestoreTerm, which B's patch does not define, so a naive merge fails to compile, and both patches rewrite the same switch/default block in Close. Confidence is 3 rather than higher because B's 'wait for goroutine' fix must be carefully scoped to 'only when no read is in progress' to avoid deadlocking A's tests that call Close/NotifyExit while a read is pending, and the two tickets are in the same subsystem (though genuinely different concerns: terminal UX vs resource lifetime). The complementary family is weak: tctl/tbot do not use prompt.Stdin(), so there is no second real consumer of NotifyExit, and the ShowMOTD context.Background() fix is better characterized as a dependent step toward A's goal than as an independent producer/consumer counterpart.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is about the Teleport kube-agent's Kubernetes secret storage: it needs the environment-variable names (KUBE_NAMESPACE, RELEASE_NAME) exposed as exported constants and the constructor to strictly validate that KUBE_NAMESPACE and TELEPORT_REPLICA_NAME are set, because a new internal cleanup command and the Helm chart depend on those exact names. Task B is a separate, plausible ticket: users deploying the agent without the official chart (or with other tooling) commonly set the standard POD_NAMESPACE variable instead of KUBE_NAMESPACE, so the backend should accept POD_NAMESPACE as a fallback source for the namespace. Both tasks must edit the same small block of code: the constants list and the validation loop at the top of the Kubernetes backend constructor. A's change renames the private constant to an exported one and keeps 'missing KUBE_NAMESPACE = hard error'; B's change adds a new constant and rewrites the same validation loop so a missing KUBE_NAMESPACE is only an error if POD_NAMESPACE is also missing. Gluing both patches together (one written against the old private name, one renaming it) leaves the file referencing a symbol that no longer exists, or two incompatible versions of the same loop, so the combined test suite fails; a single reconciled change (exported constants + accept either variable) passes both suites.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/backend/kubernetes/kubernetes.go — the const block (namespaceEnv/releaseNameEnv lines) and NewWithClient()'s env-validation loop (plus InKubeCluster() which reads the same constant)
suggestion.taskA: teleport-kube-agent backend fails if required environment variables are missing: export the KUBE_NAMESPACE and RELEASE_NAME env-var names as package constants (NamespaceEnv, ReleaseNameEnv), make NewWithClient() verify KUBE_NAMESPACE and TELEPORT_REPLICA_NAME are set and return an error otherwise, and keep Exists()/Get()/Put() working off that configuration.
suggestion.taskB: kube-agent backend cannot be used with standard downward-API deployments: many clusters (and third-party charts) expose the pod namespace via POD_NAMESPACE rather than KUBE_NAMESPACE. The Kubernetes state backend should treat POD_NAMESPACE as an accepted source for the namespace so the agent works in those environments, with tests covering 'KUBE_NAMESPACE unset but POD_NAMESPACE set' succeeding and 'both unset' failing.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by deployment compatibility with a widely-used Kubernetes convention (POD_NAMESPACE via the downward API), not by A's goal. A's ticket is about correctness of validation and exposing the constants so the chart/cleanup tooling can reference them; B's ticket is about accepting an alternative variable name so non-chart deployments work. A maintainer could file either without knowing about the other, and B is not a step toward A — it changes behavior A doesn't care about (what happens when KUBE_NAMESPACE is absent but another variable is present).
suggestion.conflict: Both patches edit the same const block and the same validation loop in NewWithClient(). A's patch renames namespaceEnv to NamespaceEnv on those exact lines while keeping strict 'KUBE_NAMESPACE must be set' semantics; B's patch, written against the base, adds podNamespaceEnv to the same const block and rewrites the same loop to fall back to POD_NAMESPACE. Naively merging yields either a compile failure (B's lines still reference the old private name A renamed) or two contradictory versions of the loop; semantically, A's requirement 'missing KUBE_NAMESPACE must error' directly contradicts B's test 'missing KUBE_NAMESPACE but POD_NAMESPACE set must succeed' unless reconciled.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: keep A's exported NamespaceEnv/ReleaseNameEnv constants, add B's podNamespaceEnv constant, and make NewWithClient()/InKubeCluster() resolve the namespace as KUBE_NAMESPACE if set, else POD_NAMESPACE, erroring only when neither is present. A's tests never set POD_NAMESPACE, so its 'KUBE_NAMESPACE not set' error case still passes; B's fallback tests pass as well.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the existing lib/backend/kubernetes/kubernetes_test.go suite (TestBackend_Get, TestBackend_Put, TestBackend_Exists and subtests, which after A's test patch reference the exported NamespaceEnv). B's set: new subtests in the same file, e.g. TestBackend_Exists/'namespace from POD_NAMESPACE fallback' (KUBE_NAMESPACE unset, POD_NAMESPACE set, expect success) and 'neither namespace var set' (expect error). Combined suite: run both against the merged package; base fails both (A's tests don't even compile without the exported constant; B's fallback tests fail on strict validation), each standalone solution passes its own set, the naive merge fails (compile error or loop contradiction), and the reconciled change passes everything.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A adds a truncation feature to the ASCII table library: a column can be given a maximum cell length, and any longer cell is cut to that many leading characters, followed by '...' and an optional footnote marker, with the full note printed below the table. Task B is a separate bug report about that same truncation: when a cell contains multi-byte characters (accents, CJK, emoji), cutting at a fixed number of characters must not split a character in half, or the table prints garbled text. Both tickets force edits to the exact same function — the cell-truncation helper in lib/asciitable/table.go — and the two natural implementations disagree on what 'cut to N' means: A's implementation slices the string by bytes (cell[:N]), B's must slice by characters (runes). A byte slice of a multi-byte string produces invalid, garbled text, so the two versions cannot both stand in one function.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/asciitable/table.go — the cell truncation helper (truncateCell in A's solution, i.e. the code that turns a raw cell into its rendered form using the column's MaxCellLength/FootnoteLabel), which A must create and B must also edit because its byte-based slicing is wrong for multi-byte text.
suggestion.taskA: Long free-form cells break table alignment and cannot be abbreviated: the lib/asciitable package should expose a public Column descriptor (Title, MaxCellLength, FootnoteLabel) with Table.AddColumn and Table.AddFootnote; cells longer than a positive MaxCellLength render as the first MaxCellLength characters + '...' (+ one space + the footnote label when set), zero means unbounded, column widths are computed from the rendered text, and referenced footnotes are printed once, after a blank line, as '<label> <note>'. MakeTable/AddRow/IsHeadless behavior is preserved.
suggestion.taskB: Table truncation mangles multi-byte text: a cell containing characters outside ASCII (e.g. 'héllo wörld', '日本語のテキスト', '🚀 ship it') must be truncated by character count, never by byte count — with a limit of 4, 'héllo wörld' must render as 'héll...' and must never contain a half-character (invalid UTF-8). The truncation must stay consistent with the footnote-label behavior (the marker is appended after the ellipsis) and the column width must reflect the rendered cell.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a classic Unicode-safety bug ticket that a different developer would file after A's feature lands: international users' names, labels, and reasons are common in Teleport, and byte-based string slicing is a well-known Go pitfall. B is motivated entirely by character-encoding correctness of the truncation output, not by A's goals (footnotes, column descriptors, tctl output) — it makes sense as its own ticket against any implementation of 'truncate a cell to N characters', and its tests only assert on rendered cell text. It is not 'the other half of A': A's spec never mentions multi-byte text, and B does not require footnotes to exist at all (its tests can use a column with no footnote label).
suggestion.conflict: A's natural solution slices by bytes: cell[:MaxCellLength]. On B's test input 'héllo wörld' with limit 4, byte-slicing cuts inside the é (a 2-byte character) and yields invalid UTF-8 ('hÃ©l...'), failing B's tests. B's solution must instead convert to runes and take the first MaxCellLength runes. Both solutions edit the same truncateCell code path in lib/asciitable/table.go, and the two slicing strategies are mutually exclusive in a single function — naively gluing A's byte slice with B's rune slice (or auto-merging, which keeps one version of the function) leaves one side's tests failing.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Implement truncation once, rune-based: take the first MaxCellLength runes of the cell, append '...', then append ' ' + FootnoteLabel when the label is non-empty. Because A's test data ('Trains are much better than cars' limit 25, 'for ever and ever' limit 2, 26 y's limit 25) is pure ASCII, rune-counting produces byte-identical output, so A's TestTruncatedTable/TestFullTable/TestHeadlessTable still pass, and B's multi-byte tests pass as well. Widths continue to be computed from the rendered cell string.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestTruncatedTable, TestFullTable, TestHeadlessTable from lib/asciitable/table_test.go (fail on base: the Column type, AddColumn and AddFootnote do not exist, so the package doesn't even compile). B's set: a new test in lib/asciitable (e.g. TestTruncatedMultibyteTable) asserting rune-based truncation of accented/CJK/emoji cells, including no invalid UTF-8 in the output and correct ellipsis/label placement (fails on base for the same missing-API reason, and fails against A's byte-slicing solution). Combined suite = A's three tests + B's tests run against the merged code: a naive merge (A's byte slice retained, or B's rune slice dropped) fails B's tests; the reconciled rune-based implementation passes everything.

notes: Key structural facts: (1) A's gold patch touches two files — lib/asciitable/table.go (the library feature, which is what A's fail_to_pass tests exercise) and tool/tctl/common/access_request_command.go (a consumer: new 'requests get' subcommand, ls table rebuilt on AddColumn/AddFootnote, printJSON helper). (2) The library is used by ~20 call sites (tool/tctl/common/collection.go, status_command.go, token_command.go, user_command.go, tool/tsh/*), all via MakeTable/MakeHeadlessTable/AddRow, so A's API is genuinely additive for existing users — no existing call site is forced to change, which weakens any complementary pairing that needs a second independent consumer. (3) The strongest independent B is the rune/Unicode truncation ticket, which collides with A exactly in the truncation helper A must create; confidence is held at 3 rather than higher because B's scope must be carefully kept to the truncation slicing (not column-width display metrics, which would drag in AddRow and the header separator and make the conflict murkier), and because B's motivation is only fully real once A's feature exists — though it reads fine as a standalone bug ticket about 'truncation must not split characters'. (4) Complementary is not viable: the natural producer/consumer split is already contained within A's own patch, so any B there is a decomposition.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A says the 'are we on EC2?' check is wrong: it only looks at whether the metadata address answers with HTTP 200, so a captive-portal or any other service that answers 200 with its own page makes Teleport believe it is on EC2. A's fix rewrites the check to actually fetch the instance ID and verify it matches the real EC2 ID format (i- followed by hex digits), and it removes the plain HTTP status probe entirely. Task B is a separate operations ticket: the check hardcodes a 250-millisecond deadline, which is too short on slow/high-latency networks and not tunable for CI, so make that deadline configurable through a new option on the client constructor. Both tickets must rewrite the exact same function (IsAvailable) and the same constructor (NewInstanceMetadataClient) in lib/utils/ec2.go: A replaces the probe body with a metadata fetch plus format validation, while B keeps the probe and only changes where its timeout comes from. The two versions of the function cannot both be true at once.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/utils/ec2.go — InstanceMetadataClient.IsAvailable (body: the 250ms deadline and what the check does) and NewInstanceMetadataClient (option plumbing for the client struct)
suggestion.taskA: EC2 availability check is unreliable: it does a bare HTTP GET to the instance metadata endpoint and treats any HTTP 200 as 'on EC2'. A captive portal or other intercepting service returning 200 with HTML causes Teleport to believe it is on EC2 and use the HTML as the node hostname (visible as raw HTML in `tsh ls`). Fix: determine availability by retrieving the EC2 instance ID within a short timeout and validating it against the EC2 resource ID format (i-{8 or 17 hex digits}); remove the direct status-code HTTP probe; support functional options on NewInstanceMetadataClient (e.g., WithIMDSClient) so the internal IMDS client can be swapped for testing.
suggestion.taskB: The EC2 metadata availability check hardcodes a 250ms timeout, so on high-latency links (or in CI with a slow mock metadata service) a genuine EC2 instance can be misdetected as non-EC2, and there is no way to tune it. Add a functional option to NewInstanceMetadataClient (e.g., WithAvailabilityTimeout(d time.Duration)) that sets the deadline used by IsAvailable, defaulting to the current 250ms. This is a pure tunability/latency ticket — it says nothing about response content, false positives, or hostname parsing.
suggestion.independence_rationale: Tunable timeouts are a classic standalone ops ticket filed by someone who hit the latency limit, not by someone investigating the captive-portal false positive. B is motivated by when the check gives up (deadline), A by what the check believes (content). B is not 'the other half of A': A's fix does not require configurability, and B's fix does not require content validation. A maintainer could file either ticket without knowing the other exists.
suggestion.conflict: A's IsAvailable must fetch the instance-id body and regex-validate it, and A explicitly deletes the status-code probe and its http.Client{Timeout: 250ms}. B's IsAvailable is the status-code probe whose timeout becomes a struct field set by a new option. The two bodies are mutually exclusive implementations of the same method on the same lines: a naive merge that keeps A's body leaves B's timeout option unused (B's slow-server test fails), and one that keeps B's probe body makes A's 'mistake some other service for instance metadata' case pass 200-with-garbage as available (A's test fails). The constructor hunks also collide (both add variadic option plumbing to NewInstanceMetadataClient).
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One IsAvailable that uses A's approach (fetch instance-id, validate against the i-{hex} regex) under a deadline that is a struct field defaulting to 250ms and settable via B's WithAvailabilityTimeout option; NewInstanceMetadataClient accepts both options (WithIMDSClient from A, WithAvailabilityTimeout from B). Both suites then pass: A's fake-IMDS cases behave per content, B's cases behave per configured deadline.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestEC2IsInstanceMetadataAvailable (httptest fake IMDS injected via WithIMDSClient; asserts false for 200-with-garbage and closed server, true for old/new instance-id formats). B's set: a new test, e.g. TestEC2IsAvailableTimeout, using a mock server with a controllable response delay and WithAvailabilityTimeout — a server slower than the configured deadline must yield false, faster must yield true. Combined suite runs both against the merged code: the naive merge fails at least one side (unused timeout option or probe-based true-on-garbage), only the reconciled implementation passes everything.

notes: Base state verified: lib/utils/ec2.go at the base commit has the bare HTTP-probe IsAvailable (250ms, status 200), no functional options on NewInstanceMetadataClient, and the instanceMetadataURL constant; A's test patch fails on base both by compilation (WithIMDSClient missing) and behavior (200-with-'Hello there!' returns true). Existing DI seams (aws.InstanceMetadata interface, service.WithIMDSClient, ec2.Config.Client, integration/helpers DisabledIMDSClient) already cover testability at the service layer, which is why the complementary angle is weak. The contradictory pair's shared region is real and tight (IsAvailable body + constructor option plumbing), and the conflict is both textual (same lines rewritten differently) and semantic (status-probe vs content-validation), but B ('make the 250ms deadline configurable') is a somewhat contrived ticket — plausible, not inevitable — hence confidence 3 rather than higher. A stronger variant of B: 'IsAvailable should honor the caller's context deadline instead of imposing its own 250ms cap', which collides with A introducing the 250ms context.WithTimeout on the same lines.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A says: the shared ASCII table library has no way to build a table that fits the terminal width, so add a new builder function there and rewire the tctl resource listings (nodes, apps, databases, kubes, desktops) to use it. Task B says: 'tctl get databases' does not show which database engine (mysql, postgres, sqlite...) each entry is, so add a Type column to that listing. Both tasks must rewrite the same ~10-line function that assembles the database listing table. A's rewrite changes its structure (collect rows first, then call the new truncated-column builder with 4 headers); B's rewrite changes its content (5 headers including Type, one extra cell per row). Gluing the two edits together produces a broken or duplicated function, so only a single reconciled rewrite — B's new column built through A's new builder — can satisfy both.
suggestion.shared_region: tool/tctl/common/collection.go, func (c *databaseCollection) writeText (base lines 654-663); A's gold patch replaces its body with rows + asciitable.MakeTableWithTruncatedColumn, and B must edit the same body to add the Type header/cell

Add a public builder to lib/asciitable that takes a column order, rows, and the name of a column designated for truncation: that column absorbs the terminal width the others leave unused (falling back to 80 when the terminal size is unknown), its oversized cells are cut and end with '...', and other columns are capped proportionally. The tsh node/app/database listings must build their truncated tables through this shared builder instead of a private copy, and the tctl text listings should use it too.
suggestion.taskB: tctl get databases prints Name, Protocol, URI and Labels but not the database engine type, so an operator cannot tell at a glance which rows are MySQL, Postgres, or SQLite. Add a Type column to the tctl databases text listing, populated from the database resource's type, the same way the verbose tsh database listing already shows it.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a plain 'missing column in a CLI listing' ticket with its own user-facing motivation (identifying engines in tctl get databases); the tsh verbose database table already displays Type, giving in-repo precedent. It says nothing about terminal width, the asciitable library, or truncation, and is fully solvable without any of A's changes (just add a header and a cell).
suggestion.conflict: Both patches rewrite the exact same function body. A's version: headers {Name, Protocol, URI, Labels}, rows collected then passed to MakeTableWithTruncatedColumn. B's version: headers {Name, Protocol, Type, URI, Labels} with a GetType() cell, built with plain MakeTable. Naively concatenating/auto-merging yields either a merge conflict, a duplicated function, or a 4-column table receiving 5-cell rows (the extra cell silently dropped or the layout wrong) — B's test asserting the Type column fails against the naive merge.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One writeText that collects 5-cell rows (name, protocol, type, uri, labels) and calls asciitable.MakeTableWithTruncatedColumn with headers {Name, Protocol, Type, URI, Labels} and truncated column 'Labels'. This keeps B's new column and A's terminal-fitting layout.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: lib/asciitable table tests (TestMakeTableWithTruncatedColumn and its subtests, TestTruncatedTable, TestFullTable, TestHeadlessTable) plus the tsh listing tests. B's set: a new test in tool/tctl/common that builds a databaseCollection with a sample database (e.g. mysql) and asserts writeText output contains the 'Type' header and the engine value, written layout-agnostically so it passes under both B's plain table and the reconciled truncated table. Combined suite runs both against the merged code: base fails both, each standalone solution passes its own set, the naive merge fails B's assertion, and the reconciled function passes everything.

notes: Two cautions. (1) The most tempting contradictory B — 'show the app's Teleport version in tctl get apps' — is a decomposition of A: A's gold patch already adds the Version column to appCollection.writeText and the GetTeleportVersion() method on the Application interface precisely for that, so it was rejected in favor of the database Type column, which A does not touch. (2) A's app.go change (GetTeleportVersion on the Application interface) is a small auxiliary piece; adding another method to that same interface would be a weak conflict because additive interface changes merge cleanly. The complementary family's soundness hinges on B's ticket naming the shared builder's exact signature; if B were free to write its own private helper (as tsh originally did), B alone would pass and the seed would break — the ticket text must pin the contract. Both families are rated 3: real, precise shared structure, but each needs careful ticket wording to stay sound and independent.

suggestion.simple_explanation:
Task A is the original ticket: when a user changes their own traits (logins, database users) in the web UI, the currently active web session keeps the old certificate data until they log out and back in. A's fix adds a 'reload user' option to the session-renewal flow: a new flag on the renewal request, a new branch at the top of the renewal logic that refetches the user from the backend (bypassing the cache) and rebuilds the certificate with fresh traits, plus the matching flag on the web UI's renew endpoint.

Task B is a separate, independently-motivated ticket: the renewal logic currently treats 'assume an approved access request' and 'switch back to my base roles' as two independent if-blocks that both execute when both are requested, so the last block silently wins and the user gets confusing, unvalidated behavior. B's fix makes the auth layer reject a renewal that sets both options at once (a single validation point, with a clear error), and adds a test that calls the renew endpoint with both set and expects that rejection.

They collide because both tasks must rewrite the same decision block in the renewal function: A restructures the two existing if-blocks into an if/else-if chain with reload-user first (so the three options stay mutually exclusive in code), while B needs to insert a 'both assume and switchback set -> error' check into that same chain. A's fix also edits the web renew handler's validation line to reject any two options set together, which would block B's test request before it reaches the auth layer. Naively merging both changes yields either duplicate, contradictory validation or code where B's expected auth-layer rejection never happens, so the combined test suite fails; a single reconciled change (reject the assume+switchback pair once, at the auth layer, and keep the web handler from pre-blocking that specific pair) passes everything.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/auth/auth.go, func (a *Server) ExtendWebSession — the mode-selection block starting at 'if req.AccessRequestID != ""' (line ~1990) through 'if req.Switchback' (line ~2016); plus the validation line in lib/web/apiserver.go, func (h *Handler) renewSession (line ~1760) and the renewSessionRequest struct (line ~1741)
suggestion.taskA: Update user traits when renewing session: when a user updates their traits (logins, database users) via the web UI, the active web session keeps stale certificate data until logout/re-login. Add a way to renew the current web session so it refetches the user record from the backend (not the cache) and issues a new SSH/TLS certificate embedding the updated traits (e.g. under the logins and db-users trait extensions), while preserving the existing assume-access-request and switchback behaviors and the session login time.
suggestion.taskB: Session renewal silently combines 'assume approved access request' with 'switchback': the renewal handler validates only some option pairs at the web layer, and the core renewal logic executes the access-request block and the switchback block as two independent if-statements, so a request that sets both is not rejected and the outcome is whatever the last block happens to do. File: make the auth layer reject a renewal request that sets AccessRequestID and Switchback together with a clear bad-parameter error, and add a regression test that POSTs to the web renew endpoint with both fields set and asserts the request is rejected.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B reads as a standalone validation/correctness ticket about the existing assume+switchback combination — a maintainer could file it without knowing anything about trait reloads or the web UI. It is motivated by the pre-existing dual-if structure in ExtendWebSession and the narrow pre-existing web-layer check ('AccessRequestID and Switchback cannot be both set' was already there for the other pair), both of which exist at the base commit. It is not 'the other half of A': A's feature (reload user) is orthogonal to B's goal (reject an invalid combination), and B's fix is complete and valuable even if A never existed.
suggestion.conflict: Both solutions must restructure the same if-block sequence in ExtendWebSession. A's gold change converts 'if AccessRequestID / if Switchback' into 'if ReloadUser / else if AccessRequestID / else if Switchback', i.e. it keeps the blocks mutually exclusive in code and lets exactly one run. B's change must make the AccessRequestID+Switchback combination an explicit error inside that same chain. Additionally, A's web-layer change rewrites the renewSession validation line to reject ANY two of the three options set together, which intercepts B's test request (both assume and switchback set) at the HTTP layer with A's generic error instead of letting it reach the auth layer where B's test expects B's rejection. Two agents editing these same lines independently produce either contradictory duplicate validation or a merge where B's auth-layer check is unreachable/absent, so the combined suite fails.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: in ExtendWebSession, keep A's if/else-if structure (ReloadUser first, then AccessRequestID, then Switchback) but add, at the top of the mode selection, an explicit check 'if req.AccessRequestID != "" && req.Switchback -> trace.BadParameter(...)' satisfying B; in the web renewSession handler, keep A's 'only one field can be set' validation for the pairs involving ReloadUser but do not pre-reject the AccessRequestID+Switchback pair (or make its error semantics match B's) so B's test request reaches the auth layer and is rejected there with the expected error. All of A's tests (reload-user traits, multi-request stacking, switchback) and B's test (combined pair rejected) then pass together.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the four fail_to_pass tests in lib/auth/tls_test.go (TestWebSessionWithoutAccessRequest, TestWebSessionMultiAccessRequests, TestWebSessionWithApprovedAccessRequestAndSwitchback, TestExtendWebSessionWithReloadUser). B's set: a new test (e.g. in lib/web/apiserver_test.go, in the style of the existing TestUserContextWithAccessRequest which POSTs to webapi/sessions/renew) that creates an approved access request, POSTs a renewal with both AccessRequestID and Switchback set, and asserts a bad-parameter rejection from the auth layer. Base code fails both sets (no ReloadUser field/branch; no auth-layer rejection of the pair). Each solution alone passes its own set. Naive merge fails the combined suite because A's web-handler validation intercepts B's request before the auth layer (wrong error/no rejection at the expected point), or the auto-merged if/else-if chain drops B's check. The reconciled single change passes the union.

notes: Repo is at the true base commit (WebSessionReq has no ReloadUser; ExtendWebSession has two independent if-blocks; web renewSessionRequest has only AccessRequestID+Switchback; webassets/ is an empty submodule so the frontend is not in this tree). The contradictory pairing is structurally real — both tasks genuinely must rewrite the same mode-selection block in lib/auth/auth.go ExtendWebSession and the same validation line in lib/web/apiserver.go renewSession — but B is somewhat constructed (a validation hardening ticket in A's exact neighborhood), and the clean failure mode of the naive merge depends on B's test asserting the auth-layer rejection while A's web-layer validation intercepts it; that subtlety is why confidence is 3, not 4. The complementary family is essentially a decomposition of A's web plumbing and does not meet the independence bar.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A fixes the Standard Ebooks import script so it can read the new dictionary-style feed data, and as part of that fix it hardcodes the book's language to 'eng' (English) and makes the script refuse any non-English book. An independent Task B, motivated by the script's own comment saying 'we're just gonna handle English for now, and have it error if Standard Ebooks ever adds non-English works', asks the script to actually support non-English books by translating the feed's language code (e.g. French 'fre', German 'ger') into Open Library's language codes. Both tasks must rewrite the exact same few lines: the language-check block and the 'languages' field of the import record. A's version says 'always write eng, reject everything else'; B's version says 'look up the real language and write that'. Those two statements cannot both be true in the same code, so blindly combining the two changes breaks one of the two test suites. A single reconciled change — a lookup table that maps English variants to 'eng' and other languages to their proper codes — satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: scripts/import_standard_ebooks.py, function map_data(): the language-handling block (lines ~34-40, the marc_lang_code computation and ValueError guard) and the 'languages' entry of the import_record dict (line ~50). Both A's and B's patches rewrite these same lines.
suggestion.taskA: Bug: map_data in scripts/import_standard_ebooks.py crashes with AttributeError on Standard Ebooks feed entries because the feed now delivers dictionary-based data while the function uses attribute access (entry.id, entry.language, ...). Fix map_data to read the entry as a dict (keys: id, title, dcterms_language, published, authors, content, value, term, tags, links), set publisher to ['Standard Ebooks'] and languages to ['eng'], extract the cover from the first link whose rel is IMAGE_REL and assert it is an absolute https:// URL, and drop the now-unused BASE_SE_URL constant.
suggestion.taskB: Feature/bug: Standard Ebooks has started publishing non-English titles, and the import script rejects every one of them with 'Feed entry language ... is not supported' because map_data only accepts English and hardcodes the language. Support non-English works: translate the language code carried by the feed entry (e.g. 'fre', 'ger', 'en-GB') into Open Library's MARC language codes via a mapping, and only error on codes that genuinely have no mapping. (Motivated by the code's own standing comment: 'we're just gonna handle English for now, and have it error if Standard Ebooks ever adds non-English works.')
suggestion.independence_rationale: B reads as a natural catalog-expansion ticket a maintainer would file on its own: the base code literally documents English-only support as a temporary limitation with an explicit error for non-English works, which is the seed of a real 'please support non-English imports' ticket. It does not mention the dictionary-format bug, the cover URL change, or anything else from A; its motivation is the language limitation, not the data-format migration. A different developer working from the same base commit could file B without knowing A exists.
suggestion.conflict: A's patch rewrites the language block to: read entry.get('dcterms_language'), raise ValueError unless it starts with 'en-', and set 'languages': ['eng'] (a literal). B's patch rewrites the same block to: look up the entry's language in an ISO-to-MARC mapping table and set 'languages': [mapped_code]. Both edits occupy the same lines and express mutually exclusive policies (hardcode English + reject the rest vs. map and accept other languages). Naively merging — e.g., applying B's mapping logic onto A's result, or concatenating both patches — either leaves two competing 'languages' assignments (last one wins, failing the other suite), reintroduces attribute access that A's dict-based test rejects, or produces a textual conflict on the same lines; the combined suite fails.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent map_data that (1) reads the language from the dict key 'dcterms_language' (with a fallback to attribute access so B-style entries also work), (2) consults a mapping table that sends all 'en-*' variants to 'eng' and includes other languages (fre->fre, ger->ger, ...), and (3) raises only for unmapped codes. A's test (en-GB entry -> languages ['eng']) and B's tests (e.g. fre entry -> ['fre'], unmapped code -> ValueError) both pass.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: scripts/tests/test_import_standard_ebooks.py::test_map_data (dict-based SAMPLE_1 entry, asserts full record incl. languages ['eng'], cover URL, publisher). B's set: new tests in the same file calling map_data with entries whose language is non-English (e.g. 'fre', 'ger') asserting the mapped MARC code, plus an unmapped-code case asserting ValueError. Base fails both (AttributeError on dict / ValueError on non-English). A alone passes A's set; B alone passes B's set. Naive merge fails the combined suite (conflicting language policy on the same lines). Reconciled version passes the combined suite.

notes: Contradictory family is the real signal here, anchored on the language block in map_data: the base code's own comment ('we're just gonna handle English for now, and have it error if Standard Ebooks ever adds non-English works') is a ready-made, independently-motivated ticket (B) that collides line-for-line with A's hardcode-to-'eng' requirement. Confidence is 3 rather than 4 because of authoring friction: B's tests must use an entry format the base code accepts (attribute-style) to stay independent of A's dict migration, and the reconciled change must accept both dict and attribute access (or the ticket must be phrased to use the dict format, in which case B's solution partially overlaps A's — acceptable for a mutex seed but worth noting). Other candidate B's (cover URL prefixing, adding rights/edition_name fields, fixing filter_modified_since's e.updated_parsed) are either the inverse of A or pure decomposition, so they were rejected. Complementary was checked against the actual import pipeline (Batch, ImportItem.single_import, parse_data, add_book.load, StandardEbooksProvider, templates) and found no missing consumer side, hence not viable.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A refactors the autocomplete endpoints in openlibrary/plugins/worksearch/autocomplete.py into one shared base class with per-type subclasses, and in doing so it drops the result-ordering instruction (sort by edition count) that the works endpoint currently sends to the search engine. An independent task B — 'the works picker on the edition edit form shows suggestions in an arbitrary order; it should show the most-editioned works first' — requires that same works endpoint to send its results ordered by edition count. Both tasks must rewrite the same works_autocomplete request-building code (the GET method / its base), and A's version deliberately has no ordering while B's version must. Glue the two changes together naively and the ordering is lost, so B's test fails; only a reconciled design (an ordering option on the shared request path, set by the works subclass) passes both.
suggestion.shared_region: openlibrary/plugins/worksearch/autocomplete.py — the works_autocomplete GET request construction (in the base code: the works_autocomplete.GET params dict containing 'sort': 'edition_count desc'; after A: the shared autocomplete.GET that builds the Solr params and the works_autocomplete subclass). Both A and B must edit this same request-building region.
suggestion.taskA: The original ticket: deduplicate the work/author/subject autocomplete endpoints into a reusable autocomplete page class, make work results expose name equal to the work title and a full_title (title + ': ' + subtitle), and resolve embedded work OLIDs (e.g. OL123W) case-insensitively with a database fallback.
suggestion.taskB: A separate ticket: 'Works autocomplete on the edition edit form returns suggestions in an arbitrary order. The dropdown should be ranked by popularity so the most-editioned matching work appears first — send the works autocomplete Solr query with results sorted by edition_count descending.' It never mentions the deduplication or the name/full_title changes.
suggestion.independence_rationale: Result ordering in a search endpoint is a user-facing concern completely orthogonal to A's maintenance goal (dedup) and its data-shaping goal (name/full_title). A maintainer looking only at the works dropdown would file the ordering ticket on its own; it is motivated by what the user sees, not by the internal structure A is changing. It is not 'the other half' of A — A does not ask for any particular ordering, it merely stops sending one as a side effect of the refactor.
suggestion.conflict: In the base code works_autocomplete.GET sends 'sort': 'edition_count desc'. A's refactored shared GET builds its Solr params without any sort key (the gold patch deletes that line), so A's solution cannot satisfy B's test that the works request is sorted by edition_count. B's solution (add the sort back into the works request) and A's solution (a sort-free shared GET) edit the same params construction; a naive merge keeps A's sort-free GET and silently drops B's sort, failing B's assertion.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Extend the shared autocomplete.GET to pass an optional per-subclass sort (e.g. a class attribute sort = None on the base, included in the Solr params when set), and set sort = 'edition_count desc' on works_autocomplete. A's tests (which assert the exact query, fq list, q_op, rows and the name/full_title shaping, and never assert the absence of sort) still pass, and B's test asserting the works request is sorted by edition_count also passes.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the two fail_to_pass tests in openlibrary/plugins/worksearch/tests/test_autocomplete.py (test_autocomplete, test_works_autocomplete), which pin the exact Solr query string, the fq/q_op/rows kwargs, the OLID fallback, and the name/full_title output. B's set: a new test that instantiates works_autocomplete, mocks Solr, calls GET, and asserts the request was made with sort='edition_count desc' (and that returned docs come back in that order). Combined suite: run both against the merged code — it passes only if the shared request path carries the works sort; a naive merge of the two independent patches fails B's sort assertion while A's tests pass, which is exactly the collision signal.

notes: Base commit confirmed: works_autocomplete.GET sends 'sort': 'edition_count desc' and sets name from the record key (d['key'].split('/')[-1']); authors_autocomplete has no 'fl' field restriction; subjects_autocomplete builds fq as a string; there is no publishers/_autocomplete endpoint and the edition form's publisher input (openlibrary/templates/books/edit/edition.html line ~118) is plain text. The strongest collision found is the sort-parameter region of the works request: A's refactor removes it, so any ticket that wants/relies on edition-count ordering of works suggestions must edit the same lines. This is a genuine same-region conflict but B reads slightly like a regression-prevention ticket (the ordering exists in base code and is dropped by A), which caps confidence at 3. The complementary publisher-endpoint pairing rests on the pre-existing {key, name} JSON convention shared by all autocomplete endpoints and the JS in autocomplete.js; A does not create that contract, so the 'must agree' coupling is weak (confidence 2). Other candidate collisions considered and rejected as weaker: A's base doc_wrap name-from-title vs a publisher subclass (no shared-line edit in base code), and the find_olid_in_string utility (A replaces two OLID finders with one; an independent M-suffix finder would be a decomposition of A's utility change).

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A changes the importer's acceptance gate: book records that have a title, source records, and a strong identifier (ISBN or LCCN) should be accepted even when author, publisher, and date are missing, and a leftover filler value for publishers (['????']) should be cleaned off before storage. Task B is a separate data-quality bug: the importer has a step that fills in missing details from BookWorm's staged metadata, but that step only fills fields that are completely absent. When a record carries filler values like authors [{'name': '????'}] or publish_date '????', the fill step treats them as 'already present' and skips them, so promise-item editions never get their real author or date. The collision: A's fix relocates that fill-in function out of the core load path (deleting the old copy and its call site inside load()) and installs a new copy in the import API's parse step, while B's fix edits the fill condition inside the old copy of that same function. Paste both changes together and either B's fix is stranded on deleted code, or A's relocation loses B's placeholder handling; only one reconciled version of the function (relocated, AND treating '????' as missing) satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.shared_region: openlibrary/catalog/add_book/__init__.py :: supplement_rec_with_import_item_metadata() and its call site in load() (lines ~990-1013 and ~1035-1037). A deletes this function from add_book/__init__.py, removes the load() call, and re-adds a modified copy in openlibrary/plugins/importapi/code.py (parse_data); B must edit the fill condition ('if not rec.get(field)') of the same function in add_book/__init__.py.
suggestion.taskA: The /api/import validator (import_validator.validate) rejects promise-item records that are sparse but carry a strong identifier. Accept a record if it is complete (non-empty title, source_records, authors, publishers, publish_date) OR if it has title, source_records, and at least one strong identifier (isbn_10, isbn_13, or lccn as non-empty lists of non-empty strings); raise ValidationError otherwise (a list containing only '' does not count). Additionally, import normalization should strip the placeholder publishers value ['????'] so downstream logic sees the field as empty.
suggestion.taskB: BookWorm metadata supplementation for promise items silently does nothing for records that contain placeholder values. supplement_rec_with_import_item_metadata() only fills a field when it is absent or falsy, so a record with authors=[{'name': '????'}] or publish_date='????' is never enriched from the staged import_item row, and promise editions ship without real author/date data even when BookWorm has it. Fix the supplementation so placeholder '????' values are treated as missing and overwritten with the staged metadata.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B targets the enrichment step (pulling real metadata in from BookWorm's staged rows) and is motivated by a data-quality symptom ('promise editions are missing authors/dates that BookWorm has'), while A targets the acceptance gate (which records pass validation at all) and placeholder cleanup. A developer fixing B never needs to change validation policy, and a developer doing A's validator work never needs to touch supplementation. B's bug exists and is reproducible at the base commit without any of A's changes: the base fill condition 'if not rec.get(field)' demonstrably skips truthy placeholder values.
suggestion.conflict: A's gold solution deletes supplement_rec_with_import_item_metadata from add_book/__init__.py, removes its call in load(), and adds a new copy (with a different import_fields list) in importapi/code.py invoked from parse_data. B's solution modifies the fill condition of the function where it currently lives, in add_book/__init__.py. Naively merging: B's hunk has no target in A's tree (function deleted), the relocated copy lacks B's placeholder-aware condition, and the load() call site B's tests exercise is gone. The combined suite fails: B's supplementation tests fail against A's tree, and a merge that keeps A's deleted call site broken fails A's pipeline tests.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: (1) validator accepts complete OR strong-identifier records; (2) normalize_import_record strips the ['????'] publishers placeholder; (3) a single supplementation function lives in the relocated position (import API parse step) and its fill condition treats '????' placeholder values as missing (e.g. skip-fill only when the field is absent, empty, or a placeholder); (4) load() no longer carries the old call. All of A's and B's tests then pass against the merged code.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: openlibrary/plugins/importapi/tests/test_import_validator.py (test_validate_strong_identifier_minimal, test_validate_multiple_strong_identifiers, test_validate_not_complete_no_strong_identifier, plus existing complete-record tests) and the updated TestNormalizeImportRecord cases in openlibrary/catalog/add_book/tests/test_add_book.py. B's set: new tests for supplement_rec_with_import_item_metadata that mock ImportItem.find_staged_or_pending to return staged BookWorm data and assert a rec with authors=[{'name': '????'}] / publish_date='????' gets those fields replaced (fails at base because the fill condition skips truthy placeholders). Combined suite runs both against the merged tree; it passes only if the surviving supplementation path both exists where A moved it and carries B's placeholder-aware fill logic. Authoring note: B's tests should assert behavior through a stable entry point (the function by name, or parse_data/load) since the reconciled location differs from the base location.

notes: Task A's gold patch is multi-part: (1) validator dual-model acceptance, (2) normalize_import_record placeholder handling, (3) relocation of supplement_rec_with_import_item_metadata from add_book.load() to importapi.parse_data with an expanded field list, (4) new stats.gauge helper, (5) promise script changes (no more '????' authors/publish_date, stage incomplete records, completeness gauges). Parts 3-5 are prime decomposition material and were deliberately avoided for task B. The strongest genuinely independent B found is the placeholder-aware supplementation fix, which collides with part 3 (function relocation/deletion) — a real same-function conflict, but the collision is partly structural (A deletes B's edit target) rather than semantic (two incompatible behaviors on the same lines), hence confidence 3 rather than 4-5. A weaker alternative B (e.g. 'also strip publish_places == ["????"] in normalize_import_record') edits A's exact lines but reconciles trivially, so it does not meet the mutex bar. Complement family: not viable without decomposition; the producer (promise script) and consumer (validator) sides of the sparse-record contract are one ticket in reality.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A adds a new date-window helper (within_date_range) into the date-utilities file, inserted right after the existing 'goal year' function, so the My Books banner only shows Dec 1–Feb 1. Task B is a separate bug report: in December, the reading-goal JSON endpoint and progress partial report last year's goal instead of the new year's, because the goal-fetching code defaults to the plain calendar year while the pages use a December-rollover 'goal year'. Fixing B requires changing that same 'goal year' function (e.g. making its date injectable so the December rollover can be tested and reused), which means editing the exact lines that A's new function is inserted beside. Two developers editing the same spot in the same file collide: the changes overlap textually and a naive merge breaks the file, while one reconciled change (new helper added AND goal-year function updated) satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: openlibrary/utils/dateutil.py, the region of get_reading_goals_year() (lines 114-118) and the lines immediately after it: A's patch inserts within_date_range() directly after line 118 using lines 118-120 as context; B's fix must modify get_reading_goals_year()'s body (add an injectable 'now' parameter so the Dec rollover is testable and reusable from checkins.py). The two hunks overlap at line 118.
suggestion.taskA: The My Books 'Yearly Reading Goal' banner must be manually added/removed every year. Automate it: the banner should appear on the My Books page only between December 1 and February 1 of each year when the user has no goal set. This requires a reusable, testable date-window check (within_date_range) that ignores the year, is inclusive of boundary days, and accepts an optional current date for testing.
suggestion.taskB: Bug: in December, the /reading-goal JSON endpoint and /reading-goal/partials page return the previous calendar year's goal and progress, while the My Books page shows the new year's goal. The default year in get_reading_goals() (checkins.py) uses the plain calendar year, but the rest of the goal UI uses a 'goal year' that rolls over on December 1. Make the default goal year consistent with the December rollover, and make the rollover logic testable by allowing the current date to be injected.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a user-visible data-correctness bug (wrong year of goal/progress shown in December) with its own motivation, reproducible without any banner work: the codebase genuinely contains two different 'goal year' definitions (dateutil.get_reading_goals_year with Dec rollover vs checkins.get_reading_goals defaulting to datetime.now().year). A maintainer would file this from seeing inconsistent December data in the goal API/UI. It never mentions the banner or date-window checking; it is not a step toward A's goal.
suggestion.conflict: A's insertion hunk lands immediately after get_reading_goals_year() with its closing lines as context; B's fix modifies get_reading_goals_year()'s body (same lines). Auto-merging produces a git conflict at that hunk; naively concatenating both edits yields duplicated/overlapping definitions in the same function region, which is broken or at minimum fails the combined suite. The two edits cannot both stand verbatim in the same lines.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change to dateutil.py: (1) update get_reading_goals_year() to accept an injectable 'now' (defaulting to datetime.now()) preserving the Dec-1 rollover, and (2) add within_date_range() right after it. checkins.py's get_reading_goals() default year is then derived from the same rollover rule. A's test_within_date_range and B's December/January default-year tests both pass against this single file state.
