suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: openlibrary/utils/tests/test_dateutil.py::test_within_date_range (plus existing dateutil tests as regression). B's set: new unit tests for the default-year behavior of get_reading_goals (mock get_current_user and YearlyReadingGoals.select_by_username_and_year, as openlibrary/tests/core/test_db.py already does for that table): with a mocked December date the default returns the next year's goal; with a January date the current year's. Combined suite = both sets against the merged dateutil.py/checkins.py. Base commit fails both (within_date_range missing; December default year wrong). Each standalone solution passes its own set. Naive merge of the two overlapping hunks fails; the reconciled change passes all.

notes: Contradictory is the stronger family here. The real structural hook is that A's gold patch inserts within_date_range() immediately after get_reading_goals_year() in dateutil.py, and an independent December goal-year bug (checkins.get_reading_goals defaulting to calendar year while templates use the Dec-rollover year) forces B into the same function/region. The conflict is a same-hunk overlap: A's insertion context lines are B's modification lines. Confidence capped at 3 because (a) 'naive merge fails' depends on the overlapping hunks actually conflicting (they do under git 3-way merge since B edits lines 114-118 and A's hunk uses 118-120 as context), and (b) B's test must mock the DB layer, which is doable following openlibrary/tests/core/test_db.py patterns. Complementary is real but weaker: banner vs chip are adjacent elements of the same feature area, and the integration test requires template-rendering test infrastructure that does not exist in the repo (openlibrary/tests contains only accounts/catalog/core/data/solr; no render_template usage). A's own fail_to_pass suite is pure-Python (test_dateutil.py), so A's side is easy to score; B's side in either family is the harder-to-author half.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A fixes a 500 error on the list-creation form: when a form is POSTed, the server must read the submitted body as the sole source of values (ignoring the URL query string), and a helper that 'unflattens' dotted form fields must let later values overwrite earlier ones. Task B is a separate feature ticket: the HTML list form should support 'tags' the way the JSON list API already does (the API endpoint accepts tags and the test suite exercises them, but the form silently drops them). Both tasks must rewrite the same function, ListRecord.from_input(), which builds the list record from the HTTP request: A replaces its input-reading logic (body vs query, defaults dict, unflatten), while B adds a 'tags' field to the same defaults and to the same constructor call at the end of the function. Two agents working from the same base each produce a complete but different version of that function; gluing the changes together yields either a version without tags (B's tests fail) or one without body handling (A's tests fail). One reconciled version that reads tags from whichever input source A established passes both suites.
suggestion.shared_region: openlibrary/plugins/openlibrary/lists.py — ListRecord.from_input() (the web.input()/defaults call and the final ListRecord(...) constructor call, which A rewrites entirely and B must extend), plus the ListRecord dataclass fields and to_thing_json() for B
suggestion.taskA: Fix: POSTing the list create/edit form to /lists/add returns 500 when the body conflicts with URL query parameters. When a request body is present it must be parsed (urlencoded, '+' = space) and used exclusively as the input source; only when the body is empty should the query string (web.input) be used. Defaults (key/name/description/seeds) may only fill values absent from the body, and must not pre-seed ancestors of nested keys (e.g. seeds) before unflattening. After unflattening, seeds may arrive as nested entries or comma-separated strings and must normalize to a list of valid seed items. The unflatten helper's setvalue() must let a later simple (non-nested) value overwrite an earlier one.
suggestion.taskB: Feature: the HTML list form (/lists/add and /lists/OLxL/edit) should let users set tags on a list, matching the existing JSON list API which already accepts a 'tags' array (see lists_json.POST and the list API tests that create a list with tags ['t1','t2']). Currently ListRecord has no tags field, the form has no tags input, and tags submitted via the form are silently dropped. Add tags to the ListRecord dataclass, read it in from_input(), include it in to_thing_json(), and add a tags input to the list edit template.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by an existing asymmetry in the codebase, not by A: the JSON API (lists_json.POST -> user.new_list(tags=...)) and its tests already support tags, while the HTML form path (ListRecord) does not. A maintainer would file 'form should support tags like the API' on its own; nothing in B's motivation mentions the 500 error, body/query precedence, or unflatten. B's template and dataclass changes stand alone even if A never happened.
suggestion.conflict: A's patch rewrites from_input() end to end: it replaces the web.input(...) call with a branch that parses web.data() and merges {} | DEFAULTS | unflatten(form_data), and rewrites the final ListRecord(key=..., name=..., description=..., seeds=...) construction. B's patch edits the same lines: it adds tags to the same defaults/web.input call and to the same ListRecord(...) construction. The two final versions of the function are mutually exclusive — A's version has no tags at all (B's tests fail), B's version still reads only web.input and ignores the body (A's test_from_input_with_data fails). Naively concatenating/auto-merging the two patches produces a function containing both input strategies or a syntax error, so the combined suite fails.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One from_input() that (1) decides the input source exactly as A requires (non-empty web.data() -> parse_qs of the body, else web.input), (2) includes 'tags' in DEFAULTS and in the body-parsed values, and (3) passes tags into the ListRecord constructor; ListRecord gains a tags field (default []) and to_thing_json() emits it. A's setvalue overwrite fix is kept as-is since B doesn't touch it.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: openlibrary/plugins/openlibrary/tests/test_lists.py TestListRecord::test_from_input_no_data, test_from_input_with_data, test_from_input_seeds (mock web.data/web.input). B's set: new tests in the same file — test_from_input_with_tags (web.data() -> b'', web.input returns tags=['t1','t2'], assert ListRecord.tags == ['t1','t2']) and test_to_thing_json_includes_tags. Combined suite runs both against the merged code: base fails both; A-alone fails B's tags tests; B-alone fails A's with-data test; only the reconciled from_input passes everything.

notes: The contradictory pairing is the natural one. Shared region is ListRecord.from_input() in openlibrary/plugins/openlibrary/lists.py: A rewrites the whole method (input source + constructor call) and B (tags support, motivated by the pre-existing JSON-API/form asymmetry in lists_json.POST and test_listapi.py::test_create) must edit the same defaults and constructor lines. Confidence is 3 rather than 4 because B's edit is additive (a new field) rather than semantically opposed, so the 'collision' is 'two competing rewrites of one function' resolved by taking the union — real, but milder than a true semantic mutex. A second, weaker contradictory option exists in utils.py setvalue(): A makes simple keys last-value-wins; a ticket defending/documenting first-value-wins (the base code's comment) would edit the exact same 3 lines in opposite directions — but that B reads as defending status quo against A, i.e. a decomposition, so it was not chosen. Complementary family: not viable; A adds no interface, and no existing consumer (lists_edit.POST, the list JSON API, the edit template) forms a contract that a second independent ticket must co-design with A. The template type/list/edit.html already submits nested seeds--i--key fields, so B's tags input can be modeled on real form structure. Also note: A's requirement that from_input detect body presence via web.data() (not web.ctx.env or the request method) constrains any reconciled implementation but does not affect B's independence.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Ticket A asks the maintainers to modernize the Internet Archive download helper in openlibrary/catalog/get_ia.py: replace the old-style urllib HTTP calls with the newer requests library, so callers get a response object with .content (bytes) and .text (string) instead of a file-like object with .read(). Ticket B, filed independently by someone else, notices that every download from archive.org is sent with Python's default, anonymous 'urllib' browser identifier, which the Internet Archive has a policy of blocking/throttling; the rest of the codebase (openlibrary/catalog/utils/query.py, openlibrary/solr/update_work.py) already sends a descriptive 'Mozilla/5.0 (openlibrary; ...)' User-Agent, but this one helper does not. B asks that urlopen_keep_trying identify Open Library on every request. Both tickets force edits to the exact same function body: A rewrites the line that performs the HTTP call (urllib.request.urlopen -> requests.get), while B must attach a header to that same call, which in the old urllib world means constructing a urllib.request.Request with a header dict. An agent solving B alone keeps the urllib implementation and only adds the header; an agent solving A alone rewrites it to requests without any custom header. Gluing the two patches together yields code that either performs the HTTP call twice (both the old urllib line and the new requests line present) or, if the old line is dropped, silently loses the User-Agent header — one side's tests fail either way. A single reconciled change — a requests-based urlopen_keep_trying that accepts and forwards a headers/User-Agent argument — satisfies both tickets at once.
suggestion.shared_region: openlibrary/catalog/get_ia.py, function urlopen_keep_trying (lines 29-39 at base), plus the header-bearing call site at line 157 in get_from_archive_bulk (urllib.request.Request with a Range header) and the two urlopen_keep_trying call sites in openlibrary/catalog/marc/marc_subject.py (load_binary line 56, load_xml line 69)
suggestion.taskA: Refactor openlibrary/catalog/get_ia.py to use requests instead of urllib: urlopen_keep_trying must return a requests.Response exposing .content/.text, all .read() call sites become .content/.text, and the Range request in get_from_archive_bulk is built with requests headers instead of urllib.request.Request.
suggestion.taskB: Identify Open Library to the Internet Archive: downloads made through openlibrary/catalog/get_ia.py (urlopen_keep_trying, and the Range request in get_from_archive_bulk) go out with Python's default anonymous urllib User-Agent, while the rest of the catalog code (catalog/utils/query.py, solr/update_work.py) already sends 'Mozilla/5.0 (openlibrary; <module>)'. Make every IA fetch from get_ia.py carry that descriptive User-Agent header so archive.org can attribute and not throttle the traffic.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a classic, self-contained ops ticket: 'our crawler is anonymous and gets throttled; tag our requests like the rest of the codebase does'. It has its own motivation (IA's user-agent policy, traffic attribution), its own precedent (query.py and update_work.py already set User-Agent), and its own success criterion (the outgoing request carries the header). It says nothing about which HTTP library should be used — a B-only agent would naturally implement it on top of the existing urllib code, e.g. by wrapping the URL in a urllib.request.Request with a User-Agent header. It is not 'the other half of A': A is a library-migration refactor, B is an HTTP-identification fix, and either is worth doing even if the other never happens.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches edit the same 10-line function. A's solution changes the return contract from a urllib file object (.read()) to a requests.Response (.content/.text) and rewrites the HTTP-call line; B's solution keeps urllib and changes how the request object is constructed (plain url -> urllib.request.Request(url, headers={'User-Agent': ...})). Naively concatenating/auto-merging the two diffs leaves two competing implementations of the same call (urllib line + requests line) or drops the header entirely. The combined test suite then fails: A's tests monkeypatch urlopen_keep_trying to return a MockResponse with .content/.text and assert MarcXml/MarcBinary parsing works (base code fails these because it calls .read() on the mock); B's tests assert the outgoing request carries the Open Library User-Agent (base code fails because urllib sends the default agent). A merged-but-unreconciled tree passes neither both at once: if the urllib implementation wins, A's .content/.text contract is broken; if the requests implementation wins without a headers parameter, B's header assertion is broken.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: urlopen_keep_trying(url, headers=None, **kwargs) implemented with requests.get(url, headers=headers, **kwargs), raising on 403/404/416, returning a requests.Response; get_from_archive_bulk passes its Range header via the headers argument instead of urllib.request.Request; load_binary/load_xml in marc_subject.py read f.content / f.text. This is exactly the shape of the gold patch (which already adds the headers/**kwargs parameters) and satisfies both A's response-object contract and B's User-Agent requirement (callers pass the Open Library User-Agent, or the function defaults to it).
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the existing openlibrary/tests/catalog/test_get_ia.py suite (test_get_marc_record_from_ia, test_no_marc_xml, test_incorrect_length_marcs) after A's test patch, which swaps the mock to return a MockResponse exposing .content/.text — these fail on base code (.read() on MockResponse) and pass only with A's requests-based implementation. B's set: a new test that runs urlopen_keep_trying against a local/stubbed HTTP endpoint (or monkeypatches the HTTP layer) and asserts the request carries the 'Mozilla/5.0 (openlibrary; ...)' User-Agent, failing on base code. Combined suite: run both against the merged tree; it passes only if the single urlopen_keep_trying both returns a requests.Response with .content/.text AND sends the Open Library User-Agent, i.e. only the reconciled implementation.

notes: Strongest structure in the repo for this pair: (1) urlopen_keep_trying is a shared helper imported by marc_subject.py, so A's change has a real cross-file blast radius; (2) the codebase already has an established User-Agent convention ('Mozilla/5.0 (openlibrary; <module>) Python/<ver>' in catalog/utils/query.py and solr/update_work.py) that get_ia.py violates, giving task B a genuine, pre-existing motivation; (3) the gold patch itself adds headers=None/**kwargs to urlopen_keep_trying and converts the urllib.request.Request Range call in get_from_archive_bulk into a headers dict — evidence the real fix anticipated exactly the header-passing need B expresses, which strengthens the collision on the same lines. Caveats keeping confidence at 3 rather than 4-5: B's standalone tests are somewhat artificial (verifying an outgoing header requires stubbing the HTTP layer, and the repo's autouse no_requests fixture blocks real requests), and a B-only agent's patch might edit only the call sites (e.g. in marc_subject.py) rather than the function body, softening the line-level conflict; the sharpest collision is on the urlopen_keep_trying body and the get_from_archive_bulk Request construction, which a B author fixing 'all IA fetches' would plausibly touch. A's tests are the given fail_to_pass set; B's tests must be authored as part of the seed.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a ticket about the shape of the 'getArtists' API response: the server should return artists grouped under letter indexes with proper metadata fields (MusicBrainz ID and sort name always present), instead of reusing the wrong response structure. Task B is a separate, real bug: the same 'getArtists' endpoint accepts an 'ifModifiedSince' parameter (a standard Subsonic caching hint meaning 'only give me data if it changed after this time') but the code silently ignores it and always returns the full list. Both tickets force edits to the exact same function in the same file (the artist-index builder and the GetArtists handler in server/subsonic/browsing.go). A's fix rewrites that function into a shared helper plus a new ID3-specific builder; B's fix changes the same lines to make the endpoint honor the timestamp and return an empty payload when nothing changed. If two agents work blindly, A's restructure and B's caching edit land on the same lines and cannot be auto-merged; and if B is applied first and then A's patch is applied, the code won't even compile because A's patch rewrites the very lines B changed. Only a single reconciled change (shared helper returning indexes + last-scan time, ID3 builder, and an ifModifiedSince check in GetArtists) satisfies both tickets at once.
suggestion.shared_region: server/subsonic/browsing.go — the getArtistIndex function (lines 30-58) and the GetArtists handler (lines 75-86). Task A's gold patch rewrites getArtistIndex into a shared getArtist helper plus getArtistIndexID3 and changes GetArtists's call site; Task B's fix must edit the same lines to thread and honor ifModifiedSince.
suggestion.taskA: Subsonic artist response lacks proper structures and consistent field serialization: the Subsonic response model uses the *Indexes type for the Artist field and does not define specific structures for artist groups in ID3 format; MusicBrainzId and SortName in ArtistID3 carry omitempty so they are dropped from XML/JSON even when set. Fix: change Subsonic.Artist to a new *Artists type, add IndexID3 (name attr + artist list) and Artists (index list, lastModified attr, ignoredArticles attr) structs, and serialize MusicBrainzId/SortName without omitempty.
suggestion.taskB: The getArtists Subsonic endpoint ignores its ifModifiedSince parameter. Per the Subsonic API spec, when a client sends ifModifiedSince and the library has not been scanned since that time, the endpoint must return an empty artists response (client keeps its cached copy); navidrome currently always returns the full artist list, wasting bandwidth and breaking client-side caching. Fix: parse ifModifiedSince in GetArtists (as GetIndexes already does) and, when the library's last scan time is not after it, return an empty Artists payload (with lastModified/ignoredArticles) instead of querying the artist index.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a protocol-compliance/caching bug in the getArtists endpoint, not a piece of A. Its motivation is client caching and the Subsonic spec, not response structure or field serialization: it makes sense even if the response kept its current *Indexes shape (the same bug exists today in GetIndexes-style behavior and would exist for any response type). It is a classic, believable maintainer ticket ('getArtists ignores ifModifiedSince') and never references the Artists/IndexID3 structures or the omitempty fields that A is about. The overlap is purely locational — both happen to live in the same handler function.
suggestion.conflict: A's gold patch deletes and rewrites getArtistIndex (splitting it into getArtist + getArtistIndex + getArtistIndexID3) and changes GetArtists's single call line from api.getArtistIndex(r, musicFolderId, time.Time{}) to api.getArtistIndexID3(...). B's minimal fix edits those same lines: it changes GetArtists to read ifModifiedSince := p.TimeOr("ifModifiedSince", time.Time{}) and adds an early-return/empty-payload branch based on the library's last scan time inside getArtistIndex. The two diffs touch identical lines, so a naive textual merge either fails to apply (B's changed lines are gone after A's rewrite) or produces code where the ifModifiedSince logic is stranded in the legacy getArtistIndex path that GetArtists no longer calls — the endpoint still ignores the parameter, so B's tests fail against the merged code.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: (1) add responses.Artists/IndexID3 and drop omitempty from ArtistID3.MusicBrainzId/SortName (A); (2) extract a shared getArtist(r, libId, ifModifiedSince) helper returning (model.ArtistIndexes, lastScanMillis, error) with the ifModifiedSince short-circuit inside it (A's structure + B's semantics); (3) keep getArtistIndex for GetIndexes and add getArtistIndexID3 for GetArtists; (4) in GetArtists, parse ifModifiedSince via p.TimeOr and pass it through, so an unmodified library yields an empty Artists payload. Both A's snapshot tests and B's behavior tests pass on this single change.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the snapshot suite TestSubsonicApiResponses (server/subsonic/responses/responses_test.go) — new 'Artist' Describe blocks asserting the artists/index/artist XML+JSON shapes and that musicBrainzId/sortName are always serialized. B's set: new ginkgo specs in the subsonic API suite (e.g. browsing_test.go) that call GetArtists with a mocked library whose LastScanAt is set: (a) no ifModifiedSince -> full artist list; (b) ifModifiedSince older than last scan -> full list; (c) ifModifiedSince newer than last scan -> empty Artists payload with lastModified/ignoredAttributes set. Combined suite: run both against the merged code. Base commit fails both (no Artists struct / omitempty present; ifModifiedSince ignored). A-alone fails B's test (c); B-alone fails A's snapshot tests. A naive merge (A's rewrite applied over B's edits, or vice versa) leaves the ifModifiedSince logic off the code path GetArtists actually uses, failing B's test (c) — only the reconciled change passes everything. Caveat: the shared tests.MockDataStore currently returns an empty (panicking) Library repository, so B's author must add a MockLibraryRepo (a small, independent test-infrastructure addition).

notes: Base commit confirmed: Subsonic.Artist is *responses.Indexes (responses.go:38), ArtistID3.MusicBrainzId/SortName have omitempty (responses.go:210-211), GetArtists ignores ifModifiedSince (browsing.go:78), while GetIndexes already parses it (browsing.go:63) — which is exactly what makes B a believable standalone ticket. The strongest collision is at the GetArtists call site and getArtistIndex body: A's patch rewrites both, and B's minimal fix edits the same lines. Confidence is 3 rather than 4 because (a) the conflict is locational (same function) rather than a true semantic mutex — a careful merge tool might survive if B's diff is small, though B-first + A-apply does not compile; (b) B requires adding a MockLibraryRepo to the shared tests package since the current mock returns an empty panicking Library repository; (c) A's gold patch's own refactoring (extracting getArtist) is what B would naturally have used, so the 'reconciliation' is essentially A's structure plus B's one behavioral line. Complementary family is weak: A is a closed producer-side change with its own snapshot tests; no independent consumer exists in the repo. Snapshot tests are unix-only (build tag), so combined-suite scoring should run on Linux/macOS.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A moves the app's list of known audio/image file types out of a hardcoded Go file (consts/mime_types.go) into a data file (resources/mime_types.yaml) loaded at startup, and deletes the old Go file. An independent Task B — 'Navidrome does not recognize .m4p (protected AAC) files as audio; add support' — would naturally be solved by adding one line to the same hardcoded table in consts/mime_types.go. The two changes collide because A deletes the very file B edits: a blind merge hits a delete/modify conflict (or, if both files are kept, the app has two competing sources of truth for the same format table). A reconciled change instead adds the new format to the yaml file A introduces.
suggestion.shared_region: The audio-format table and its registration into the system MIME registry: consts/mime_types.go (audioFormats map + init()) at the base commit, which A deletes and replaces with resources/mime_types.yaml + conf/mime/mime_types.go. B's edit target is the audioFormats map in consts/mime_types.go.
suggestion.taskA: Lossless/audio format definitions are hardcoded in consts/mime_types.go and can't be changed without a code release. Move them into a data resource (resources/mime_types.yaml with 'types' and 'lossless' sections), load it via a config-load hook in a new conf/mime package exposing LosslessFormats, register the MIME types with the standard library, and point server/serve_index.go at the new source.
suggestion.taskB: Users report that .m4p files (iTunes protected AAC) in their library are ignored by the scanner and not playable — Navidrome doesn't know the format. Add .m4p as a recognized audio type (MIME type audio/mp4, not lossless) so IsAudioFile accepts it and streaming serves the right Content-Type. (At the base commit the obvious fix is one entry in the audioFormats table in consts/mime_types.go.)
suggestion.independence_rationale: 'Add support for format X' tickets are routine, standalone maintenance work for a music server and are motivated entirely by user reports about .m4p files — nothing about the yaml refactor. A different developer would file and fix it without knowing about Task A, and at the base commit the only sensible place to make the fix is the existing hardcoded format table, which is exactly the file A removes.
suggestion.conflict: A's solution deletes consts/mime_types.go; B's solution modifies its audioFormats map. Git auto-merge of the two independent patches is a delete/modify conflict that cannot be applied, and a naive 'keep both files' merge leaves two sources of truth registering the same MIME table, with B's format absent from A's yaml — so B's behavior tests (TypeByExtension('.m4p') == 'audio/mp4', IsAudioFile('x.m4p') == true) fail against A-only code and A's 'definitions must come from the yaml resource' intent is violated by keeping the Go table.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's structure (conf/mime + resources/mime_types.yaml, delete consts/mime_types.go) and fold B's request into the data: add '.m4p: audio/mp4' under the yaml 'types' section only (not under 'lossless'). Then A's tests still pass (exactly the nine lossless formats, .dsf/.flac registered) and B's behavior tests pass (.m4p registered, recognized as audio).
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestMime (conf/mime) and the TestServer suite (server/serve_index_test.go, losslessFormats key sourced from mime.LosslessFormats). B's set: new behavior tests, e.g. in model — IsAudioFile('test.m4p') is true — plus a MIME-registry assertion that TypeByExtension('.m4p') == 'audio/mp4' and that 'm4p' is NOT in the lossless list. Base commit fails both sets (conf/mime doesn't exist; .m4p unregistered). Each solution alone passes only its own set. The combined suite is scored against the merged tree: the naive merge fails (unresolvable delete/modify conflict / B's format missing from yaml), the reconciled merge passes everything.

notes: Key structural facts at base commit: consts/mime_types.go holds the audioFormats/imageFormats tables, registers them in the stdlib MIME registry in init(), and builds consts.LosslessFormats (sorted); the only production consumer is server/serve_index.go line 57; behavioral consumers (model.IsAudioFile/IsImageFile, MediaFile.ContentType, Stream.ContentType, subsonic helpers) all go through mime.TypeByExtension, which is why a 'support format X' ticket lands on the same table A deletes. Caveat keeping the contradictory seed at confidence 3 rather than 4: if a naive merge is done by 'keeping both files' instead of git auto-merge, the combined test suite would actually pass (both inits run, AddExtensionType just overwrites), so the failure of the naive merge depends on the delete/modify conflict being unresolvable — a real but structural, not semantic, collision. B's format must be chosen non-lossless (e.g. .m4p) so it doesn't break A's exact-nine-lossless-formats assertion; a lossless addition (e.g. .dff) would make the combined suite unsatisfiable unless A's test is also amended.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A introduces a brand-new typed in-memory cache (a generic 'SimpleCache') in the shared cache utilities and rewires the 'now playing' tracker to use it. A separate, independently-motivated ticket B — 'let a player clear its now-playing entry when playback stops, instead of leaving it listed until the track's time runs out' — also has to touch that same now-playing tracker and, to do so, needs the cache to support deleting a key, which the new SimpleCache as designed by A does not expose. Both tasks therefore land on the same code: the SimpleCache interface/implementation in utils/cache and the playTracker in core/scrobbler. A defines the cache's method set without a delete operation; B's feature requires adding one. Glued naively, B's 'stop' call has no method to invoke (or B's delete is added to a cache type A has already replaced), so the combined behavior breaks; a single reconciled change that adds the delete capability to the shared cache and wires it into the tracker satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: utils/cache/simple_cache.go (the SimpleCache[V] interface + simpleCache impl + NewSimpleCache) together with core/scrobbler/play_tracker.go (playTracker.playMap field, newPlayTracker constructor, and NowPlaying/GetNowPlaying). A creates/rewrites this region; B must extend the same cache with a delete/remove operation and call it from the same tracker.
suggestion.taskA: Add a generic, strongly-typed TTL cache (SimpleCache[V] with Add, AddWithTTL, Get, GetWithLoader, Keys and a NewSimpleCache[V] constructor) to the shared utils/cache package, and migrate the now-playing tracker and the cached genre repository off their direct, untyped ttlcache usage onto it so reads no longer need type casts.
suggestion.taskB: Now-playing entries can only disappear on their own once the track's duration (plus a few seconds) elapses; there is no way for a player to clear its entry when a track is stopped, skipped, or the player disconnects, so the 'Now Playing' list keeps showing stale entries. Add a StopNowPlaying(playerId) operation to the PlayTracker that immediately removes that player's now-playing entry.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone product ticket about now-playing UX/lifecycle (stale entries lingering), motivated entirely by player behavior — it never mentions the cache refactor, generics, or type safety. A maintainer would file it on its own. It is not 'the other half of A': A is about the shape of the cache abstraction and migrating existing callers; B is about a new user-facing capability (removing an entry) that A does not provide. The overlap is only that both happen to need to modify the now-playing tracker and, consequently, the cache it uses.
suggestion.conflict: A's SimpleCache[V] interface is fixed at five methods (Add, AddWithTTL, Get, GetWithLoader, Keys) and A's tests pin that exact surface; A also replaces playTracker's *ttlcache.Cache field with cache.SimpleCache[NowPlayingInfo]. B's StopNowPlaying needs to delete a key, which requires a Remove/Delete method on the cache. Working independently, B either (a) adds the delete to the old ttlcache-based tracker and then cannot compile/operate once A has swapped the field to SimpleCache (which has no delete), or (b) adds a delete method to the SimpleCache interface/impl — the very lines A authored — so the two edits to the same interface definition and the same playTracker field/constructor cannot both stand as-is. Naively concatenating A's patch and B's patch yields either a missing-method compile failure or a duplicated/divergent cache definition.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Extend the shared SimpleCache[V] interface and its simpleCache implementation with a Delete(key string) (or Remove) method backed by ttlcache's delete, keep A's other four methods and NewSimpleCache unchanged, and implement playTracker.StopNowPlaying by calling playMap.Delete(playerId). The now-playing tracker keeps A's SimpleCache[NowPlayingInfo] field and constructor; B's feature is layered on top. One coherent change to the cache + tracker satisfies both A's typed-cache tests and B's stop-now-playing tests.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the SimpleCache specs in utils/cache (run under TestCache) — Add/Get, AddWithTTL expiry, GetWithLoader success and error propagation, Keys. B's set: a new scrobbler spec, e.g. StopNowPlaying removes the entry so a subsequent GetNowPlaying no longer lists that player, and stopping an unknown player is a no-op. Combined suite = both, run against the merged code. Base fails both (no SimpleCache; no StopNowPlaying). A-alone passes A's tests but B's stop test fails (no delete). B-alone (against old ttlcache) passes B but A's typed-cache tests fail. Only the reconciled change — SimpleCache with a delete method plus the tracker wiring — passes the full combined suite.

notes: Key structural facts at the base commit: (1) A's gold patch already migrates two of the three ttlcache consumers (play_tracker, cached_genre_repository) and leaves cached_http_client untouched; the HTTP client needs SetCacheSizeLimit, which SimpleCache does not expose, so it is the only 'independent consumer' and it does not fit cleanly. (2) There is a genuine latent bug in scanner/cached_genre_repository.go: Put's GetByLoader loader returns the input g.ID (empty for a brand-new genre) instead of the ID assigned by the underlying GenreRepository.Put, so new genres get cached with an empty ID. A rewrites exactly these lines, so a separate 'fix genre ID caching' ticket would collide on the same region — but its fix (return the persisted ID) is behaviorally compatible with A's typed rewrite, making it a weak/soft conflict rather than a hard mutex, and it risks reading as a step of A's migration. (3) The strongest contradictory pairing is the now-playing 'StopNowPlaying/delete' feature vs A's fixed five-method SimpleCache interface, both converging on utils/cache/simple_cache.go + core/scrobbler/play_tracker.go; the conflict is real but soft (an interface-extension collision) and reconciles trivially by adding a Delete method, hence confidence 3 rather than higher. (4) Complementary is weak because A's own patch already contains the consumer side, leaving only the size-limited HTTP client as an independent partner, and that partner needs a contract change A does not make.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A asks to simplify the database layer: instead of the program keeping two separate database connections (one for reading, one for writing) behind a custom wrapper object, it should keep a single standard connection, and the backup/restore/prune operations should become ordinary package-level functions. Task B is a separate robustness ticket: after a backup file is created, the program should verify that the file is a valid, undamaged database (an integrity check), and if not, delete the corrupt file and report an error, because users have found backups that fail to restore. Both tasks must edit the same code: the function that copies the database into a backup file, and the backup function wrapping it. A rewrites that region (turning the methods into free functions with new names and new callers), while B adds a verification step inside that very same function. Applied blindly together, the result is either two incompatible versions of the same function, or the verification step attached to a method that no longer exists — the code fails to compile or backups are no longer verified. One careful change — a free backup function that copies the database, then verifies the copy and deletes it if verification fails — satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.shared_region: db/backup.go — the backupOrRestore function and the Backup entry point (method func (d *db) Backup / func (d *db) backupOrRestore at base; rewritten to free functions plus package-level Backup/Restore/Prune by A)
suggestion.taskA: Simplify the database access layer: db.Db() should return the standard *sql.DB directly; remove the custom db.DB interface and its read/write-split implementation; make Backup(ctx) (string, error), Restore(ctx, path) error, and Prune(ctx) (int, error) public package-level functions in the db package; persistence.New must accept a *sql.DB and build its query helper via dbx.NewFromDB with db.Driver; delete persistence/dbx_builder.go; add exported db.Dialect ("sqlite3") and db.Driver ("sqlite3_custom") variables, register/open the connection with Driver, and use Dialect for the migration tool's dialect setting.
suggestion.taskB: Database backups can silently be corrupt: after a backup file is written, nothing checks that it is actually a valid database, so a backup taken during an unclean shutdown or disk error can later fail at restore time with a confusing error. Add a verification step to the backup flow: after the database is copied to the backup file, open the backup file and run an integrity check (PRAGMA integrity_check); if the check reports any problem, delete the bad backup file and return an error from the backup operation. Expose the check as a reusable package-level function (e.g. db.VerifyBackup(path string) error) and add tests: a good backup file verifies, a file containing garbage fails verification, and Backup() refuses to leave behind a backup file that fails verification.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a data-safety ticket about the backup feature's output quality — it is motivated by corrupt/unrestorable backup files, a classic ops complaint, and says nothing about the db.DB interface, read/write splitting, or the persistence layer. A maintainer responsible for the backup/restore commands (cmd/backup.go, db/backup.go) would file it independently of the architectural cleanup. It is not 'the half of A that A didn't do': A's goal is simplifying the connection layer, B's goal is guaranteeing backup file validity; B would be filed even if A never existed (it would then just edit the existing (d *db) Backup method).
suggestion.conflict: Both patches rewrite the same lines of db/backup.go. A deletes func (d *db) backupOrRestore and func (d *db) Backup and replaces them with a free backupOrRestore plus new package-level Backup/Restore/Prune. B modifies the body of func (d *db) Backup / backupOrRestore to add the integrity-verification step (and adds VerifyBackup). Naively merging (3-way auto-merge or concatenating the changes) either conflicts on the same function, produces duplicate/incompatible definitions that do not compile, or leaves B's verification call inside the deleted method so the new package-level Backup never verifies — in every case the combined test suite fails.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: A single db/backup.go where backupOrRestore is a free function (per A) that, in the backup direction, after the SQLite backup copy completes, opens the destination file, runs PRAGMA integrity_check, and on failure deletes the file and returns an error; package-level Backup/Restore/Prune (per A) wrap it; VerifyBackup(path) (per B) is the reusable exported check. A's callers (cmd/backup.go, cmd/root.go) and B's verification tests both pass against this one version.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: TestDB and TestPersistence (the instance fail_to_pass) — at base they fail to compile because they reference package-level Prune/Backup/Restore, db.Dialect, Db() as *sql.DB, and GetDBXBuilder; A's gold patch makes them pass. B's set: new specs in package db (e.g. db/verify_test.go or additions to db/backup_test.go) run under the same TestDB suite: VerifyBackup succeeds on a freshly created valid backup file, fails on a file filled with garbage, and Backup() returns an error and removes the file when the destination pre-exists as an invalid database. At base, B's tests fail (VerifyBackup does not exist; no verification behavior). Combined suite = TestDB (A's backup/db specs + B's verification specs) + TestPersistence, all run against the merged code: it passes only if the collision in db/backup.go was reconciled into one backupOrRestore/Backup implementation that both has A's package-level shape and B's verification step.

notes: The contradictory family is the stronger fit. The collision is real but somewhat mechanical: both tasks legitimately edit the Backup/backupOrRestore region of db/backup.go because A reshapes it (method→free function, new package-level wrappers) and B adds behavior inside it (integrity verification). B's base-failure is guaranteed by compilation (VerifyBackup absent); A's base-failure is guaranteed by its test patch referencing Dialect, package-level Backup/Restore/Prune, and Db() as *sql.DB. One caveat for the authoring step: B's test 'Backup() refuses to leave a corrupt file' should be designed so it fails at base for the right reason (missing verification/VerifyBackup symbol), not by relying on SQLite's own error when the destination is garbage, since the base code path may already error in that scenario. The complementary angle is weak because cmd/pls.go at base already works through db.Db(); a B that merely 'uses the new API' is mostly a consumer of A rather than an independent contract partner. Also note A's patch touches consts.DefaultDbPath (removes _cache_size/_synchronous/_txlock pragmas) — that line is an incidental change, not a natural shared region for any independent ticket.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A changes how the server identifies a player: instead of storing the raw browser string, it stores a cleaned-up 'user agent' value, and it renames the registration function's third argument from 'type' to 'userAgent'. Task B is a classic separate bug: when Navidrome runs behind a reverse proxy, every player's recorded IP address is the proxy's IP, not the real client's IP; the fix is to read the real IP from the X-Forwarded-For/X-Real-IP headers, changing what is passed as the registration function's fourth argument. Both fixes must edit the same two adjacent lines in the same middleware function that computes these two values and calls the registration function. Applied independently, each agent rewrites that one call expression with the other agent's change missing, so a naive merge keeps only one of the two fixes and the combined tests fail; only a single reconciled line that uses both the cleaned-up user agent and the proxy-aware IP passes everything.
suggestion.shared_region: server/subsonic/middlewares.go, func getPlayer — base lines 146-147: `ip, _, _ := net.SplitHostPort(r.RemoteAddr)` and `player, trc, err := players.Register(ctx, playerId, client, r.Header.Get("user-agent"), ip)` (the IP computation and the Register call expression)
suggestion.taskA: The original ticket: replace the loosely defined player 'type' field with an explicit user-agent based identity. The Player model must expose UserAgent (json tag userAgent) instead of Type; the player repository lookup must become FindMatch(userName, client, typ) replacing FindByName(client, userName); Register must accept a userAgent argument, use FindMatch to find an existing player, return the player's transcoding profile (or nil) and persist the player with UserAgent set, Client/UserName unchanged and LastSeen updated. The old Type field, FindByName method and typ parameter must be fully removed, not kept for compatibility. Includes the DB migration renaming the player.type column to user_agent and the middleware passing a canonicalized user agent to Register.
suggestion.taskB: Bug: player IP addresses are wrong behind a reverse proxy. The subsonic API's player middleware records the proxy's IP (the direct TCP peer) as the player's IPAddress instead of the real client IP. Fix the getPlayer middleware so the IP it registers comes from the X-Forwarded-For header (first entry) or X-Real-IP when present, falling back to the direct peer address otherwise. (Note: the main web router already applies chi's RealIP middleware, but the subsonic API path does not use it for player registration.)
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a stock, real-world ticket for any self-hosted app behind a proxy, and the codebase has genuine structure for it: server/server.go already uses middleware.RealIP for the main router while the subsonic getPlayer middleware uses raw r.RemoteAddr — an observable inconsistency. B's motivation (wrong IPs in the player list / stats) never involves player identification, user agents, the Type field, or FindMatch; a different developer would file it without knowing about A. It is not a step toward A's goal.
suggestion.conflict: A's solution rewrites the Register call in getPlayer to pass a canonicalized user agent as the third argument (e.g. `players.Register(ctx, playerId, client, canonicalUserAgent(r), ip)`). B's solution rewrites the same call to pass a proxy-aware IP as the fourth argument (e.g. `players.Register(ctx, playerId, client, r.Header.Get("user-agent"), realIP(r))`). Both edits touch the same expression on the same line (and the adjacent ip-computation line). A naive 3-way merge resolves the hunk to one side or the other: keeping A's line drops B's IP fix (B's tests fail because the registered IP is still the direct peer), keeping B's line drops A's canonical user agent (A's tests fail). The two changes cannot both stand in the merged expression without being combined.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One reconciled getPlayer implementation: compute `ip` from X-Forwarded-For/X-Real-IP with RemoteAddr fallback (B), compute `userAgent` by parsing/canonicalizing the User-Agent header (A), and make a single call `players.Register(ctx, playerId, client, userAgent, ip)` with all of A's other changes (UserAgent field, FindMatch, migration) in place. This satisfies both tickets at once.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the gold fail_to_pass tests in core/players_test.go (Register exposes UserAgent with json tag userAgent and drops Type; Register uses FindMatch, persists the player, returns transcoding or nil). B's set: new tests in server/subsonic/middlewares_test.go at the middleware level — a mock core.Players that captures the Register arguments; assert that when the request carries X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.9 (with a different RemoteAddr) the captured ip is 10.0.0.9, same for X-Real-IP, and without either header the captured ip is the peer address. B's tests must be written at the middleware level (not against core.Register, whose base implementation ignores the ip argument, which would make the base pass). Combined suite: run A's core tests plus B's middleware tests against the merged code; base fails both; A-alone fails B's; B-alone fails A's; only the reconciled getPlayer (plus A's full changes) passes all. B's solution must not add getPlayer to the scrobble routes in api.go — that wiring belongs to A.

notes: Contradictory is the stronger family here (confidence 3, not higher, because the collision is a single-expression line conflict and soundness depends on test-placement discipline: B's tests must assert on the middleware's Register arguments, and B's fix must stay out of api.go route wiring which A also touches). A's gold patch is broad (model, persistence, migration, scrobbler, subsonic server), which widens the set of plausible B tickets but also raises the risk that a B solution drifts into A's territory (e.g. adding getPlayer to scrobble routes) — the authoring step should pin B's scope to middlewares.go only. The base state was verified: getPlayer uses raw RemoteAddr and raw user-agent header; server.go already uses chi RealIP for the main router; scrobble routes currently lack the player middleware; core.Register ignores the ip argument at base.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is about Windows log files being unreadable: it adds a small utility (CRLFWriter) that converts lone line-feed characters into Windows-style line endings, and it adds a new function called SetOutput in log/log.go that lets the rest of the program point the logger at a different destination, wrapping that destination with the CRLF converter on Windows. Task B is a different, independently-motivated complaint: the logging library (logrus) decorates its output with colored text using special invisible 'ANSI escape' characters, and when log output is redirected to a file or captured by the OS service manager, those invisible characters show up as garbage in the file. B's fix is to strip those escape sequences before the bytes reach the destination — and the natural, minimal place to do that is the very same SetOutput function in log/log.go that A introduces. Both tickets therefore land on the same function: A's version wraps the writer with a line-ending converter, B's version wraps it with an escape-sequence stripper. Pasted side by side, the code contains two definitions of the same function and no longer compiles; only a single SetOutput that applies both wrappers (strip escapes, then convert line endings) satisfies both tickets.
suggestion.shared_region: log/log.go — the SetOutput(w io.Writer) function (A adds it at ~line 132, right after SetRedacting; B's fix must modify that same function's body to also strip ANSI escape codes before handing the writer to the underlying logger).
suggestion.taskA: Log output on Windows uses line feeds only and is unreadable in standard editors. Provide a CRLFWriter(w io.Writer) io.Writer utility in the log package that converts every bare LF to CRLF unconditionally (platform-agnostic), passes existing CR+LF pairs through unchanged including when the pair is split across two Write calls, and reports the number of input bytes (not the expanded count) from each Write. Also provide SetOutput(w io.Writer) so the default logger's destination can be changed, applying the CRLF conversion on Windows.
suggestion.taskB: Log output contains invisible color-control characters when redirected. The logger's text formatter emits ANSI color escape sequences, so when Navidrome runs as an OS service or its stderr is redirected to a file, the captured log is full of garbage characters and cannot be parsed by log tools. Add an option to strip ANSI escape sequences from log output before it is written to the configured output destination (i.e., in the log package's output plumbing, wrapping the destination writer with an ANSI-stripping writer).
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by a completely different defect (color escape codes polluting redirected/captured logs — a very common real-world complaint for any service that logs via a colored formatter) and would be filed by someone who never heard of the Windows line-ending problem. It does not require CRLFWriter, does not mention Windows line endings, and is not a step toward A's goal; it only happens to need the same output-destination hook (SetOutput) that A introduces, because that is the single choke point where the logger's writer is assigned. The collision is structural, not a decomposition of A.
suggestion.conflict: Both solutions define/modify the same function SetOutput in log/log.go with different bodies: A's body wraps w with CRLFWriter on Windows then calls defaultLogger.SetOutput(w); B's body wraps w with an ANSI-stripping writer then calls defaultLogger.SetOutput(w). A naive merge (concatenating or auto-merging the two patches) yields either two func SetOutput declarations in the same package (compile error) or one body that lacks the other's wrapper, so the combined test suite fails (missing CRLF conversion or missing ANSI stripping).
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: A single SetOutput that composes both wrappers in one pipeline, e.g. w = stripANSI(w); if runtime.GOOS == "windows" { w = CRLFWriter(w) }; defaultLogger.SetOutput(w). Order is behaviorally safe here (ANSI sequences contain no LF bytes, so stripping before or after CRLF conversion yields the same bytes); a single agent or two coordinating agents can pick one order and both tickets' tests pass.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the fail_to_pass TestLog suite — the new log_test-package specs for CRLFWriter (bare LF -> CRLF, existing CRLF passthrough, CRLF split across two Write calls, Write returns input length and nil error) plus the existing Logger/Levels specs. B's set: a spec (in the same TestLog ginkgo suite, so it runs in the same binary) that calls log.SetOutput(buf), emits a log entry through the default logger, and asserts the captured bytes contain no ANSI escape sequences (and that plain text is intact). Soundness: base commit has no SetOutput at all, so both suites fail to compile against base; A's gold patch passes A's set; B's patch (SetOutput that only strips ANSI) passes B's set; the naive merge fails to compile (duplicate SetOutput); the reconciled single SetOutput passing both wrappers makes the combined suite pass.

notes: Key structural facts at the base commit (23bebe4): log/log.go has no SetOutput and no CRLFWriter; defaultLogger is a package-private *logrus.Logger with only SetDefaultLogger (used by log_test.go) as the writer-adjacent hook; logrus's default TextFormatter emits ANSI colors, which makes the B ticket (strip ANSI in output plumbing) a believable standalone issue. The contradictory pair's collision is a same-function-definition conflict (duplicate SetOutput) rather than a semantic one, which is the strongest kind of naive-merge failure (compile error). Confidence kept at 3 rather than higher because B's fix is not forced to touch SetOutput by existing code — a B author could instead fix ANSI stripping at the formatter level (e.g. configuring the logrus formatter), which would avoid the collision entirely; the authoring step should pin B's spec to the output-writer plumbing. Also note A's gold patch is broader than its stated interface (it adds the LogFile option, INI config parsing, MSI build changes); those extra pieces are why the complementary family here degenerates into decomposition.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A fixes the real-time event stream so that a browser tab does not receive back the update it just caused: the server learns each tab's unique ID (from a request header, stored in a cookie) and the event broker skips the originating tab when forwarding events. Task B is a separate, realistic ticket: the 'serverStart' event that the server pushes to a newly connected tab should include the server's version, so the web UI can detect it is running an outdated cached interface and prompt the user to refresh. Both tasks must edit the exact same line of code in the event broker: the line that builds and enqueues the serverStart message when a new client subscribes. Task A rewrites that line to use a renamed enqueue method (set -> put) as part of its restructuring, while Task B rewrites the same line to add the version field to the message. Each change alone is fine, but a naive merge of the two patches either keeps A's line and silently drops B's version (so B's test fails) or keeps B's line and resurrects the old method name (so the code no longer compiles / A's structural tests fail). A single reconciled line — new method name AND version field — satisfies both.
suggestion.shared_region: server/events/sse.go, broker.listen() — the `case c := <-b.subscribing` branch, specifically the line `c.diode.set(b.prepareMessage(&ServerStart{StartTime: consts.ServerStart}))`; plus server/events/events.go, the ServerStart struct definition
suggestion.taskA: SSE events are delivered back to the connection that originated them: when a client action triggers a real-time update, the server should not echo that update back to the originating client (identified by a per-client unique ID carried in the request context), while other sessions of the same user still receive it and unattributed events keep broadcasting to everyone. This requires threading the sender's context through the broker, filtering per client, and associated restructuring of the broker's message/enqueue internals.
suggestion.taskB: The 'serverStart' event sent to a newly connected web client should include the server's version. The UI keeps a cached copy of its static assets; when it opens the event stream it cannot tell whether the server was upgraded behind it. Including the version in serverStart lets the UI show a 'new version available, please refresh' banner. This is a pure payload/feature ticket about what the server announces on stream start, with no relation to who should or should not receive events.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by a completely different user problem (stale cached UI after a server upgrade) and would be filed by the UI/frontend maintainer, not the person fixing event echo. It never mentions client identification, filtering, or the originating connection; it only asks for one more field in a well-known event. It is not a step toward A's goal — A works perfectly without the version field, and B works perfectly without any filtering.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches rewrite the same physical line in listen()'s subscribe branch. A's patch changes `c.diode.set(...)` to `c.diode.put(...)` (and A's tests structurally enforce that diode has `put` and no `set`, and that message has exactly four unexported fields). B's patch changes the ServerStart literal on that same line to add `Version: ...`. Auto-merging/concatenating the two independent diffs cannot produce a line that has both the renamed method and the new field: one side's hunk is written against the other's pre-image, so the merge either drops B's field (B's test fails) or drops A's rename (compile error, A's structural tests fail).
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One line in listen(): `c.diode.put(b.prepareMessage(&ServerStart{StartTime: consts.ServerStart, Version: <server version>}))`, plus adding a `Version` field to ServerStart in events.go. A's discipline tests (message field list, diode put/no-set, shouldSend semantics) are unaffected by an extra field on ServerStart, and B's payload test passes.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the server/events suite (TestEvents) — shouldSend filtering cases, message-struct field discipline, diode put-only AST check, request.ClientUniqueIdFrom — plus the server/subsonic suite (TestSubsonicApi) for the consts.CookieExpiry move. B's set: a new spec in the events suite that captures the serverStart message delivered to a freshly subscribed client (or inspects prepareMessage output) and asserts the JSON payload contains the expected version string. Combined suite: run both; base fails both, A-alone fails B's version assertion, B-alone fails A's structural/filtering tests, naive merge fails (missing version or compile/structural break), reconciled code passes everything.

notes: Task A is unusually prescriptive: its tests pin the exact shape of the events package (message must have exactly fields id/event/data/senderCtx via reflection; diode must have put and must NOT retain set via source AST parsing; shouldSend must be a broker method with exact truth-table semantics). This makes the events package a poor home for most contradictory B's, because any B that adds a field to `message` or renames diode methods would make the combined suite impossible to satisfy even after reconciliation — the only sound B's are those that touch lines A rewrites without altering the pinned structures (e.g., the ServerStart literal in listen()'s subscribe branch, or the client.String() format, which A's tests do not pin). The ServerStart-version B is the strongest candidate and reflects a real later Navidrome feature, but the conflict is a same-line textual collision rather than a deep semantic mutex, hence confidence 3. The consts.CookieExpiry move also looked like a mutex candidate (A makes it a fixed constant; a 'make cookie expiry configurable' B would want a config value), but A's tests only need the constant to exist for compilation — they do not assert the response cookie's MaxAge — so a reconciled 'const default + config override' could pass both, and the conflict is weaker and more contrived than the ServerStart one. Complementary is not viable: the natural other side of the contract (UI sending the client ID) is already part of A's gold patch, making any such B a decomposition.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a ticket about the album persistence layer: when an album is read from the database, its play count should be normalized (divided by song count) only in 'normalized' mode, and the disc data should round-trip correctly. The accepted fix moves the normalization from the list-conversion helper (toModels) into the per-row post-read hook (PostScan), makes the list converter a pure copy, and adds a new dbAlbums type with its own toModels method. An independently motivated task B is a ticket from a Subsonic-API user: 'getAlbumList with type=frequent returns inconsistent play counts — the list is sorted by the raw stored play count, but the same albums shown elsewhere report a normalized play count, so the ordering and the displayed numbers disagree.' B's fix is to make the genre-less list path (GetAllWithoutGenres) return normalized play counts, which requires editing the same toModels/GetAllWithoutGenres region. A strips normalization out of that region entirely (and deletes the method B wants to keep), while B keeps the method and puts normalization back in the list path — the two edits cannot both stand.
suggestion.shared_region: persistence/album_repository.go — the dbAlbum PostScan() function and the toModels conversion region (albumRepository.toModels / the new dbAlbums.toModels) plus the GetAllWithoutGenres() call site
suggestion.taskA: Album mapping inconsistencies between database values and model fields: PostMapArgs must serialize Album.Discs to a JSON string ('{}' when empty), PostScan must unmarshal Discs only when the string is non-empty (leaving Album.Discs unmodified otherwise), PostScan must normalize PlayCount by SongCount in normalized mode and leave it unchanged in absolute mode, and a dbAlbums slice type must expose toModels() that copies fields without extra transformation.
suggestion.taskB: Subsonic getAlbumList(type=frequent) is inconsistent: the album list is ordered by the raw stored play_count, while album detail views report play counts normalized by song count (when albumplaycountmode=normalized), so the 'most played' ordering disagrees with the numbers users see. Fix: make the album list path (GetAllWithoutGenres, used by getAlbumList/frequent and getArtist) return play counts normalized according to the configured mode, consistent with the rest of the API.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B reads as a genuine API-consistency bug report filed by someone using the Subsonic 'frequent' album list — it never mentions discs, PostScan, or A's mapping cleanup. It targets a user-visible inconsistency (sort key vs displayed value) that exists at the base commit: GetAllWithoutGenres returns raw play counts while Get/GetAll normalize them. It is motivated by the API behavior, not by A's refactoring.
suggestion.conflict: A's solution deletes albumRepository.toModels, removes normalization from it, and adds a new dbAlbums type with a no-op toModels method, moving normalization into PostScan. B's solution must keep editing the same toModels/GetAllWithoutGenres region to (re)apply normalization on the list path. Naively merging both changes either duplicates the toModels declaration (the old method plus the new dbAlbums method) or leaves normalization applied twice (PostScan + list path, e.g. 6 plays / 3 songs -> 2 in PostScan, then 2/3 -> 1 in the list path), so A's 'toModels is a pure copy' test and B's 'GetAllWithoutGenres returns normalized counts' test cannot both pass.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's structure (dbAlbums.toModels as a pure copy, normalization in PostScan) and satisfy B by having GetAllWithoutGenres apply the same mode-based normalization after toModels (or by routing its rows through PostScan), so the frequent list is ordered by and reports normalized play counts. One coherent change: normalization happens exactly once, at row-read time, and the list path inherits it.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the new TestPersistence specs in persistence/album_repository_test.go (dbAlbum.Discs mapping, PostScan play-count tables, dbAlbums.toModels pure-copy). B's set: a new spec asserting GetAllWithoutGenres returns PlayCount normalized in normalized mode (e.g. 6 plays / 3 songs -> 2) and unchanged in absolute mode, plus a subsonic getAlbumList(type=frequent) ordering test. Combined suite passes only with the reconciled single-normalization design; the naive merge fails compilation (duplicate toModels) or double-normalizes (A's pure-copy and B's list-normalization expectations both break).

notes: Base-commit facts that matter: (1) A's fail_to_pass is the whole TestPersistence ginkgo suite; the new test file references dbAlbums.toModels which does not exist at base, so base fails by compilation plus behavior. (2) At base, normalization lives only in albumRepository.toModels, so Get/GetAll/Search normalize but GetAllWithoutGenres (used by subsonic getAlbumList and getArtist) does not — this real inconsistency is what makes B's ticket believable. (3) The collision is genuine but somewhat narrow: both A and B are ultimately about where play-count normalization happens, so B must be authored carefully as an API-consistency ticket (frequent list ordering vs displayed values) rather than 'normalize in GetAllWithoutGenres' phrased as a step of A. Confidence 3: plausible independent pair, needs authoring work to keep B from reading as a decomposition of A. (4) Complementary is weak: the consumer side already exists, so the 'B alone fails' bar is not met without an end-to-end test the repo's mocking style doesn't support.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A asks the mail app to stop deciding the 'verified' badge from a hardcoded list of Proton email addresses and instead use a new helper (isFromProton) that reads a server-provided IsProton flag on each message, with the badge gated by a new feature flag. Task B is a separate UI-consistency ticket: in the base code the verified badge shows next to the sender in the conversation list (column view) but is silently missing in the single-message row view, so B asks for the badge to appear in the row view too. Both tasks must modify the exact same component (ItemRowLayout): add a 'hasVerifiedBadge' prop to its props interface, add it to the function's parameter list, and insert the badge image in the same sender-line section. If two agents apply their changes blindly, the prop gets declared twice (a compile error) and the badge rendered twice, so the combined test suite fails until someone reconciles into one prop and one badge driven by the new helper.
suggestion.shared_region: applications/mail/src/app/components/list/ItemRowLayout.tsx — the Props interface (after 'onBack'), the destructured parameter list, and the sender <span> JSX block (lines ~24-38, ~40-54, ~95-101); plus the hasVerifiedBadge computation in Item.tsx (lines 106-107)
suggestion.taskA: The verified badge in the mail list is driven by a hardcoded whitelist of Proton addresses plus a DMARC check, which is inconsistent and unmaintainable. Add an isFromProton(element) utility that reads the IsProton flag the server now sends on messages and conversations, use it (behind a new ProtonBadge feature flag) to compute hasVerifiedBadge in the list item, and render the badge via a small shared VerifiedBadge component.
suggestion.taskB: The 'verified' badge appears next to the sender in the conversation list (column layout) but is missing in the single-message row layout, even though Item.tsx already computes and passes a hasVerifiedBadge value to the layout component. Show the badge in the row layout next to the sender for consistency with the column layout.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a real, pre-existing UI inconsistency discoverable in the base code alone: Item.tsx passes hasVerifiedBadge to ItemLayout, ItemColumnLayout renders it, but ItemRowLayout's Props interface has no such prop, so the value is dropped in row view. A user filing 'badge missing in single-message view' would never mention isFromProton, the IsProton flag, or the feature flag — their motivation is purely visual consistency between the two list layouts. It is not 'the part of A that A didn't do'; it exists independently of A's predicate change.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches insert 'hasVerifiedBadge?: boolean;' into the same Props interface block, 'hasVerifiedBadge = false,' into the same destructuring list, and a badge element into the same sender-span JSX region of ItemRowLayout.tsx. Naively merging (applying both diffs) yields a duplicate interface member and a duplicate binding (compile/syntax error) or two stacked badge images; additionally A changes the predicate in Item.tsx to isFromProton + feature flag while B's change assumes the old whitelist predicate, so B's badge would never appear for IsProton-flagged messages whose sender is not whitelisted.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep a single hasVerifiedBadge prop on ItemRowLayout, render the badge exactly once (via A's VerifiedBadge component), and drive it from A's reconciled predicate: !displayRecipients && isFromProton(element) && protonBadgeFeature?.Value. B's row-view requirement is then satisfied for any Proton-origin message, and A's predicate change is preserved.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the two isFromProton unit tests in applications/mail/src/app/helpers/elements.test.ts. B's set: a new component test rendering Item (or ItemRowLayout) with columnLayout=false and a verified sender, asserting the badge is present in row view and absent when not verified. Base fails both sets (helper missing; badge absent in row view). A alone passes A's set; B alone (whitelist-based, no feature flag) passes B's set. Naively merged code fails the combined suite (duplicate prop compile error). The reconciled change passes the combined suite, with B's fixture using an IsProton=1 message and the ProtonBadge feature flag enabled via the existing setFeatureFlags test helper.

notes: Both families hinge on the same base-code facts: (1) ItemRowLayout at base silently drops the hasVerifiedBadge prop that Item.tsx already passes — a genuine pre-existing inconsistency that makes contradictory B believable; (2) the old badge predicate is whitelist+DMARC-based, so a header indicator built on the whitelist (B-alone) genuinely disagrees with IsProton-based detection (A), which is what makes the complementary integration test sound. Risks: for the contradictory seed, A's gold patch itself adds the row-layout badge, so B overlaps with part of A's diff — it must be framed strictly as the pre-existing row-view gap, not 'the half of A that A didn't do', and B's test fixture must use IsProton + the ProtonBadge feature flag to pass against the reconciled code. WHITE_LISTED_ADDRESSES is shared with image auto-loading (transformEmbedded/transformRemote), so B should not touch the constant itself. Complementary B's ticket should avoid naming isFromProton explicitly (that would make B depend on A); the contract is enforced by the integration test instead. Neither pair is a ready-made 5: confidence 3 each, solid structure but requiring careful authoring to keep independence and soundness intact.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A is a pure cleanup ticket: the file-metadata helpers (called 'extended attributes' or xattrs) currently take several separate arguments in a fixed order, which is easy to get wrong, so A asks to collapse them into one named-options object, tighten the data types, and make the parsing path never crash on garbage input. Task B is a separate product ticket: the file digest stored in these xattrs is SHA-1, which is considered broken/deprecated, so B asks to stop storing SHA-1 and store a SHA-256 digest instead (the upload worker already computes SHA-256 for block hashes, so this is a natural standalone request). Both tickets must rewrite the very same function — the one that builds the xattr structure from a file — and the same small 'digests' type blocks. A changes that function's signature to an object parameter and keeps SHA-1 as the digest field; B changes the same signature and swaps the digest field to SHA-256. If two agents apply their changes blindly, the file ends up with two versions of the same function (or one signature that satisfies neither), so A's test (which feeds a SHA-1 digest and expects it back under the SHA1 key) and B's test (which feeds a SHA-256 digest and expects it under SHA256, with no SHA1) cannot both pass. One agent reconciling both can: keep A's object-parameter shape and parsing behavior, and make the digests field carry the new SHA-256 value (and/or both), so both suites pass together.
suggestion.shared_region: applications/drive/src/app/store/_links/extendedAttributes.ts — the `createFileExtendedAttributes` function (signature + `Digests` construction), the `encryptFileExtendedAttributes` wrapper, the `Digests` blocks inside the `ExtendedAttributes`/`ParsedExtendedAttributes` interfaces, and `parseDigests`; plus the production call site in applications/drive/src/app/store/_uploads/worker/worker.ts
suggestion.taskA: Refactor the extended-attribute (xattr) helpers to take a single options object (XAttrCreateParams with required `file`, optional `digests`/`media`) instead of positional arguments, introduce a `DeepPartial` utility type and use strict types for all parsing helpers, make parsing tolerant of empty/invalid/partial input (never throw, missing fields stay undefined), normalize digest names to canonical keys, and emit ModificationTime as ISO-8601 on create / Unix seconds on parse — without changing feature semantics for valid input.
suggestion.taskB: SHA-1 is cryptographically deprecated and the Drive upload worker already computes SHA-256 (block hashes use `generateContentHash` with algorithm SHA256 and `HashType: 'sha256'`), yet the file-level xattr digest stored at upload time is SHA-1 only. Stop storing the SHA-1 file digest in extended attributes and store a SHA-256 digest instead: the xattr creation path must accept and emit a SHA-256 digest under a canonical `SHA256` key, the parsing path must extract/validate it (and no longer treat SHA1 as the digest of record), and the upload worker must pass the SHA-256 digest when encrypting file xattrs.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by a real, separate concern — digest algorithm deprecation — that exists in the base code: the worker computes SHA-1 for xattrs while every block hash in the system is SHA-256, and no SHA-256 file digest exists anywhere in the drive app. A maintainer would file 'we should not be persisting SHA-1 digests' without ever touching the argument-shape or type-strictness issues A addresses. B is not 'the half of A A didn't do': A's goal (object params, strict types, resilient parsing) is fully achieved even if SHA-1 stays, and B's goal (SHA-256 digest) is fully achieved even if the positional signature stays. They are orthogonal motivations that happen to land on the same lines.
suggestion.conflict: A rewrites `createFileExtendedAttributes` to `createFileExtendedAttributes({ file, digests, media }: XAttrCreateParams)` with `digests?: { sha1: string }` emitting `Common.Digests = { SHA1 }`, and rewrites `encryptFileExtendedAttributes` to the same object shape. B rewrites the identical functions to drop the `sha1` digest parameter and add a `sha256` one (however expressed), emitting `Common.Digests = { SHA256 }`, and edits the same `Digests` type blocks and `parseDigests`. Naively merging both patches yields duplicate definitions of the same exported functions (or a signature that is both positional-with-sha256 and object-with-sha1), so A's test calling `createFileExtendedAttributes({file, digests: {sha1: 'abcdef'}})` expecting `Digests: {SHA1: 'abcdef'}` and B's test calling it with a sha256 digest expecting `Digests: {SHA256: ...}` cannot both pass against the glued code.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's object-parameter shape (`XAttrCreateParams` with `file`, `media`, and a `digests` field) and its strict types/DeepPartial parsing, but define the digests field to carry SHA-256 (e.g. `digests?: { sha256: string }`, or both `sha1?`/`sha256?` if backward compatibility with existing SHA-1 xattrs is required for parsing). `createFileExtendedAttributes` emits `Common.Digests` with the canonical `SHA256` key (and `SHA1` only if the reconciled type keeps it); `parseDigests` validates/extracts the new key while staying tolerant; the worker passes the SHA-256 digest. A's suite is satisfied by keeping the object shape, tolerant parsing, and (if sha1 kept) its normalization; B's suite is satisfied by the SHA-256 field end to end.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the existing `extendedAttributes.test.ts` updated by A's test patch — 'creates the struct from the file' (object-param call, SHA1 normalization, block sizes, media) plus the 'parses the struct' cases (empty/invalid JSON, partial fields, digest normalization). B's set: new/updated cases in the same file asserting that creating xattrs with a `sha256` digest yields `Common.Digests.SHA256` (and no SHA1 as the digest of record), that parsing `'{"Common":{"Digests":{"SHA256":"..."}}}'` extracts it, and that malformed SHA256 values are tolerated. Combined suite: run both against the merged code — base fails both (base has no object param and no SHA256), A-alone fails B's tests, B-alone fails A's object-param/SHA1 tests, and only the reconciled function passes everything.

notes: Collision mechanics verified against base: `createFileExtendedAttributes(file, media?, digests?)` and `encryptFileExtendedAttributes` are positional at base; A's gold patch rewrites both to the `XAttrCreateParams` object shape and tightens the `Digests` type blocks (`SHA1?: string` → `SHA1: string`) and all parse helpers (`any` → `MaybeExtendedAttributes`). B (SHA-256 digest) must edit exactly these functions, the same type blocks, `parseDigests`, and the same worker call site — a true same-region mutex. Supporting evidence that B is a real-world-plausible ticket: `packages/shared/lib/keys/driveKeys.ts` `generateContentHash` already uses algorithm 'SHA256' for block hashes, and the drive app contains zero SHA-256 file-digest code, so 'stop persisting SHA-1 in xattrs' is an independent, motivated gap. Caveats keeping confidence at 3 rather than 4-5: (1) this repo's jest uses babel transforms (no type-checking in tests), so the conflict must be expressed behaviorally — the reconciled function needs to accept both digest shapes (or sha256 plus tolerant sha1 parsing) for A's SHA1 test and B's SHA256 test to pass together; (2) A's own test patch hard-codes `digests: { sha1: 'abcdef' }` → `Digests: { SHA1: 'abcdef' }`, so a B that fully removes SHA1 from the create path would force the reconciler to keep SHA1 as a secondary field — workable but requires care; (3) the complementary family fails its soundness bar because the worker↔xattr contract already exists at base. If an author prefers maximum safety, B can be phrased as 'add SHA-256 to xattr digests (keep SHA1 for legacy parsing)' which reconciles cleanly with A's object-param shape.
