Gluing the two patches together either drops one side's change (B's handler missing, or A's dispatch/executeRequest-removal missing) or references a helper A deleted, so the combined test suite fails until someone writes one merged version that does A's dispatch AND B's timeout handling.
suggestion.shared_region: src/desktop/DesktopNetworkClient.ts, function DesktopNetworkClient.request() (and the surrounding executeRequest/getModule that A deletes). A rewrites request's body to dispatch directly to http/https and removes executeRequest; B must edit the same body to attach a 'timeout' listener that calls abort() on the returned ClientRequest.
suggestion.taskA: Opening a downloaded attachment from the desktop client fails. The native download must be driven through DesktopNetworkClient.request's returned request object (executeRequest must go away), the write stream must be created exactly once up front in the Tutanota temp download dir, any failure (non-200 status, response error, request error) must delete the partially written file and reject (non-200 rejects with the status code as a string), and open() must hand the path to the system shell, reject on failure, and show a confirmation dialog for executables instead of opening them.
suggestion.taskB: DesktopNetworkClient ignores the timeout option: when the server stalls after connecting, requests hang indefinitely because nothing listens for the 'timeout' event, even though callers (the download manager, the missed-notification fetcher) pass timeout: 20000. Make the client honor its timeout by aborting the request when it fires. (The SSE client currently papers over this with its own ad-hoc .on('timeout', () => req.abort()) workaround, which should not be needed once the shared client is fixed.)
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by a defect that exists at the base commit and is independently observable, with in-repo evidence: DesktopSseClient._downloadMissedNotification (src/desktop/sse/DesktopSseClient.ts ~line 461) already contains an ad-hoc timeout->abort workaround precisely because the shared client doesn't handle it. A maintainer would naturally file 'fix timeout handling in the shared DesktopNetworkClient' without any reference to attachments, downloadNative, or open(). It is not a piece of A: A's ticket is about the download/open flow, B's is about the network client's contract with its callers.
suggestion.conflict: Both patches edit the same lines of request(). A's version replaces the body with a direct https/http dispatch (downcast(opts)) and deletes getModule and executeRequest; B's version keeps the body shape but attaches req.on('timeout', () => req.abort()) (and plausibly also touches executeRequest, which A removes). Naively merging: if A's hunk wins, B's timeout test fails (no handler); if B's hunk wins, A's tests fail or the code doesn't compile (getModule/executeRequest references, wrong dispatch); a textual auto-merge of two divergent edits to the same function body cannot produce both. The two demands are not mutually exclusive in principle, but the two patches cannot coexist as-is.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent request(): const req = url.startsWith('https') ? https.request(url, downcast(opts)) : http.request(url, downcast(opts)); req.on('timeout', () => req.abort()); return req; — with executeRequest removed per A. A's download tests don't observe the extra listener, and B's timeout test passes because the handler is attached.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the four fail_to_pass tests in test/client/desktop/DesktopDownloadManagerTest.ts (downloadNative no error; downloadNative error gets cleaned up; open; open on windows). B's set: a new DesktopNetworkClientTest that mocks http/https, calls client.request(url, {timeout: 20000}), emits 'timeout' on the returned ClientRequest, and asserts abort() was called (fails on base, passes with B). Combined suite runs both against the merged code: base fails both; A-alone fails B's test; B-alone fails A's tests; only the reconciled change passes everything.

notes: Strongest structure in this task is the contradictory pair on DesktopNetworkClient.request: A rewrites it (and deletes executeRequest/getModule) while a real, independently-motivated timeout bug (evidenced by the ad-hoc workaround in DesktopSseClient._downloadMissedNotification) forces B to edit the same function body. Confidence is 3 rather than 4 because B's fix location is not 100% forced by the ticket text — though both natural placements (the client's request(), or the download manager's call site) collide with A's rewrite, so the conflict is robust to placement. Additional observation: A's gold patch leaves FileFacade's numeric statusCode === 200 comparison stale against the new string statusCode, a latent real break — but fixing it is a follow-up to A, which is why the complementary family is marked non-viable rather than a decomposition. The base test file's downloadNative tests (404/retry-after/suspension/precondition) assert the old result-object contract; A's test patch deletes them, so any B that builds on that old contract would be entangled with A's test changes.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A fixes a decryption bug: when the app loads a mail's 'details' record (body, reply-to, attachments) on its own, it can't find the right decryption key, so A removes a shortcut the crypto code uses — an in-memory table (sessionKeyCache) inside CryptoFacade that remembers keys it has already figured out and reuses them for related records. Task B is a separate security/hygiene ticket: that same in-memory table is never emptied when a user logs out, so one account's decrypted keys can linger in memory for the next account on the same device; B asks for a way to clear the table on logout. Both tickets must edit the exact same lines of CryptoFacade (the cache field, the code in resolveSessionKey that reads/writes it, and the test-only getter). A's fix deletes the table entirely; B's fix requires the table to still exist and adds a clear operation on it. Gluing the two changes together produces code that either references a deleted field or keeps a cache that A's tests explicitly forbid, so the combined test suite fails until someone reconciles the two demands (e.g., keep a cache that only stores keys for mail bodies/attachments, never for mail details, and clear it on logout).
suggestion.shared_region: src/api/worker/crypto/CryptoFacade.ts — the `sessionKeyCache` field (line ~84), the cache read at the top of `resolveSessionKey` (lines ~199-211), the cache-populating `.then()` block after resolution (lines ~231-243), the helpers `setSessionKeyCacheWithElementId`/`setSessionKeyCacheWithTuple` (lines ~276-282), the seeding in `collectAllInstanceSessionKeys` (line ~348), and the `getSessionKeyCache()` getter (line ~611). Task A deletes all of it; task B must keep the field and add a clear path into it.
suggestion.taskA: Non-legacy mail details fail to decrypt during loading: some MailDetails/MailDetailsBlob/MailDetailsDraft entities cannot be decrypted when loaded because the loader doesn't know their session key. Fix by (1) letting load/loadMultiple accept an owner-encrypted session key (single value or per-element-id map) and stamp it onto the entity (as raw bytes) before decryption, threading that parameter through EntityClient, DefaultEntityRestCache, and EntityRestClient, and using it in MailFacade.getReplyTos, MailIndexer.processNewMail, and InboxRuleHandler.checkInboxRule; and (2) making CryptoFacade.resolveSessionKey derive the key only from the instance being processed — removing the sessionKeyCache field, its getter, and all cache seeding — so a mail details entity with no key of its own throws SessionKeyNotFoundError instead of reusing a previously resolved mail key.
suggestion.taskB: Stale decrypted session keys survive logout: CryptoFacade keeps a sessionKeyCache mapping element ids to decrypted session keys for the whole lifetime of the worker, and nothing ever empties it. When a user logs out and a different account logs in on the same device/worker, the previous user's keys remain in memory. Add a clearSessionKeyCache() (or equivalent) to CryptoFacade that empties the table, wire it into the logout/worker-reset path, and add tests that the cache is populated after resolving a mail's key and empty after logout.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated by logout/memory hygiene and cross-account key leakage — a classic security-review ticket — and says nothing about mail details decryption, provided keys, or the loader API. A maintainer could file it at any time regardless of whether A exists; its premise (the cache exists and is never cleared) is true at the base commit. It is not 'the other half of A': A's ticket explicitly demands the cache be removed, while B demands it be retained and made clearable — opposite fates for the same structure, each justified by a different concern (correctness of key resolution vs. key lifetime).
suggestion.conflict: A's solution deletes the sessionKeyCache field, the getter, and every read/write of it inside resolveSessionKey, and its new test 'MailDetailsBlob does not fall back to a cached mail session key' fails whenever resolving a mail populates a cache that a later MailDetailsBlob consults. B's solution keeps the field and adds a clear method that references it (and tests that the cache is populated after mail resolution). Naively merging: B's clear/eviction code references the field A deleted (compile/runtime break), or if both versions of resolveSessionKey coexist, A's no-fallback test fails because B's cache is still consulted. The two edits to the same lines cannot both stand.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: Keep a scoped session key cache in CryptoFacade that only ever stores keys for MailBody and File instances (never for MailDetails/MailDetailsBlob/MailDetailsDraft), consulted in resolveSessionKey only for those types; add clearSessionKeyCache() and call it from the logout/worker-reset path. Then A's tests pass (a MailDetailsBlob with no own key still throws SessionKeyNotFoundError because details are never cached, and provided keys still work) and B's tests pass (cache populated after mail resolution for body/file, emptied after logout).
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the existing fail_to_pass tests — EntityRestClient Load/Loadmultiple 'applies providedOwnerEncSessionKey(s) ... before decryption', MailIndexer/MailFacade/InboxRuleHandler propagation tests, entityrestcache loadMultiple tests, and CryptoFacadeTest 'MailDetailsBlob does not fall back to a cached mail session key'. B's set: new CryptoFacadeTest cases — (1) after resolveSessionKey on a mail with a body reference, the cache contains the body's key (observable via a test-only accessor or via no second permission load), (2) after invoking the logout clear, the cache is empty and re-resolving reloads permissions. Combined suite: base fails both sets; A-only passes A's set; B-only passes B's set; the naive merge fails (broken reference or A's no-fallback test fails); only the reconciled scoped-cache-with-clear passes everything.

notes: Explored at base commit a834bd4: CryptoFacade.sessionKeyCache (field line 84, read lines 199-211, population lines 231-243 and 344-349, getter line 611) is exactly what A's gold patch deletes, and A's requirements explicitly demand that deletion — which makes the logout-hygiene ticket B a clean same-region mutex rather than a decomposition. Weaker alternative contradictory candidate: B' = 'add ownerKey support to loadMultiple for parity with load' — both A and B' would add a 4th parameter to EntityRestClient.loadMultiple/DefaultEntityRestCache.loadMultiple/EntityClient.loadMultiple with different meanings, colliding on the same signatures; viable but more artificial than the cache conflict, so not used. Another observation: MailUtils.loadMailDetails (src/mail/model/MailUtils.ts:397) loads MailDetailsBlob without a provided key and is NOT updated by A; using it as B would be a decomposition of A and was rejected. Complementary family is weak: A's changes are self-contained plumbing with no pre-existing producer/consumer contract in the repo. Overall: contradictory pair is plausible and structurally real (opposite fates for the same field/function), confidence 3 — soundness of the reconciliation (scoped cache for body/file only + clear on logout) needs verification when authoring, since A's tests assert details never resolve from any cache state.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A fixes the 'reorder pinned topics' feature: it changes the message format sent from the browser to the server (from a list of many topics to a single topic plus a position number), rewrites the server-side function that applies the reorder, and makes it reject the old list format. Task B is a separate, real maintenance ticket: every other topic action in this codebase (delete, restore, pin, lock, move...) has already been migrated from the old realtime socket call to the newer REST API, and the code even contains a TODO comment admitting no REST call exists yet for reordering pinned topics. B would add that missing REST endpoint and make the socket handler a thin deprecated wrapper around it — but to keep the existing browser client working, B would preserve the old list-based message format. Both tasks must rewrite the exact same socket handler function, and their versions are mutually exclusive: A's version rejects the list format while B's version accepts and forwards it.
suggestion.shared_region: SocketTopics.orderPinnedTopics in src/socket.io/topics/tools.js (lines 70-76), plus the underlying topicTools.orderPinnedTopics in src/topics/tools.js
suggestion.taskA: Original ticket: pinned topic reordering behaves inconsistently depending on permissions and whether the topic is actually pinned. Fix: accept only a single object payload {tid, order} where order is the zero-based position from the top of the displayed pinned list; reject null/non-object/array payloads with [[error:invalid-data]]; require category moderator/admin, else [[error:no-privileges]]; no-op if tid is not currently pinned; otherwise move the topic to that position preserving relative order of the rest. Migrate the browser client (public/src/client/category/tools.js) off the legacy array payload.
suggestion.taskB: Independent ticket: 'Migrate topics.orderPinnedTopics to the REST API v3 like the other topic tools'. All sibling socket handlers in src/socket.io/topics/tools.js (delete, restore, purge, lock, unlock, pin, unpin) are deprecated wrappers that call warnDeprecated and delegate to src/api/topics.js, and public/src/client/category/tools.js has a literal TODO: 'should also use categoryCommand, but no write api call exists for this yet'. B adds PUT /api/v3/topics/:tid/pin/order (or similar) in src/api/topics.js + src/routes/write/topics.js, implements the reorder in topicTools.orderPinnedTopics keeping the existing array-of-{tid,order} payload so the current client keeps working, and turns the socket handler into a warnDeprecated delegating wrapper.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is motivated entirely by the codebase's own ongoing socket-to-REST migration pattern, which predates and is unrelated to A's consistency bug. A maintainer filing 'finish migrating the remaining topic tools to REST' would never mention the pinned-ordering inconsistency; it is a different goal (API modernization) that happens to land on the same function. The codebase contains concrete evidence (the TODO comment and the uniform warnDeprecated pattern) that this ticket is a real, pending piece of work.
suggestion.conflict: A's solution rewrites SocketTopics.orderPinnedTopics to validate a single object and throw [[error:invalid-data]] for anything that is not one (its test suite explicitly asserts an array payload errors). B's solution rewrites the same function to accept the legacy array payload and delegate it to the new REST endpoint. Naively merging both edits yields either two definitions of the same function or one that both rejects and forwards arrays — A's 'should error with an array payload' test and B's 'socket handler delegates array to REST' test cannot both pass. The same collision exists in topicTools.orderPinnedTopics: A replaces the body with single-{tid,order} logic; B's REST controller calls the function with the array shape.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: A single reconciled change: add the REST endpoint (B's goal) but have it accept the new single-object {tid, order} contract (A's goal), implement topicTools.orderPinnedTopics once with A's semantics, make the socket handler a warnDeprecated wrapper that validates the single-object shape and delegates to the REST layer (rejecting arrays), and update the client to send the single object via the new API call. Both tickets' tests then pass: A's because arrays are rejected and the new semantics hold, B's because the endpoint exists and the socket handler is a delegating deprecated wrapper.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the four fail_to_pass tests in test/topics.js (array payload rejected, unprivileged user rejected, non-pinned tid no-op, single-object reorder works). B's set: new tests asserting (1) the REST endpoint exists and reorders pinned topics, (2) the socket handler emits the deprecation warning and delegates to the REST layer, (3) the legacy client payload shape still works end-to-end. Combined suite: on the naive merge, A's array-rejection test fails (B's handler forwards arrays) and B's legacy-shape test fails (A's handler rejects them); only the reconciled single-contract implementation passes all of A's plus B's tests together.

notes: Base commit confirmed: socket handler requires Array.isArray(data) and delegates to topicTools.orderPinnedTopics which does a bulk sorted-set write keyed by the legacy 'higher score = higher' convention; the client sends an array of {tid, order: length-index-1}. All sibling socket topic tools are warnDeprecated REST wrappers except orderPinnedTopics, and the client has an explicit TODO that no write API exists for it — this is the strongest real structure for an independent B. The contradictory seed is real but only moderate: B's payload-shape choice (keep array) is what creates the mutex, and a B author who happened to pick the single-object shape would make the tasks nearly compatible, so the conflict is not forced by the code alone. The complementary family is essentially unavailable without decomposing A. One other candidate considered (pin-expiry cleanup interacting with the pinned set) touches different functions (checkPinExpiry/getPinnedTids) and would not collide on the same lines, so it was rejected.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A adds a new bulk 'increment many scores at once' function to the database layer, and in the MongoDB adapter it inserts the new function at the exact spot right after the existing single-item increment function. A separate, real ticket B would be: 'the MongoDB single-item increment has a known race where two simultaneous first-time writes to the same member can crash with a duplicate-key error; make the retry logic actually work'. B must rewrite the body of that same single-item function, which sits in the same few lines where A inserts its new code. If two agents blindly merge, the region can end up with the old and new versions of the increment function both present (in this language, a duplicate function definition means the second one silently wins, so B's race fix vanishes) or with broken syntax. However, the two changes can in principle coexist in one file, so the collision is positional/textual rather than a hard semantic contradiction, and a test that forces the race is timing-dependent and flaky — hence low confidence.
suggestion.shared_region: src/database/mongo/sorted.js, the sortedSetIncrBy function (lines ~394-423) and the insertion point immediately after it where A's gold patch adds sortedSetIncrByBulk
suggestion.taskA: Add a backend-agnostic bulk sorted-set increment method (sortedSetIncrByBulk) to all database adapters that accepts an array of [key, increment, member] tuples, applies them in one batched operation, and returns the resulting scores in input order.
suggestion.taskB: Fix the MongoDB adapter's single-item sorted-set increment: when two concurrent first-time increments target the same key-member, the upsert can fail with an E11000 duplicate-key error; the current catch-and-retry is unreliable, so harden the duplicate-key handling (and make the bulk path consistent with it).
suggestion.independence_rationale: The E11000 upsert race is a real, documented MongoDB problem (the code already cites NodeBB issue #4467 and SERVER-14322 in comments), and a maintainer would file a reliability ticket about it without knowing anything about the bulk-increment feature. It is motivated by correctness of the existing method, not by A's goal.
suggestion.conflict: A inserts a new function at the end of sortedSetIncrBy; B rewrites sortedSetIncrBy's body. Both patches touch the same hunk boundary. A naive merge that keeps both versions of the function leaves the last definition winning, silently discarding B's fix (or producing a syntax error if the merge interleaves mid-function), so the combined test suite fails.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: rewrite sortedSetIncrBy with the hardened duplicate-key handling and add sortedSetIncrByBulk immediately after it, reusing the same upsert/unique-index logic so both single and bulk paths behave consistently.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the two new tests in test/database/sorted.js for sortedSetIncrByBulk. B's set: a test that issues concurrent first-time increments of the same member and asserts no E11000 error and correct summed score. Combined suite runs both; it passes only if the merged file has exactly one, correctly-fixed sortedSetIncrBy plus the working bulk method. Caveat: the race test is probabilistic, which weakens the seed.

notes: The complementary family is the stronger pairing here: A is a genuine producer (new db API) and B is a genuine consumer (analytics flush in src/analytics.js, secondarily src/meta/errors.js), both independently motivated by real code structure. Confidence is 3 rather than 4 because (a) B's authoring must pin the exact tuple order [key, increment, member] and the input-order return contract in the ticket text, otherwise the two agents could plausibly pick different shapes; (b) B's agent cannot pass its integration test locally without A, which is inherent to producer/consumer seeds but raises authoring risk; (c) the existing test/controllers.js call analytics.writeData(done) imposes a callback-signature constraint that B's ticket should preserve. The contradictory family is weak: the only same-region collision is A's insertion point directly after mongo's sortedSetIncrBy versus a B ticket hardening that function's E11000 upsert-race retry. The edits are textually adjacent but semantically compatible (both can coexist in one file), so 'naive merge fails' depends on a fragile duplicate-function-definition scenario rather than a true semantic mutex, and the race test would be timing-flaky. The redis and postgres adapters have no analogous pre-existing defect, so the mutex region exists in only one of three files. If a mutex seed is wanted anyway, the mongo sortedSetIncrBy boundary is the place, but I would not invest in it over the complementary pair.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A adds an optional score-range (min/max) filter to the database helper that totals the sizes of several sorted sets, and it also rewrites the profile-page code that computes a user's 'best' and 'controversial' post counts to use that new filter. An independent task B — a performance/bug ticket about that same profile-count computation (e.g. 'the profile loads one database call per category for best/controversial and the result is an array that must be summed; make it a single efficient call that returns a number') — must edit the exact same lines in the profile-count function. Both A and B therefore rewrite the same few lines that build the 'best' and 'controversial' counts, and a naive merge of the two rewrites produces duplicated or inconsistent code that fails the combined tests.
suggestion.shared_region: src/controllers/accounts/helpers.js, function getCounts() — the lines that compute counts.best and counts.controversial (and the follow-up .reduce() calls). A second, weaker shared region is the sortedSetsCardSum() function body in src/database/{redis,mongo,postgres}/sorted.js, which A rewrites to add min/max and which a DB-layer performance ticket B would also rewrite.
suggestion.taskA: Add support for inclusive min/max score ranges to the database utility sortedSetsCardSum(keys, min, max) across the redis/mongo/postgres backends, so callers can get a filtered total across many sorted sets in one call; use it to compute a user's 'best' and 'controversial' post counts on the profile.
suggestion.taskB: Performance/correctness ticket on the user profile: the 'best' and 'controversial' post counts are currently fetched with one database round-trip per visible category (a Promise.all of per-category sortedSetCount calls) and then summed in application code with a .reduce(). Consolidate this into a single efficient database call that returns a plain number, so the profile stops issuing N queries and the counts are not transiently arrays. (Motivated purely by profile load performance / a reported oddity, with no mention of any new DB range feature.)
suggestion.independence_rationale: B reads as a believable standalone performance ticket: a maintainer profiling the user page would see dozens of per-category count queries and file 'make profile counts a single query'. It does not reference min/max ranges or the DB feature. However, independence is only moderate — B's ideal solution is essentially 'call the multi-set count in one shot', which is the same optimization A performs as a consumer of its new feature, so B is close to being the consumer-side half of A rather than a fully separate effort.
suggestion.conflict: Both A and B rewrite the same getCounts() lines for best/controversial. A changes them to db.sortedSetsCardSum(..., min, '+inf') and deletes the two .reduce() lines; B changes them to a single consolidated call and also removes/replaces the .reduce() lines. Gluing the two patches together yields either a duplicated best/controversial assignment or a call that mixes A's min/max arguments with B's single-query shape, so the profile-count tests (and A's DB range tests) do not all pass on the naive merge.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: compute best and controversial each with a single multi-set, score-bounded count (A's new sortedSetsCardSum with min/max), drop the per-category Promise.all and the .reduce() post-processing (B's goal), and keep the DB-layer min/max implementation. This satisfies A's range tests and B's 'one call, returns a number' test together.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the new 'sortedSetsCardSum() should work with min/max' test plus the existing sortedSetsCardSum tests in test/database/sorted.js. B's set: a profile test asserting counts.best/counts.controversial are integers equal to the expected totals and that the count is produced by a single DB call (or simply that the profile returns correct numeric best/controversial). Combined suite = both; it passes only on the reconciled getCounts + DB implementation and fails on a naive concat/merge of the two independent patches.

notes: Honest read: this task is essentially one feature (DB min/max) plus its immediate consumer (profile best/controversial counts) bundled into a single gold patch, so the most natural 'B' is a decomposition of A rather than an independent ticket — which is exactly the failure mode to avoid. Contradictory is the stronger family but still only weak (confidence 2): the genuine shared region is getCounts() in src/controllers/accounts/helpers.js (best/controversial lines + the .reduce() calls) and, secondarily, the sortedSetsCardSum() body in the three DB backends. A real collision requires B to be an independently-motivated performance/correctness ticket targeting those same lines; because B's ideal fix overlaps with what A already does as a consumer, independence is moderate and a naive merge can be argued to partially coexist, so soundness would need care. Complementary is weak (confidence 1): the contract (sortedSetsCardSum keys/min/max) is real and A has standalone value, but A's patch already includes a consumer and B's feature can be built on the pre-existing getSortedSetRangeByScore, so B is not forced to depend on A. Existing base-code observations that support plausibility: mongo sortedSetCount returns undefined (not 0) for a falsy key while redis/postgres return 0, and the profile currently issues one sortedSetCount per category for best/controversial then .reduce()s the array — both are the kind of thing a separate maintainer ticket would target in the same region A edits.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A adds a REST endpoint to EDIT a chat message. To do that cleanly, A inserts a 'does this message even exist?' check at the very top of a shared permission function (canEditDelete in src/messaging/edit.js) that is used by BOTH editing and deleting. A plausible, unrelated ticket B is 'add a REST endpoint to DELETE a chat message' — the natural sibling of the edit endpoint. B would want the same friendly behavior (if the message id is bogus, say 'invalid message id' rather than a confusing permission error), so B's author would also reach into that same shared function and add an existence check there. The problem for a clean mutex: both A and B are just adding an existence-check line to the top of the same function, and those two additions stack on top of each other harmlessly instead of contradicting. So the code region genuinely overlaps, but the edits compose rather than collide, which is exactly what a contradictory seed needs to avoid.
suggestion.shared_region: src/messaging/edit.js — the shared canEditDelete(messageId, uid, type) function (called by both Messaging.canEdit and Messaging.canDelete); secondarily src/controllers/write/chats.js (the Chats.messages object holding edit/delete placeholders) and src/routes/write/chats.js (the commented put/delete '/:roomId/:mid' route lines).
suggestion.taskA: Add PUT /api/v3/chats/:roomId/:mid so an API client can edit a chat message. It must return 200 with the updated message on success, 400 with [[error:invalid-mid]] when the mid does not exist (reported before any permission error), 400 with [[error:invalid-chat-message]] for empty/whitespace content, and 400 with [[error:cant-edit-chat-message]] when the caller may not edit it. Also switch the browser chat client to use this REST call instead of the raw socket.
suggestion.taskB: Add DELETE /api/v3/chats/:roomId/:mid so an API client can delete a chat message. It should return 200 on success, 400 with [[error:invalid-mid]] when the mid does not exist (reported before any permission error), and 400 with [[error:cant-delete-chat-message]] when the caller may not delete it. This is the obvious sibling of the edit endpoint and would be filed by a different developer working on the same 'expose chat message management over the write API' roadmap.
suggestion.independence_rationale: A DELETE endpoint is a fully self-motivated ticket: the write API currently exposes no way to delete a chat message either (the delete route is commented out and Chats.messages.delete is a '// ...' placeholder, exactly as edit was before A). It is not 'the other half of A' — it does a different verb with different permission rules (canDelete / chatDeleteDuration / cant-delete-chat-message) and different success semantics. A maintainer plausibly files 'add edit endpoint' and 'add delete endpoint' as two separate issues.
suggestion.conflict: Both A and B must modify the shared canEditDelete function in src/messaging/edit.js to add an existence check that fires before the permission checks, and both edit the same Chats.messages object and the same route-registration lines. However, the two existence-check insertions are additive and land at the top of the function, so a naive merge keeps both and still behaves correctly — the edits do not produce two mutually-incompatible truths. That is why this is only a weak mutex: the region overlaps, but the changes compose.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: A single reconciled change adds the existence check once at the top of canEditDelete (serving both edit and delete), implements both Chats.messages.edit and Chats.messages.delete controllers, and registers both the put and delete '/:roomId/:mid' routes. This satisfies A's edit tests and B's delete tests together.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set = the fail_to_pass tests in test/messaging.js (edit via PUT /chats/:roomId/:mid: invalid-mid, empty content, not-own-message, success) plus the user-join system-message test. B's set = analogous tests for DELETE /chats/:roomId/:mid (invalid-mid, not-own, success). The combined suite runs both against the merged code; it passes only if the shared canEditDelete existence check and both route/controller implementations coexist correctly. Because the edits are additive, the combined suite is likely to pass even for a naive merge, which is the weakness of this seed.

notes: This is fundamentally a single-endpoint addition (PUT edit). The gold patch's footprint — new error string, client rewiring, controller impl, an existence check inserted into the shared canEditDelete, a new messageExists helper, route registration, and a deprecation warning on the old socket path — is cohesive and additive. The strongest candidate for an independent B is the sibling DELETE (or GET single-message) endpoint, which really does share the canEditDelete function and the controller/route files, so a contradictory seed is imaginable. But the shared edits are additive existence-check insertions that compose under a naive merge rather than producing genuinely incompatible code, so the mutex property is weak (confidence 2). The complementary family does not fit because there is no single integration test requiring both endpoints to agree on a co-designed contract. Overall this task is a weak seed for both families; it only really works as a 'two sibling endpoints touch the same permission function' story, and even that is closer to complementary-additive than to a true collision.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A adds a brand-new fact, ansible_processor_nproc, to the Linux CPU-facts function: it first copies the count parsed from the CPU info file, then upgrades it to the number of CPUs the current process is actually allowed to use (via the OS affinity call, or the nproc command if that call does not exist). Task B is a separate, real bug report: on ARM, Power and SPARC machines, when the machine's architecture fact is not yet known, the same function falls back to counting the 'vendor id' lines, which is wrong on those platforms, so ansible_processor_count comes out wrong. Both tickets must edit the same block at the end of get_cpu_facts in lib/ansible/module_utils/facts/hardware/linux.py: A appends its new nproc computation right after the vcpus line, while B rewrites the architecture-fallback branch (the if/else that decides which counting method to use) a few lines above. The collision is semantic, not just textual: A's test data encodes the OLD behavior for the SPARC scenario (count taken from the vendor-id path), so once B changes the fallback, A's own expected results no longer hold, and the two changes cannot simply be glued together.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/ansible/module_utils/facts/hardware/linux.py, LinuxHardware.get_cpu_facts — the tail of the function: the 'if collected_facts.get("ansible_architecture") != "s390x"' / ARM-PPC fallback branch (lines ~247-276) where A inserts the processor_nproc block (after the processor_vcpus line, before 'return cpu_facts') and where B must change the architecture-fallback condition/logic
suggestion.taskA: Introduce a new gathered fact ansible_processor_nproc on Linux: report how many CPUs the current process can actually use. Seed the value from the /proc/cpuinfo-derived count, prefer os.sched_getaffinity(0) when available, and fall back to running the nproc binary (resolved with get_bin_path from ansible.module_utils.common.process, executed via module.run_command) when the affinity call is missing. Existing processor facts must be unchanged.
suggestion.taskB: On ARM, PowerPC and SPARC hosts, ansible_processor_count is wrong whenever the architecture fact is not available at CPU-fact time: the code falls back to counting 'vendor id' occurrences, which those platforms do not report the same way, so the count degrades to a bogus number. Fix get_cpu_facts so the fallback counting method (the one keyed on the 'processor' field occurrences) is also used for SPARC / when architecture is unknown, so processor_count is correct without an architecture fact.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a classic, believable standalone bug ticket: it is about the EXISTING ansible_processor_count being wrong on specific architectures when the architecture fact is missing — a user-visible defect with its own reproduction (run setup with the architecture fact unavailable on an ARM/Power/SPARC box) and its own fix. It does not mention nproc, affinity, or any new fact. The existing unit test test_get_cpu_info_missing_arch even documents the expectation that counts are 'incorrect' for ARM/Power without an architecture, which is exactly the kind of known wart a maintainer would file separately. A (adding a new fact) and B (fixing an existing fact's fallback) are independently motivated; neither is a step toward the other.
suggestion.conflict: Both edits land in the same ~30-line region of get_cpu_facts. A appends its processor_nproc block immediately after the processor_vcpus computation inside the non-s390x branch; B rewrites the architecture-fallback branch (the condition that selects the counting method) that sits directly above it. More importantly they collide semantically through the shared test data: A's CPU_INFO_TEST_SCENARIOS hard-codes the OLD SPARC behavior (processor_count derived from the vendor-id path), so B's change to the fallback makes A's expected results for the sparc64 scenario false. Naively merging A's code + B's code (or A's test data + B's test data) therefore fails the combined suite: A's sparc expectation breaks under B's logic, and the two scenario files cannot both define the same scenario with different expected counts.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: A single reconciled change keeps B's corrected architecture fallback (so processor_count is right for ARM/Power/SPARC without an architecture fact) AND adds A's processor_nproc block after the vcpus computation, and updates the shared CPU_INFO_TEST_SCENARIOS so the SPARC scenario's expected_result reflects the post-B fallback while still including A's new processor_nproc key. With one coherent edit plus one consistent set of scenario expectations, both A's tests (nproc present and correct) and B's tests (correct count without architecture) pass together.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: test/units/module_utils/facts/hardware/test_linux_get_cpu_info.py::test_get_cpu_info, ::test_get_cpu_info_missing_arch, ::test_get_cpu_info_nproc (all driven by CPU_INFO_TEST_SCENARIOS, which A extends with nproc_out / sched_getaffinity / processor_nproc). B's set: a new/updated test asserting that get_cpu_facts with no/unknown ansible_architecture returns the correct processor_count for ARM/Power/SPARC cpuinfo fixtures. Combined suite: run A's three tests plus B's fallback test against the merged get_cpu_facts and a single reconciled CPU_INFO_TEST_SCENARIOS. Base code fails both (no nproc key; wrong fallback count). A-alone passes A's tests; B-alone passes B's tests. The naive merge fails because A's sparc scenario expectation contradicts B's changed fallback, so only the reconciled change (updated shared expectations + both behaviors) passes everything.

notes: Task A is a purely additive change to get_cpu_facts (new key + new import) with no new interface, which is why the complementary family is weak: the produced facts have no in-repo consumer. The contradictory family has a genuine structural hook — the same function's tail is where A inserts code and where a plausible independent bug (ARM/Power/SPARC processor_count fallback when architecture is missing, already flagged by the existing test_get_cpu_info_missing_arch) would be fixed — but the soundness is fragile: A's and B's tests share CPU_INFO_TEST_SCENARIOS, and A's SPARC expectation encodes the pre-B behavior, so the two test-data sets collide as much as the code does. This makes it a real but low-confidence (2) mutex candidate that would need careful authoring (a single reconciled scenario file) to be sound. It is not a clean decomposition: B stands on its own as a bug fix to an existing fact, independent of the new nproc fact.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A asks for a validated public way to store per-host execution state inside the play iterator: a new method set_state_for_host that checks the stored object is a real HostState before writing it, plus converting all internal writes (including the mark_host_failed function) to go through it. A plausible independent ticket B reports that a host which is already finished but still flagged as failed gets 're-failed' when the task queue manager re-marks it at the start of the next play, and the iterator then keeps handing out its last task forever instead of reporting the host as done; the fix is a guard in the failure-marking code path (mark_host_failed / _set_failed_state) that transitions such a host to the COMPLETE state. Both tickets must edit the same small region of mark_host_failed in lib/ansible/executor/play_iterator.py: A rewrites the line that stores the state (adding type validation), B changes what state is stored and how it is computed there. Gluing the two changes together naively (e.g. B's direct assignment plus A's validation wrapper applied inconsistently, or B's guard bypassing the validated setter) produces code where either the validation is bypassed or the re-failed host is never completed, so the combined tests fail; a single reconciled edit (compute the guarded state, then store it via the validated setter) passes both.
suggestion.shared_region: lib/ansible/executor/play_iterator.py, PlayIterator.mark_host_failed (lines ~491-497 at base, including the self._host_states[host.name] = s assignment) and its helper _set_failed_state
suggestion.taskA: Introduce public, type-validated methods on PlayIterator to access _host_states: set_state_for_host(hostname, state), set_run_state_for_host(hostname, run_state), set_fail_state_for_host(hostname, fail_state); route internal state writes (init, get_host_state stub, get_next_task_for_host, mark_host_failed, add_tasks) and strategy-plugin writes through them.
suggestion.taskB: Bug: a host that failed in a previous play and is already in a terminal state is re-marked failed by the task queue manager when the next play starts; the failure-marking code then leaves the host's run state non-terminal (no rescue/always to fall into), so get_next_task_for_host keeps returning the same last task for that host instead of None. Add a guard in the failure-marking path so an already-failed/terminal host is transitioned to COMPLETE and reported as failed exactly once.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a classic idempotency bug ticket about double-failure across plays (triggered by TaskQueueManager._load_play re-calling mark_host_failed for self._failed_hosts at lines 305-307 of task_queue_manager.py); it is motivated by observed misbehavior, not by the encapsulation goal. A's gold patch happens to touch mark_host_failed only to swap the storage line for the new setter and does not fix the re-failure behavior, so B is not a piece of A. The collision is real but modest: the two edits sit on adjacent lines of the same function rather than being mutually exclusive designs, so the conflict is more 'same hunk, must be merged coherently' than 'cannot both be true'.
suggestion.conflict: A's edit replaces the storage line in mark_host_failed with a validated setter call and adds the validation methods; B's edit changes the state computation/assignment in the same function (guard for already-terminal hosts, possibly assigning a new HostState or setting run_state to COMPLETE). Naively concatenating both diffs yields either duplicate/conflicting assignments to the same line, or B's direct _host_states write bypassing A's validation, so one of the two test sets fails.
suggestion.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent mark_host_failed: fetch a copy of the state, apply B's guard (if the host is already failed/terminal, set run_state to COMPLETE and skip re-entering rescue/always logic), then store the result via A's set_state_for_host so validation applies; keep the _removed_hosts append.
suggestion.test_strategy: A's set: the modified test/units/executor/test_play_iterator.py::TestPlayIterator::test_play_iterator_add_tasks (uses set_state_for_host) plus new unit tests asserting the three setters raise on wrong types and update state. B's set: a new unit test building a PlayIterator, marking a host failed twice (simulating TQM re-marking across plays), asserting get_next_task_for_host returns None and is_failed stays True. Combined suite passes only if the guard and the validated setter coexist in mark_host_failed.

notes: Base commit verified: play_iterator.py still has direct _host_states writes at lines 222, 255, 278, 496, 590 and no set_*_for_host methods; strategy/__init__.py still pokes _host_states at lines 135, 160, 1165, 1174, 1183, 1193. A's gold patch itself already converts the strategy call sites, which narrows the room for an independent B: the cleanest independent B is the clear_host_errors insufficiency (flag cleared but run state stuck), which A does not fix.
